category.name: Linux
category.description: Files, permissions, users, processes, the shell, networking, storage and package managers.

questions.text:
On a Linux host running Docker Engine with kernel 6.17.0-20-generic, what does this command print?

docker run --rm ubuntu:24.04 uname -r
options: The default kernel version of Ubuntu 24.04, which ships inside the image
An error, because a container has no kernel of its own to report
The kernel version of a small VM that Docker Engine starts for containers
questions.explanation: A container is a group of host processes; the image supplies only userspace files, never a kernel. Every container sees the host kernel. (Docker Desktop on macOS or Windows differs: there the containers share the kernel of a Linux VM.)

questions.text: Which kernel mechanism enforces the limits set by docker run --memory 64m --cpus 1.5?
questions.explanation: cgroups limit and account for resources. Inside such a container on cgroup v2, /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max reads 67108864 and cpu.max reads 150000 100000. Namespaces control what a process can see, not how much it may use.

questions.text:
What does the PID column show for the ps process in the output of this command?

docker run --rm alpine ps
options: 1, because ps is the first process in a new PID namespace
The same PID that the host's ps would show for it
0, because PID 0 is reserved for the container's init
Nothing, because ps cannot read /proc inside a container
questions.explanation: Docker starts each container in a new PID namespace, so its first process is PID 1 there and sees no host processes. On the host, the same process has an ordinary, different PID.

questions.text: Which namespace lets a container have its own hostname, separate from the host's?
questions.explanation: The UTS namespace isolates the hostname and NIS domain name. Docker sets it to the short container ID by default (docker run --rm alpine hostname prints something like 87891a48e4d9), or to the value of --hostname.

questions.text: You must test a kernel module against a kernel version different from the one your server runs. Which environment fits?
options: A Docker container built from an image of the target distribution
A virtual machine that boots the target kernel
A Podman container in rootless mode
A container started with --network none for isolation
questions.explanation: Containers always run on the host kernel, so no image or flag can give them another kernel, and loading a module from one affects the host. A VM boots its own guest kernel, so you can choose any version.

questions.text: Why is a virtual machine usually considered a stronger security boundary than a container?
options: Containers cannot use cgroups, so one container can exhaust host memory
VM disk images are encrypted, but container images are stored in plain text
Containers always run as root, but VM processes never do
Each VM has its own kernel, while all containers share the host kernel
questions.explanation: A kernel bug reachable from inside a container can compromise the whole host, because every container calls into the same kernel. A VM attacker must also escape the hypervisor. This is why many platforms run containers inside VMs.

questions.text: What is the relationship between a Docker image and a container?
options: An image is a read-only stack of layers; a container adds a writable layer and runtime state
An image is a running container that has been paused and saved
A container is a compressed copy of an image that is unpacked when it starts
An image holds the kernel, while a container holds the application files
questions.explanation: Many containers can run from one image at once. Each gets its own thin writable layer on top of the shared read-only image layers, plus its own processes, namespaces and network settings.

questions.text:
You run the commands below. What does the second command print?

docker run --name w alpine sh -c 'echo data > /keep.txt'
docker run --rm alpine cat /keep.txt
options: cat: can't open '/keep.txt': No such file or directory
An error saying the name w is already in use
questions.explanation: The file was written to the writable layer of container w only. A new container starts from the unchanged image. The data is still in w (docker cp w:/keep.txt - or docker start w would find it) until w is removed.

questions.text: In docker diff output, what do the letters A, C and D mean?
options: Archived, Cached and Detached files in the image
Added, Changed and Deleted paths in the container's writable layer
Paths from the Application, Config and Data volumes
Files that are Accessible, Corrupted or Dangling
questions.explanation: docker diff compares a container's filesystem with its image. After rm /etc/motd and creating /keep.txt it shows C /etc, D /etc/motd and A /keep.txt. Volume contents are not included.

questions.text:
You build this Dockerfile. Which instructions add a filesystem layer on top of the alpine base layers?

FROM alpine:latest
ENV MODE=prod
COPY app.txt /app/
RUN apk add --no-cache curl
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["cat", "/app/app.txt"]
questions.explanation: Instructions that change files (RUN, COPY, ADD) create layers. ENV, EXPOSE and CMD only change image metadata and appear as 0B entries in docker history. Here the image has one base layer plus two new ones.

questions.text: A Dockerfile has RUN head -c 50000000 /dev/urandom > /big.bin followed by RUN rm /big.bin. How big is the resulting image compared with the base?
options: About 50 MB larger, because the first layer still contains the file
About the same, because the second step deletes the file
About 100 MB larger, because the delete step copies the file again
The build fails, because a later step cannot delete a file from an earlier one
questions.explanation: Layers are immutable. The rm only adds a whiteout marker in a new layer, so the 50 MB stays in the earlier layer. To keep an image small, create and delete temporary files in the same RUN instruction.

questions.text:
With this Dockerfile, you edit only app.py and rebuild. Which steps run again instead of coming from the cache?

FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
options: Every step, because the build context changed
Only RUN pip install, because it is the slowest step
COPY . . and the steps after it
No steps, because CMD is the only one that uses app.py
questions.explanation: Docker reuses each cached step until one has different inputs; that step and all later ones are rebuilt. Copying requirements.txt on its own first means the dependency install is reused until the requirements file itself changes.

questions.text: Why do Dockerfile best practices say to write RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl as one instruction rather than two?
options: Two RUN instructions in a row are a syntax error
apt-get install cannot run unless it is chained with &&
A single instruction makes apt-get download packages in parallel
A cached apt-get update layer could be reused with an edited install line, giving stale package lists
questions.explanation: If RUN apt-get update is its own step, its cached layer is reused for months, and a later edit to the install line runs against old package indexes. Combining them, and deleting /var/lib/apt/lists/* in the same step, avoids this and saves a layer.

questions.text:
An image has the instructions below. What does docker run --rm img there print?

ENTRYPOINT ["echo", "hi"]
CMD ["world"]
questions.explanation: In exec form, CMD supplies default arguments to ENTRYPOINT. Arguments after the image name replace CMD, so echo hi there runs. With no arguments it prints hi world. To replace the entrypoint itself, use --entrypoint.

questions.text: An image uses the shell form ENTRYPOINT echo hi together with CMD ["world"]. What does docker run --rm img there print?
options: An error, because shell form and exec form cannot be mixed
questions.explanation: A shell-form ENTRYPOINT runs as /bin/sh -c 'echo hi', and both CMD and command-line arguments are ignored. Use the exec form (a JSON array) when the entrypoint should accept arguments.

questions.text:
The build context contains arch.tar.gz. What ends up in the image after these two instructions?

ADD arch.tar.gz /added/
COPY arch.tar.gz /copied/
options: Both directories contain the unpacked files from the archive
Both directories contain the file arch.tar.gz
/added/ contains arch.tar.gz and /copied/ contains the unpacked files
/added/ contains the unpacked files and /copied/ contains arch.tar.gz
questions.explanation: ADD auto-extracts local tar archives (and can fetch URLs, which it does not unpack). COPY copies files as they are. Prefer COPY unless you need ADD's extra behaviour, because it is more predictable.

questions.text:
What is the main benefit of the multi-stage build below?

FROM golang:1.21-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN go build -o /server .

FROM alpine:3.18
COPY --from=builder /server /usr/local/bin/server
CMD ["server"]
options: The final image contains the binary but not the Go toolchain or the source code
The two stages are built in parallel on two different hosts
The final image runs the Go compiler at start-up to rebuild the binary
The builder stage becomes a shared base layer of the final image
questions.explanation: Only what COPY --from=builder copies reaches the last stage; the stage named builder is discarded. A Go toolchain image is hundreds of megabytes, while the final Alpine-based image can be under 20 MB.

questions.text: A project has a .dockerignore file containing .env, and the Dockerfile uses COPY . /src/. What happens to .env?
options: It is copied but made read-only
It is not sent to the build context, so it never reaches the image
It is copied, and only docker push leaves it out
The build fails because an ignored file is matched by COPY
questions.explanation: .dockerignore filters what the client sends to the builder. Ignored files cannot be copied by any instruction, which keeps secrets and bulky folders such as .git or node_modules out of images and speeds up builds.

questions.text:
/etc/apk in the alpine image contains files. What do the two commands list?

docker volume create v
docker run --rm -v v:/etc/apk alpine ls /etc/apk
docker run --rm -v "$PWD/emptydir":/etc/apk alpine ls /etc/apk
options: Both list nothing, because a mount hides the image's directory
Both list the image's files, because mounts are layered under the image
The first lists nothing; the second lists the image's files
The first lists the image's files; the second lists nothing
questions.explanation: When an empty named volume is first mounted, Docker copies the image's contents at that path into it. A bind mount always shows the host directory as it is, hiding whatever the image had there.

questions.text: You run docker run -v /srv/missing:/data alpine true and /srv/missing does not exist on the host. What happens?
options: Docker refuses to start the container because the source is missing
Docker creates a named volume called missing
Docker creates /srv/missing on the host, owned by root, and mounts it
The mount is skipped and /data is an ordinary directory in the container
questions.explanation: The -v syntax creates a missing bind-mount source as a root-owned directory. The --mount type=bind,... syntax does not, and fails with bind source path does not exist, which catches typos in paths.

questions.text: A PostgreSQL container was started with -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data. You run docker rm -f on it and start a new container with the same -v option. What happens to the database files?
options: They are lost, because removing a container deletes its volumes
They are still there, because named volumes outlive containers
They are restored from the image's original data directory
They survive only if the container was stopped before removal
questions.explanation: A named volume lives under /var/lib/docker/volumes/ until you delete it with docker volume rm, docker volume prune or docker compose down -v. Only the container's writable layer is deleted with the container.

questions.text: What happens when a process in a container tries to write to a mount created with -v pgdata:/data:ro?
options: The write succeeds, but it goes to the container's writable layer
The write succeeds, and Docker discards the change when the container stops
The container is stopped with exit code 137
The write fails with Read-only file system
questions.explanation: The :ro option makes that mount read-only inside the container; other paths are not affected. Use it when the container only needs to read, such as served web pages or configuration files.

questions.text: You start docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx. How do you reach the web server from the host?
options: http://localhost:80, because -p maps the container port onto the same host port
http://localhost:8080, but only from inside another container
Only at the container's private IP address on port 8080
questions.explanation: -p 8080:80 publishes container port 80 on host port 8080 on all host addresses. Add an address to restrict it, as in -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80. Repeat -p to publish several ports.

questions.text: An image's Dockerfile has EXPOSE 8000. You start it with docker run -d --name web img. What does docker port web print?
options: Nothing, because EXPOSE alone does not publish a port
An error, because exposed ports must be published
questions.explanation: EXPOSE only documents the port in the image metadata. Publish it with -p, or use -P to publish all exposed ports on random high host ports (for example 8000/tcp -> 0.0.0.0:32768).

questions.text: A container is started with -p 127.0.0.1:18080:8000. Who can connect to host port 18080?
options: Any machine on the network, because Docker ignores the address
Only other containers on the default bridge
Only clients on the host itself, through the loopback address
Nobody, because a published port must be 1024 or higher on both sides
questions.explanation: The optional address before the host port chooses the host interface to listen on. Binding to 127.0.0.1 keeps a development database or admin panel off the network while still letting curl http://127.0.0.1:18080/ work on the host.

questions.text: Two containers, app and db, are started on the default bridge network. Inside app, ping db fails with bad address 'db'. What fixes it?
options: Publish a port on db with -p
Run both containers on a user-defined network created with docker network create
Add EXPOSE to the db image
questions.explanation: Docker's embedded DNS resolves container names only on user-defined networks, not on the default bridge. After docker network create appnet and --network appnet on both containers, app can reach db by name.

questions.text: What does Docker do with -p 8080:80 when the container also uses --network host?
options: It maps port 80 to 8080 using NAT, as usual
It fails to start the container
It assigns a random port, as with -P
It discards the published port and prints a warning
questions.explanation: With --network host the container uses the host's network namespace, so a service listening on port 80 is directly on host port 80. Docker prints WARNING: Published ports are discarded when using host network mode.

questions.text: What network interfaces does a container started with --network none have?
options: None at all, not even loopback
lo and an eth0 with no default route
The same interfaces as the host
questions.explanation: --network none gives the container its own network namespace with only lo. ip -o link inside it lists just lo. Use it for batch jobs that must not reach the network.

questions.text: What is the difference between docker run and docker exec?
options: docker run attaches to a running container; docker exec creates a new one
docker exec restarts a stopped container; docker run only works on images
They are aliases; exec is kept for backward compatibility
docker run creates a new container from an image; docker exec runs an extra command in a running container
questions.explanation: docker exec -it web sh opens a shell next to the main process of the running container web. It fails if the container is stopped. docker run -it --rm alpine sh starts a fresh container and removes it when the shell exits.

questions.text: A container started with --memory 32m --memory-swap 32m tries to allocate 200 MB. What do docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}' and the exit status show?
options: 1 false, because malloc returns an error
137 true, because the kernel OOM killer sent SIGKILL
143 true, because Docker sent SIGTERM
0 false, because the excess memory goes to swap
questions.explanation: When a cgroup exceeds its memory limit, the kernel kills a process in it. Exit code 137 is 128 + 9 (SIGKILL), and OOMKilled is true. Setting --memory-swap equal to --memory gives the container no swap.

questions.text: docker stop web takes ten seconds and the container exits with code 137. The main process is a Python server running as PID 1. Why?
options: PID 1 in a PID namespace ignores SIGTERM unless it installs a handler, so Docker sends SIGKILL after the 10 s timeout
Python flushes its buffers for 10 s before it exits
docker stop always waits 10 s and then sends SIGKILL
The container's cgroup blocks all signals until the timeout ends
questions.explanation: The kernel does not apply default signal actions to a namespace's init process. Running with --init puts a small init (tini) at PID 1 that forwards signals; then docker stop returns at once and the exit code is 143 (SIGTERM).

questions.text:
What does the last line print?

docker run --rm alpine sh -c 'exit 3'
echo $?
options: 0, because the container was created and removed successfully
1, because any failure inside a container becomes 1
3, because docker run returns the container's exit status
125, because the container command failed
questions.explanation: docker run in the foreground exits with the main process's status, which makes containers usable in scripts and CI. Docker itself uses 125 when the daemon fails to run the container, 126 when the command cannot be invoked and 127 when it is not found.

questions.text: Which hypervisor is a Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor?
questions.explanation: A Type 2 hypervisor is an application on a host operating system, like VirtualBox or VMware Workstation. Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisors such as ESXi, Hyper-V and Xen run directly on the hardware, with no general-purpose OS beneath them.

questions.text: What distinguishes paravirtualization from full virtualization?
options: Paravirtualization emulates every hardware device in software
The guest is modified or uses special drivers to call the hypervisor directly
Paravirtualization can only run one guest per host
Full virtualization requires a modified guest kernel
questions.explanation: In full virtualization, an unmodified guest runs as if on real hardware. A paravirtualized guest knows it is virtualized and uses hypercalls or paravirtual devices, such as virtio network and disk drivers, which avoid slow device emulation.

questions.text: Which /proc/cpuinfo flags show that an x86 CPU has hardware virtualization extensions?
questions.explanation: grep -Ew 'vmx|svm' /proc/cpuinfo checks for VT-x or AMD-V, and lscpu prints a Virtualization: line. The hypervisor flag means the reverse: you are already inside a VM. vme is an old virtual-8086 feature.

questions.text: How do KVM and QEMU divide the work of running a VM on Linux?
options: KVM is a user-space emulator; QEMU is the kernel module that runs guest code
KVM and QEMU are two names for the same program
KVM kernel modules use the CPU's virtualization extensions via /dev/kvm; QEMU in user space emulates the devices and manages the VM
QEMU runs Linux guests and KVM runs Windows guests
questions.explanation: lsmod shows kvm plus kvm_intel or kvm_amd, which expose /dev/kvm. QEMU uses it to run guest code natively on the CPU and provides the virtual disks, NICs and firmware. libvirt manages QEMU/KVM VMs on top.

questions.text: What happens if you start a QEMU x86-64 VM on a host where KVM is unavailable (for example, no /dev/kvm)?
options: QEMU refuses to run any x86 guest
The VM runs at the same speed through paravirtualization
QEMU switches to running the guest as a container
QEMU can fall back to TCG software emulation, which works but is much slower
questions.explanation: qemu-system-x86_64 -accel help lists tcg and kvm. TCG translates guest instructions in software, which is how QEMU also emulates other architectures. With -accel kvm (or -enable-kvm) guest code runs directly on the CPU.

questions.text: virsh list shows no VMs, but you know a VM called web exists. What is the likely reason?
options: virsh list shows only running domains; web is shut off, so use virsh list --all
web was deleted when it was shut down
virsh list shows only VMs created in the current shell session
The VM is listed only by virsh dominfo --all
questions.explanation: By default virsh list prints running domains; --all adds inactive ones and --inactive shows only those. Also check the connection: qemu:///system and the per-user qemu:///session have separate sets of VMs.

questions.text: What is the difference between virsh shutdown web and virsh destroy web?
options: shutdown deletes the VM; destroy only stops it
destroy deletes the VM's disk images; shutdown keeps them
shutdown asks the guest OS to shut down cleanly; destroy stops it at once, like pulling the power cord
They are identical, but destroy needs root
questions.explanation: virsh destroy terminates the domain immediately without deleting its definition or storage, so it can be started again. virsh shutdown depends on the guest reacting (ACPI or guest agent) and may take time or fail if the guest ignores it.

questions.text: What does virsh undefine web do to a shut-off VM?
options: Shuts the VM down and keeps it registered
Removes the VM's libvirt definition but, by default, leaves its disk images in place
Deletes the VM's definition and all its disk images
Resets the VM's configuration to its defaults
questions.explanation: undefine removes the domain's XML configuration from libvirt. Disk images are deleted only with options such as --remove-all-storage or --storage. To create a domain from XML use virsh define, and to change one use virsh edit.

questions.text: You run virsh setmem web 4G --config while web is running. When does the change take effect?
options: Immediately, without changing the stored configuration
Immediately, and it is also saved for the next boot
At the next boot of the VM, because --config changes the persistent configuration
Never, because memory can only be changed with virsh edit
questions.explanation: In virsh, --config changes the persistent definition used at the next start, --live changes the running domain, and both can be given together. setmem cannot exceed the domain's maximum memory, which virsh setmaxmem changes.

questions.text: A VM uses NAT networking. It can browse the internet, but a laptop on the LAN cannot connect to the VM's web server. What is the usual fix?
options: Switch the VM to host-only networking
Switch the VM to internal networking
Give the VM a second NAT adapter
Add a port-forwarding rule on the host, or use bridged networking
questions.explanation: With NAT, the VM shares the host's address, and outside machines cannot start connections to it unless a port is forwarded. In bridged mode the VM gets its own LAN address. Host-only and internal networks cut off the LAN entirely.

questions.text: Inside a VM, top shows a high st value. What does it mean?
options: The VM's virtual CPUs were ready to run but the hypervisor was running something else
The VM's disks are stalled waiting for storage
The kernel is starting processes faster than they can be scheduled
Processes in the VM are stopped with SIGSTOP
questions.explanation: Steal time (st, %steal in iostat) is time a virtual CPU wanted to run but the hypervisor gave the physical CPU to another VM or task. High steal points to an overloaded host, not to a problem inside the guest.

questions.text: What is a key difference between Podman and Docker?
options: Podman uses its own image format that Docker cannot run
Podman runs without a central daemon and supports rootless containers
Podman can only run on Fedora and RHEL
Podman containers run in lightweight VMs instead of namespaces
questions.explanation: Docker's CLI talks to the dockerd daemon, which normally runs as root. Podman forks containers directly from the CLI and is designed for rootless use. Both use OCI images, and most docker commands work with podman.

questions.text: Which command creates an ext4 filesystem on the partition /dev/sdb1?
questions.explanation: mkfs.ext4 takes the block device, not a mount point. mkfs -t ext3 would build the wrong filesystem type, and format is not a Linux command.

questions.text: What happens to the existing files on /dev/sdb1 when you run mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1?
options: They are lost, because a new empty filesystem replaces the old one
They are converted to the ext4 format
They are moved to a lost+found directory
They are kept, because mkfs only writes free space
questions.explanation: Creating a filesystem writes fresh metadata (superblock, inode tables, journal) over the old structures, so existing data is no longer reachable. Back up first and double-check the device name.

questions.text: Which command sets the label mydata on an existing ext4 filesystem without reformatting it?
questions.explanation: e2label changes the label in place, and running it with only the device prints the current label. mkfs.ext4 -L sets a label but also wipes the filesystem, and blkid -L looks a device up by label.

questions.text:
In the /etc/fstab line below, which value is the mount options field?

/dev/sdb1   /mnt/external   ext4    defaults    0   2
questions.explanation: The fields are device, mount point, filesystem type, options, dump and fsck pass. defaults is the standard set of options such as read-write.

questions.text:
In the /etc/fstab line below, what does the final 2 mean?

UUID=1234-ABCD   /mnt/mydata   ext4   defaults   0   2
options: Mount the filesystem two seconds after boot
Keep two backup copies with dump
Check the filesystem with fsck after the root filesystem
Allow two retries if mounting fails
questions.explanation: The sixth field is the fsck pass order: 1 is usually the root filesystem, 2 means check after root, and 0 means do not check. The fifth field, 0 here, disables dump backups.

questions.text: Why is UUID=... usually preferred over /dev/sdb1 in /etc/fstab?
options: UUIDs make the filesystem mount faster at boot
Only UUIDs are accepted for ext4 filesystems
UUIDs encrypt the connection to the device
/dev/sdX names can change between boots, but the UUID does not
questions.explanation: Adding or removing disks can renumber /dev/sdX names, causing the wrong device to mount or a boot failure. The UUID is stored in the filesystem itself, so it follows the filesystem wherever the disk appears.

questions.text: Which command prints the UUID and filesystem type of /dev/sdb1?
questions.explanation: blkid reads the filesystem signature and prints UUID= and TYPE=. e2label shows only the label, df shows usage and fdisk -l shows partition layout. lsblk -f is another way to see UUIDs.

questions.text: Which command mounts the filesystem with UUID 1234-abcd on /mnt?
questions.explanation: mount accepts UUID= (or LABEL=) as the source, followed by the mount point. A bare UUID is treated as a path and fails.

questions.text: You just added a line to /etc/fstab. What should you run before rebooting to catch mistakes?
questions.explanation: mount -a tries to mount everything listed in /etc/fstab, so a typo shows up now instead of breaking the next boot; findmnt --verify also checks the file. fsck checks filesystems, not configuration files.

questions.text: Which /etc/fstab option mounts an external drive at boot when it is connected, but lets boot finish normally when it is not?
questions.explanation: nofail tells the boot process not to treat a missing device as an error, while still mounting it when present. noauto would skip the mount at boot even when the drive is connected.

questions.text: Which mount option stops the kernel from updating a file's access time every time it is read?
questions.explanation: noatime skips access-time updates, reducing writes on busy filesystems; the usual default, relatime, already limits them. nosuid and nodev are security options, and sync makes writes synchronous.

questions.text: You want to browse a disk taken from a damaged system without being able to change its files through the mount. Which command is appropriate?
questions.explanation: ro mounts the filesystem read-only; noexec still allows writes. ext4 may still replay a dirty journal on an ro mount, so add noload or use blockdev --setro when the device itself must stay untouched.

questions.text: What does the noexec mount option do?
options: Ignores device files on the filesystem
Hides executable files from directory listings
Prevents programs on the filesystem from being executed directly
questions.explanation: With noexec, binaries stored on that filesystem cannot be run, which is useful for removable media or /tmp. Files can still be read and written.

questions.text: What does the nosuid mount option do?
options: Ignores set-user-ID and set-group-ID bits on files in that filesystem
Prevents users other than root from mounting it
questions.explanation: With nosuid, a setuid program on that filesystem runs with the caller's own privileges, so a planted setuid-root binary cannot be used to gain root.

questions.text: The root filesystem was mounted read-only during recovery. Which command makes it writable without rebooting?
questions.explanation: remount changes the options of an already-mounted filesystem in place, here switching it to read-write. Unmounting / on a running system is not an option.

questions.text: Which command makes the contents of the image file ubuntu.iso browsable at /mnt/iso?
questions.explanation: The loop option attaches the regular file to a loop device so it can be mounted like a disk; recent mount versions add it automatically for regular files. A bind mount only mirrors an existing path, and copying the file does not expose its contents.

questions.text: Which command makes the existing directory /var/log also accessible at /mnt/logs?
questions.explanation: A bind mount attaches an existing directory tree at a second location. loop is for image files, and a tmpfs mount would create an empty in-memory filesystem.

questions.text: The directory /mnt/external contains oldfile.txt. What happens to it when you mount /dev/sdb1 on /mnt/external?
options: It is copied onto the USB drive
It is hidden until the filesystem is unmounted
It appears alongside the USB drive's files
questions.explanation: Mounting places the new filesystem over the directory, hiding the original contents without touching them. They reappear after umount, which is why empty mount points are recommended.

questions.text: sudo umount /mnt/external fails with "target is busy". What is a common cause?
options: The filesystem has errors that need fsck
A process has its working directory or an open file there
The device was mounted with nofail
The command must be spelled unmount
questions.explanation: The kernel will not detach a filesystem that is in use. cd out of the mount point or close the program, then try again.

questions.text: Which command shows which processes are using the mount at /mnt/external?
questions.explanation: fuser -vm lists processes with files or working directories on that filesystem; lsof +f -- /mnt/external gives similar output. findmnt and df describe the mount itself, not its users.

questions.text: What does umount -l /mnt/external do?
options: Lists processes that keep the mount busy
Forces the unmount and kills processes using it
Unmounts every filesystem listed in /etc/fstab
Detaches the mount point now and finishes cleanup once it is no longer busy
questions.explanation: A lazy unmount removes the filesystem from the directory tree immediately and releases it once the last user finishes. Prefer a normal unmount after closing the users when you can.

questions.text: Why should you unmount a USB drive before unplugging it?
options: Linux caches writes, and unmounting ensures they are written to the device
Unmounting erases temporary files from the drive
The drive cannot be detected again otherwise
Unmounting checks the drive for viruses
questions.explanation: A copy may finish while data still sits in the page cache. umount flushes pending writes and closes the filesystem cleanly; sync flushes too but does not replace unmounting.

questions.text: Which utility lists mounted filesystems as a tree with their sources, types and options?
questions.explanation: findmnt shows the mount hierarchy, and findmnt /mnt/point checks a single mount. blkid reports filesystem signatures and fdisk -l shows partition tables.

questions.text: Which command shows the filesystem type, such as ext4 or nfs4, of the filesystem that holds /mnt/data/report.txt?
questions.explanation: df -T adds a Type column for the filesystem containing each given path. file describes the file's contents, stat -c %s prints its size and ls -l shows its permissions and owner.

questions.text: In /proc/filesystems, what does nodev in front of tmpfs mean?
options: tmpfs is mounted with the nodev option
tmpfs is not backed by a block device
tmpfs is listed but not supported by the kernel
questions.explanation: /proc/filesystems lists the types the running kernel supports. nodev marks types such as proc, sysfs and tmpfs that need no block device; lines without it, such as ext4, are mounted from a disk or image.

questions.text: You rename the image logo.png to logo.txt. What does file logo.txt report?
options: ASCII text, because the name ends in .txt
data, because the name and contents disagree
PNG image data, read from the file's contents
An error, because the extension is not registered
questions.explanation: file identifies type from the contents, mainly "magic" byte signatures, not from the name. Linux in general does not rely on extensions to decide what a file is.

questions.text: What should you do before running fsck to repair the ext4 filesystem on /dev/sdb1?
options: Mount it read-write so changes can be saved
Run mkfs.ext4 to reset its metadata
questions.explanation: Repairing a mounted filesystem can corrupt it further because the kernel is changing it at the same time. Unmount first, or for the root filesystem use a rescue or live environment.

questions.text: e2fsck /dev/sdb1 reports a damaged superblock. The ext4 filesystem uses 4 KiB blocks. Which command checks it using the first backup superblock?
questions.explanation: ext4 keeps backup superblocks in several block groups; with 4 KiB blocks the first is at block 32768. dumpe2fs lists them, and mkfs.ext4 prints them when creating the filesystem. mkfs.ext4 -b would reformat the device.

questions.text: What does tune2fs -l /dev/sdb1 display?
options: Live I/O statistics for the device
The files in the filesystem's root directory
Superblock details such as block count, UUID and features
The options it is currently mounted with
questions.explanation: -l lists superblock contents for ext2, ext3 and ext4. Mount options are shown by findmnt, and I/O statistics by tools such as iostat.

questions.text: Which statement about resizing an ext4 filesystem with resize2fs is true?
options: It can shrink a mounted filesystem, but growing requires unmounting
It can grow a mounted filesystem, but shrinking requires unmounting
It also changes the size of the underlying partition
It only works on ext2, so ext4 must be converted first
questions.explanation: ext4 supports online growth, but resize2fs shrinks only unmounted filesystems. It never changes the partition: grow the partition first before enlarging, and shrink the filesystem before shrinking the partition.

questions.text: Which command converts an existing ext2 filesystem to ext3 by adding a journal?
questions.explanation: tune2fs -O has_journal enables the journal feature in place, keeping the data. mkfs.ext3 would create a new, empty filesystem.

questions.text: Which filesystem added journaling to the ext family for the first time?
questions.explanation: ext3 is ext2 plus a journal, which records pending changes so the filesystem can recover quickly after a crash. ext4 kept journaling and added larger limits and extents.

questions.text: An ext4 machine loses power in the middle of heavy writes. What happens when the filesystem is mounted again?
options: The journal is replayed to restore consistent metadata; uncommitted writes may be lost
Every file written since the last fsck is rolled back to its earlier content
The filesystem must be recreated with mkfs.ext4 before it can be used
Nothing special happens, because ext4 writes all data synchronously
questions.explanation: The journal (handled by jbd2) lets the kernel finish or discard interrupted transactions without a full fsck. It protects filesystem structure; data still in the page cache at the crash can be lost unless the application used fsync.

questions.text: Which Linux filesystem uses copy-on-write and natively supports snapshots and subvolumes?
questions.explanation: Btrfs writes changed data to new locations instead of overwriting, which makes cheap snapshots possible. ext4 and XFS are journaling filesystems without built-in snapshots.

questions.text: Which filesystem, originally developed by Silicon Graphics, is known for high performance with large files and parallel I/O?
questions.explanation: XFS was created by SGI and scales well under concurrent workloads. JFS came from IBM and ReiserFS is a historical filesystem known for handling many small files.

questions.text: What is the role of the Virtual File System (VFS) in the Linux kernel?
options: It stores files in RAM instead of on disk
It shares files with other machines over a network
It gives programs one interface to many filesystem types
It encrypts data before it reaches the disk
questions.explanation: The VFS layer translates system calls like open and read into operations for ext4, XFS, NFS and others, so applications do not need filesystem-specific code.

questions.text: Copying a 6 GB video to a USB stick fails, although the stick has plenty of free space. The stick is most likely formatted with which filesystem?
questions.explanation: FAT32 limits individual files to 4 GiB minus 1 byte. exFAT, NTFS and ext4 all support much larger files.

questions.text: A FAT32 USB stick mounted by root shows every file owned by root, and chown on it fails. How do you let the user with UID 1000 write to it?
options: Run tune2fs -o user_xattr on the device
Add usrquota to its mount options
questions.explanation: FAT stores no Unix owners or permission bits, so the driver presents one owner for every file, chosen at mount time with uid= and gid= (and umask for the mode). tune2fs only works on ext filesystems.

questions.text: A program needs temporary files that survive a reboot. Which directory is intended for that?
questions.explanation: /tmp is commonly cleared at boot and /run holds volatile runtime data, while /var/tmp is meant to persist between reboots. /proc is a kernel pseudo filesystem.

questions.text: /tmp has mode drwxrwxrwt (1777). Why can't user bob delete alice's file /tmp/a.txt?
options: bob lacks write permission on a.txt itself
tmpfs does not allow files to be deleted
The sticky bit lets only a file's owner, the directory owner or root remove it
questions.explanation: The trailing t is the sticky bit. Normally anyone with write permission on a directory can delete any entry in it; on a sticky directory, unlinking or renaming an entry also requires owning it (or the directory), or being root.

questions.text: Where should an administrator install a program compiled from source so it does not clash with distribution-managed packages?
questions.explanation: The package manager owns /usr/bin and /bin. /usr/local (or /opt) is reserved for locally installed software, and /etc is for configuration, not binaries.

questions.text: Why should you never store persistent files in /proc or /sys?
options: They are mounted read-only for all users
They are wiped and rebuilt by a nightly job
They are encrypted with a per-boot key
They are kernel-generated pseudo filesystems, not disk storage
questions.explanation: /proc and /sys expose live kernel and process state. Their contents are created on the fly and disappear at shutdown.

questions.text: How do block device files differ from character device files under /dev?
options: Block devices are virtual, while character devices are physical
Block devices move fixed-size blocks, while character devices move byte streams
Block devices are root-only, while character devices are world-readable
Block devices hold directories, while character devices hold files
questions.explanation: Disks like /dev/sda are block devices accessed in fixed-size chunks. Keyboards, terminals and serial ports are character devices; ls -l marks them with b and c.

questions.text: Which file on an NFS server defines which directories are shared and which clients may access them?
questions.explanation: Each line in /etc/exports names a directory followed by the allowed clients and options, such as /opt/shared 192.168.1.0/24(rw,sync,root_squash). Clients use /etc/fstab to mount shares.

questions.text: After editing /etc/exports, which command applies the changes without restarting the NFS service?
questions.explanation: exportfs -r re-reads /etc/exports and syncs the active export table. -v only displays current exports and -u unexports a directory.

questions.text: What does the root_squash export option do?
options: Gives client root full root access to the export
Prevents the server's root user from reading the export
Forces all client users to log in as root
Maps requests from root on the client to an anonymous unprivileged user
questions.explanation: With root_squash, UID 0 on a client becomes nobody (or nfsnobody) on the server. no_root_squash disables this protection and should be avoided unless truly needed.

questions.text: Which export option maps every client user, not just root, to the anonymous user?
questions.explanation: all_squash makes all access use one server-side identity, which can be chosen with anonuid and anongid. It suits simple public drop-box shares.

questions.text: What does the sync option in /etc/exports mean?
options: The client caches all writes locally
The server commits changes to storage before replying to the client
The export is mirrored to a second server
questions.explanation: sync is the safe choice: a reply means the data is stored. async replies earlier for speed but can lose data if the server crashes.

questions.text: Why is NFSv4 generally easier to put behind a firewall than NFSv3?
options: It needs no open ports at all
It uses a single main TCP port, 2049
It runs over HTTPS on port 443
questions.explanation: NFSv4 is a stateful protocol that carries everything over TCP port 2049. NFSv3 relies on extra services such as rpcbind on port 111 and mountd, often on varying ports.

questions.text: Which command mounts the export /opt/shared from the server 192.168.1.100 on /mnt/nfs_shared?
questions.explanation: The source is written server:/path, followed by the local mount point. Reversing them or splitting the host from the path makes mount fail, and a bind mount only works with local directories.

questions.text: From a client, which command lists the directories that the NFS server 192.168.1.100 advertises?
questions.explanation: showmount -e queries the server's export list (most useful with NFSv3-style services). exportfs runs on the server itself, and findmnt shows local mounts.

questions.text: Mounting 192.168.1.100:/opt/shared fails with mount.nfs: access denied by server, although port 2049 on the server is reachable. What is the most likely cause?
options: The client's address is not covered by the export's entry in /etc/exports
The server firewall is blocking TCP port 2049
The user's UID differs between the client and the server
The client did not include noatime in its mount options
questions.explanation: The server answered and refused, which points at the export rules: wrong client subnet, wrong path or exports not reloaded. A blocked port gives a timeout instead, and UID mismatches only show up as permission errors after mounting.

questions.text: The server exports /opt/shared with ro, and a client mounts it with default options. What happens when a client user runs touch /mnt/nfs_shared/new.txt?
options: It succeeds, because the client mounted the share read-write
It succeeds locally, and the file is discarded at unmount
It makes every NFS mount on the client read-only
questions.explanation: Export options are enforced by the server, whatever the client asks for in its own mount options. The server rejects the write, and the client reports it as a read-only filesystem error.

questions.text: An NFS share is mounted with default options and the server crashes. What happens to client processes that read files on the share?
options: They receive an I/O error immediately
They block, and the client keeps retrying until the server returns
They read cached copies from the client's local disk
The client unmounts the share automatically
questions.explanation: The default hard option retries requests indefinitely, logging "server not responding, still trying". soft returns an error after retrans retries instead, which avoids hangs but can cause data loss for writes.

questions.text: A laptop has an NFS share in /etc/fstab and hangs at boot when away from the office network. Which options fix this?
questions.explanation: _netdev marks the mount as network-dependent, nofail stops a missing server from failing the boot, and x-systemd.automount mounts the share on first access instead of at boot.

questions.text: User alice has UID 1000 on an NFS client but UID 2000 on the server, and the export uses the default sec=sys authentication. Why does she get "Permission denied" on her own files in the share?
options: NFS ignores file permissions for non-root users
The server always maps users to nobody
NFS sends the numeric UID 1000, which the server does not treat as alice
Usernames longer than four characters are not supported
questions.explanation: With sec=sys, ownership checks use the numeric UIDs and GIDs the client sends. Keep them consistent through central identity management such as LDAP, or assign matching IDs manually.

questions.text: Files on an NFSv4 mount show the owner nobody even though the UIDs match. What is a likely cause?
options: The NFSv4 ID-mapping domain in /etc/idmapd.conf differs between client and server
The client mounted the share with noatime
questions.explanation: NFSv4 maps names using a domain; if the client and server domains differ, names cannot be mapped and owners appear as nobody or 4294967294. Squash options can produce the same symptom.

questions.text: A client shows "Stale file handle" after the server's exported directory was renamed and recreated. How do you fix it on the client?
options: Leave the directory, then unmount and remount the share
Run fsck on the NFS mount point
Delete and recreate the local mount point directory
questions.explanation: The client still holds references to the old directory objects. Remounting obtains fresh handles; use fuser -vm or lsof if the unmount reports that the target is busy.

questions.text: Which of these is an absolute path?
questions.explanation: An absolute path starts at the root directory /, so it points to the same place no matter where you are. The others are relative paths resolved from the current working directory.

questions.text: Your current directory is /home/user/Documents. Which relative path refers to /home/user/notes/todo.txt?
questions.explanation: .. moves up one level to /home/user, and notes/todo.txt continues from there. notes/... and ./notes/... look inside Documents, and ../.. climbs too far, to /home.

questions.text: How can you recognize a hidden file in a Linux directory listing?
options: It has no read permission for others
It is owned by the root user
Its name begins with a dot (.)
questions.explanation: By convention any file whose name starts with . (such as .bashrc) is hidden from a plain ls. Permissions and ownership have nothing to do with it; ls -a reveals these files.

questions.text: Which command lists all files, including hidden ones, in long format with permissions, owner and size?
questions.explanation: -a includes entries starting with a dot and -l gives the long format. ls -l alone hides dotfiles, and ls -lh only changes how sizes are printed.

questions.text: mkdir projects/2024/q1 fails with "No such file or directory" because projects does not exist yet. Which command creates the whole path?
questions.explanation: -p creates every missing parent directory and does not complain if the path already exists. mkdir has no -r option, -m only sets the mode, and touch creates files, not directories.

questions.text: You run cp project /backup/ where project is a directory. What happens?
options: cp skips it with a message that -r was not specified
The directory and all its contents are copied to /backup/project
Only the files at the top level of project are copied
An empty directory named project is created in /backup
questions.explanation: Without -r (or -a), GNU cp refuses to copy directories and prints -r not specified; omitting directory 'project'. Use cp -r project /backup/ to copy the whole tree.

questions.text: Which cp command copies the directory project recursively while preserving permissions, timestamps and symbolic links?
questions.explanation: -a (archive) recurses and preserves mode, ownership, timestamps and symlinks. -r recurses but gives the copies new timestamps and the copying user's ownership, -v only prints progress, and -i only prompts before overwriting.

questions.text: Which command copies file.txt into /backup/ but asks for confirmation before overwriting an existing file?
questions.explanation: -i (interactive) prompts before overwriting. -f forces the copy, -p preserves mode and timestamps, and -u copies only when the source is newer, none of which ask first.

questions.text: What does mv oldname.txt newname.txt do when both names are in the same directory?
options: Copies the file and keeps both names
Fails because mv only moves files between directories
Creates a hard link called newname.txt
questions.explanation: mv both moves and renames. Within one filesystem it just changes the directory entry, so the data and inode stay the same and oldname.txt no longer exists afterwards.

questions.text: Which command removes the directory old_logs together with everything inside it?
questions.explanation: rm -r recurses into the directory and deletes it with its contents. Plain rm refuses to remove directories, rmdir only removes empty ones, and old_logs/* leaves the directory itself (and its hidden files) behind.

questions.text: What does adding -f to rm -r change?
options: It makes rm descend into subdirectories
It moves the files to a trash folder instead of deleting them
It overwrites the file data before deleting it
It never prompts and ignores files that do not exist
questions.explanation: -f (force) suppresses confirmation prompts and errors about missing files. Recursion comes from -r; rm has no trash and does not securely erase data, which is why rm -rf must be used with care.

questions.text:
How many files does this command create?

touch file{1..4}{a..f}
questions.explanation: Brace expansion produces every combination: 4 numbers times 6 letters gives 24 names, file1a through file4f, and touch creates each one.

questions.text:
What does this command do?

cp config.yml{,.bak}
options: It fails, because a brace list cannot contain an empty item
It copies config.yml and a file named .bak into the current directory
It copies config.yml to a new file named config.yml.bak
It creates a directory config.yml that contains .bak
questions.explanation: Brace expansion runs before cp and turns the word into config.yml config.yml.bak (empty item, then .bak), so cp receives a source and a destination. It is a common shortcut for making a backup copy.

questions.text:
What does this nested brace expansion print?

echo {A,B{1..3},C}
questions.explanation: The inner range {1..3} expands with the prefix B to B1 B2 B3, and those words sit in the outer list between A and C.

questions.text: In a directory containing file.txt, file1.txt and file12.txt, which files does ls file?.txt list?
questions.explanation: In a glob, ? matches exactly one character. file.txt has none in that position and file12.txt has two, so only file1.txt matches. In a regular expression, by contrast, ? means "zero or one of the preceding element".

questions.text: Which filename is matched by the glob file[12].txt?
questions.explanation: [12] matches a single character that is either 1 or 2. file12.txt would need two characters in that position, and 3 or _ are not in the set.

questions.text: In Bash with default settings, what does echo *.txt print in a directory that contains no .txt files?
options: An error saying no files were found
The names of all files in the directory
questions.explanation: Globs only match existing files. When nothing matches, Bash leaves the pattern unchanged (unless nullglob or failglob is set), so echo prints *.txt. Brace expansion, by contrast, always generates its words.

questions.text: A directory contains .env, a.txt and b.log. In Bash with default settings, what does echo * print?
questions.explanation: A leading dot must be matched explicitly, so * skips hidden files (unless dotglob is set). That is also why rm -r dir/* leaves dotfiles behind; .* would match .env.

questions.text: While viewing a file with more, what does pressing Enter do?
options: Jumps to the next search match
questions.explanation: Enter advances one line and Space advances one page. Moving backward is limited in more (b works only on files, not pipes), while less supports full navigation in both directions.

questions.text: While reading a log in less, which keys search backward from the current position for the text ERROR?
questions.explanation: In less, /pattern searches forward and ?pattern searches backward; n repeats the last search. b scrolls back one page and is not a search command.

questions.text: Why is less usually a better choice than cat for reading a very large log file?
options: It shows one screen at a time and lets you scroll backward and search
It compresses the file so it loads faster
It shows only the last 10 lines of the file
It lets you edit the file in place
questions.explanation: cat dumps the whole file to the terminal at once. less pages the content, supports backward movement and /pattern searches, and does not modify the file.

questions.text: What does head -n 2 a.txt b.txt print?
options: The first 2 lines of a.txt followed by those of b.txt, with no separator
Only the first 2 lines of a.txt, because the second name is ignored
An error, because head accepts only one file at a time
The first 2 lines of each file, each block preceded by a ==> name <== header
questions.explanation: With several files, head (and tail) prints a header line such as ==> a.txt <== before each file's lines. Without -n the default is 10 lines; -q suppresses the headers.

questions.text: What does tail -n +2 data.csv output?
options: Every line from line 2 to the end, skipping the header line
The last 2 lines of the file
The file with every second line removed
questions.explanation: A leading + makes tail start output at that line number instead of counting from the end. It is a common way to drop a CSV header.

questions.text:
Which lines of data.csv does this pipeline print?

tail -n +50 data.csv | head -n 11
options: The last 50 lines, then the first 11 lines
questions.explanation: tail -n +50 starts output at line 50 and head -n 11 keeps the next 11 lines, which are lines 50 through 60.

questions.text: The directory dest/ already exists. After running rsync -a src dest/ (no trailing slash on src), where does the file src/f1 end up?
options: Nowhere; rsync requires a trailing slash on a directory source
questions.explanation: Without a trailing slash, rsync copies the directory itself into the destination. rsync -a src/ dest/ copies only the contents of src, so the file would land at dest/f1.

questions.text: Which command makes /dest/ an exact mirror of /src/, removing files that no longer exist in the source?
questions.explanation: --delete removes destination files that are absent from the source. Without it rsync only adds and updates files; --dry-run changes nothing and -P only shows progress.

questions.text: What does rsync --dry-run (-n) do?
options: Copies only files whose checksums differ
Shows what would be transferred without changing anything
Deletes extra files in the destination
questions.explanation: A dry run simulates the transfer and lists the actions (add -v to see them). It is a good habit before a run that uses --delete.

questions.text: Which rsync option compresses data during the transfer to save bandwidth?
questions.explanation: -z compresses data in transit, which helps over slow links such as SSH to a remote host. -a is archive mode, -v is verbose and -n is a dry run.

questions.text: A large rsync transfer keeps getting interrupted. Which option shows per-file progress and keeps partially transferred files so the next run can resume?
questions.explanation: -P combines --progress and --partial, so you can watch each file and avoid restarting large files from zero after an interruption.

questions.text: Why is rsync usually preferred over cp for repeated backups of the same directory?
options: It always compresses files stored on the destination
It can copy files that cp is not permitted to read
It keeps old versions of every changed file
It skips files that are already up to date at the destination
questions.explanation: rsync compares source and destination (by size and modification time by default) and transfers only what changed, so later runs are much faster. It does not bypass permissions or keep version history by itself.

questions.text: What is the main difference between df and du?
options: df counts files, while du counts directories
df reports usage per filesystem, while du sums the given files and directories
df reads only /, while du reads every mounted filesystem
df reports memory usage, while du reports disk usage
questions.explanation: df asks each mounted filesystem for its size, used and available space. du walks a directory tree and adds up what the files occupy, which is how you find space hogs.

questions.text: Which command prints a human-readable size summary for each file and directory in the current directory?
questions.explanation: du -s gives one total per argument and -h uses K, M and G units; the glob passes each non-hidden item as an argument. df -h . reports the whole filesystem, not individual items.

questions.text: When running du on /, which option keeps it from descending into other mounted filesystems such as /proc or a network share?
questions.explanation: -x (--one-file-system) skips directories on different filesystems. -s summarizes, -a lists files too and -c prints a grand total.

questions.text: Why should you use sort -h rather than sort -n on the output of du -sh *?
options: sort -h is faster on large inputs
sort -n sorts in reverse order by default
sort -n ignores unit suffixes, so it treats 900K as larger than 2.0G
questions.explanation: -n compares only the leading number (900 versus 2.0). -h understands human-readable suffixes, so du -sh * | sort -hr correctly lists the largest items first.

questions.text: Creating a file fails with "No space left on device", yet df -h shows the filesystem only 40% full. What should you check next?
options: free -h, because RAM may be full
df -i, because the filesystem may have run out of inodes
du -sh /tmp, because temporary files are not counted by df
ls -l, because the directory may be read-only
questions.explanation: Every file needs an inode. On filesystems with a fixed inode count, such as ext4, millions of tiny files can use them all while blocks remain free. df -i shows inode usage.

questions.text: You delete a 10 GB log file with rm, but df shows no space was freed. What is the most likely reason?
options: A running process still has the file open
rm only removes the filename after a reboot
df caches its results for an hour
Log files are always stored in a reserved area
questions.explanation: rm removes the name, but the inode and data are kept until every open file descriptor is closed. lsof +L1 lists such deleted-but-open files; restarting the process that writes the log releases the space.

questions.text: With disk quotas, what distinguishes a soft limit from a hard limit?
options: The soft limit applies to inodes and the hard limit applies to blocks
The soft limit applies to groups and the hard limit applies to users
The soft limit can be exceeded for a grace period; the hard limit can never be exceeded
The soft limit only produces log entries and is never enforced
questions.explanation: A user above the soft limit gets a grace period (set with edquota -t) before writes are refused. The hard limit is an absolute ceiling. Both block and inode limits have soft and hard values.

questions.text: Which mount options must be added to an ext4 filesystem's /etc/fstab entry to enable user and group quotas?
questions.explanation: After adding usrquota,grpquota and remounting, quotacheck -cug creates the quota files and quotaon starts enforcement. uquota is XFS's spelling for user quotas, and acl enables access control lists, not quotas.

questions.text: Which command opens an editor to set the soft and hard quota limits for user alice?
questions.explanation: edquota edits limits. quota -u only displays a user's usage, repquota reports on all users of a filesystem, and quotaon turns enforcement on for a filesystem.

questions.text: In repquota /home output, user bob's line shows +- right after his name. What does that mean?
options: bob has exceeded both his block and inode hard limits
bob's block usage is over its soft limit, but his file count is not
bob's block quota is disabled, but his inode quota is enabled
bob is under every limit and his grace period was reset
questions.explanation: The first character refers to block limits and the second to inode (file) limits; + means usage is above the soft limit. bob can keep writing until he hits the hard limit or the grace period shown in the grace column expires.

questions.text: Which piece of information is stored in the directory entry rather than in the file's inode?
questions.explanation: A directory entry maps a name to an inode number; the inode holds the metadata and data block pointers but not the name. That is why one inode can have several names (hard links).

questions.text: Which command shows each file's inode number in the first column?
questions.explanation: -i prints inode numbers, and -l adds the long listing. -n shows numeric UIDs and GIDs, -s shows allocated blocks and -F appends type indicators.

questions.text: What does a file's ctime record?
options: When its inode metadata (or content) last changed
When the file was last read
When the file was last copied
questions.explanation: ctime is the status change time, updated by changes such as chmod, chown or writing to the file. It is not creation time; reads update atime and content changes update mtime.

questions.text: You run ln report.txt copy.txt and then delete report.txt. What happens to copy.txt?
options: It still works and shows the same content
questions.explanation: Without -s, ln creates a hard link, a second name for the same inode. The data is kept until the last name is removed, so copy.txt is unaffected.

questions.text: You create a new file report.txt and then run ln report.txt copy.txt. What link count does stat report.txt show?
questions.explanation: The inode now has two directory entries pointing at it, so its link count is 2. A symlink would not change the target's link count.

questions.text: After ln -s a.txt link, what does ls -li a.txt link show?
options: The same inode number for both names, and a link count of 2
Different inode numbers, and a.txt still has a link count of 1
The same inode number, with link marked by an l type
Only a.txt, because symlinks have no inode of their own
questions.explanation: A symlink is a separate small file with its own inode that stores the path a.txt. It adds no directory entry for the target's inode, so the target's link count is unchanged.

questions.text: Why does ln /mnt/usb/data.txt ~/data.txt fail when /mnt/usb is a separate filesystem?
options: Hard links only work within one directory
USB drives do not support links of any kind
Inode numbers are only meaningful within one filesystem
questions.explanation: A hard link is a directory entry pointing at an inode number, and those are unique only within a filesystem, so ln fails with "Invalid cross-device link". A symbolic link, which stores a path, works instead.

questions.text: What happens when you run ln dir1 dir2, where dir1 is a directory?
options: dir2 becomes a second name for dir1
ln refuses, because hard links to directories are not allowed
dir2 is created as a symbolic link to dir1
dir1 is copied recursively to dir2
questions.explanation: GNU ln prints "hard link not allowed for directory". Directory hard links could create loops in the tree and confuse .. and tools that walk it; use ln -s dir1 dir2 for a second path to a directory.

questions.text: What happens to a symbolic link when its target file is deleted?
options: The symlink keeps a copy of the target's data
The symlink remains but is dangling and fails when accessed
The system refuses to delete the target
questions.explanation: A symlink stores only a path. Once nothing exists at that path, opening the link gives "No such file or directory", although the link itself is still listed.

questions.text: The symlink /opt/app/current stores the relative target releases/v2. Where does the system look for that target?
options: In the current working directory of the process using the link
In /opt/app, the directory that contains the symlink
questions.explanation: Relative symlink targets are resolved from the directory containing the link, so this one points to /opt/app/releases/v2 no matter where you run commands from.

questions.text: Which command prints the fully resolved, canonical absolute path that the symlink mylink points to?
questions.explanation: readlink -f follows every link in the chain and prints an absolute path. Plain readlink prints the stored target text, which may be relative, and stat -L shows the target's metadata rather than its path.

questions.text: The symlink mylink currently points to fileA.txt. Which command makes it point to fileB.txt instead?
questions.explanation: A symlink cannot be edited in place. -f replaces the existing link and -n stops ln from descending into mylink if it points to a directory. Without -f, ln fails with "File exists".

questions.text: Which command finds .log files under /var whose contents were modified within the last 7 days?
questions.explanation: -mtime -7 means modified less than 7 days ago; +7 means more than 7 days ago. -atime checks access time and -mmin counts minutes, not days.

questions.text: What does find . -type f -newer file2 list?
options: Files created after file2 was first created
Regular files modified more recently than file2
Files that are larger than file2
Files with a higher inode number than file2
questions.explanation: -newer compares modification times against the reference file. Adding -type f restricts results to regular files.

questions.text: With GNU find, which files does find . -type f -size +2000 match?
options: Files using more than 2000 blocks of 512 bytes (about 1 MB)
questions.explanation: A -size number without a suffix counts 512-byte blocks, rounded up. Suffixes change the unit, for example -size +10M for more than 10 MiB or c for bytes.

questions.text: You want find to ask before deleting each matching .bak file. Which command does that?
questions.explanation: -ok works like -exec but prompts before each command and runs it only on a y answer. -delete and -exec rm remove matches without asking.

questions.text: You create report.txt and immediately run locate report.txt, but it finds nothing. Why?
options: locate only searches the current directory
locate needs the -i option for exact names
locate ignores files owned by regular users
locate searches a prebuilt database that has not been updated yet
questions.explanation: locate is fast because it queries a database built by updatedb, which usually runs periodically. Newly created files appear after the next update; find searches the live filesystem.

questions.text: In Bash, ls is an alias for ls --color=auto. Which command shows the alias as well as every ls executable found in PATH?
questions.explanation: type is a shell builtin, so it knows about aliases, functions and builtins, and -a lists every match. which is an external program that only searches PATH for files, even with -a.

questions.text:
On a server with a non-hybrid CPU, lscpu prints the lines below. How many logical CPUs does the kernel schedule on?

Thread(s) per core:  2
Core(s) per socket:  8
Socket(s):           2
questions.explanation: Logical CPUs = sockets × cores per socket × threads per core = 2 × 8 × 2 = 32, which lscpu also prints as CPU(s). CPUs that mix performance and efficiency cores (such as recent Intel desktop chips) break this simple product.

questions.text: Which command prints the number of logical CPUs listed in /proc/cpuinfo?
questions.explanation: /proc/cpuinfo has one block per logical CPU, each starting with a processor line, so counting them matches nproc (when no CPU affinity limit applies). The first cpu cores line gives the cores per socket, and physical id names a socket.

questions.text:
free -h prints the output below. Is the system short of memory?

               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:            31Gi       8,5Gi       2,9Gi        75Mi        20Gi        22Gi
Swap:          2,0Gi          0B       2,0Gi
options: Yes, only 2.9 GiB is free, so new programs will start swapping
No, about 22 GiB is available because most of the page cache can be reclaimed
Yes, buff/cache is using 20 GiB that programs can never get back
No, because swap is empty and 2 GiB of swap is always enough
questions.explanation: Linux fills idle RAM with page cache. The available column (from MemAvailable in /proc/meminfo) estimates how much memory new programs can use without swapping, including reclaimable cache. free alone is not a useful measure.

questions.text: Which command shows which block devices are rotational hard disks rather than SSDs?
questions.explanation: The ROTA column is 1 for a rotational disk and 0 for SSD or NVMe, and -d hides partitions. lsblk -f shows filesystem type, label, UUID and mount points; lsblk -m shows device permissions.

questions.text: You need the filesystem type and UUID of every partition, for example to write an /etc/fstab entry. Which command shows them without root?
questions.explanation: lsblk -f adds FSTYPE, LABEL, UUID, free space and mount points to the device tree. blkid shows similar data but may need root to probe devices it has not cached.

questions.text: Which command shows the kernel driver in use for each PCI device, such as a network card or GPU?
questions.explanation: lspci -k adds Kernel driver in use: and Kernel modules: lines under each device. That is the quickest way to see whether, for example, an NVIDIA GPU uses nvidia or nouveau. lspci -t shows the bus tree, and lsmod has no -k option.

questions.text: lsusb prints Bus 001 Device 002: ID 05e3:0610 Genesys Logic, Inc. Hub. What is 05e3:0610?
options: The USB vendor ID and product ID
The bus number and port number
The major and minor device numbers
questions.explanation: USB and PCI devices carry a vendor ID and a product (device) ID in hexadecimal. They are the best search terms for driver support. lspci -nn prints the PCI equivalent, such as [8086:4668].

questions.text: Which command shows each installed RAM module with its size, speed and slot, and why does it need sudo?
options: free -h, because it reads root-only kernel memory
lscpu --caches, because the RAM layout is stored in the CPU
cat /proc/meminfo, because the file is readable only by root
sudo dmidecode -t memory, because it reads the firmware's SMBIOS tables, which only root can read
questions.explanation: dmidecode decodes the SMBIOS/DMI tables provided by the firmware: system, board, BIOS and memory slots. As a normal user it fails with /sys/firmware/dmi/tables/smbios_entry_point: Permission denied. free and /proc/meminfo only show totals.

questions.text:
ls -l /dev/null /dev/nvme0n1 prints the lines below. What do the first characters c and b mean?

crw-rw-rw- 1 root root   1, 3 Oct 25 10:10 /dev/null
brw-rw---- 1 root disk 259, 0 Oct 25 10:10 /dev/nvme0n1
options: c is a character device and b is a block device
c is a configuration file and b is a binary file
c means the device is closed and b means it is busy
c is a container device and b is a bus device
questions.explanation: Device files have a type, permissions and a major/minor number pair that selects the driver. Block devices such as disks are accessed in blocks; character devices such as terminals and /dev/null are byte streams. The disk group controls raw disk access.

questions.text: What do the first four bytes of every ELF executable contain?
options: The magic number 0x7f followed by ELF
#! followed by the interpreter path
The size of the file in bytes
questions.explanation: head -c 4 /bin/ls | od -c prints 177 E L F (177 is octal for 0x7f). The kernel and file use this magic number to recognise ELF; scripts instead start with #!.

questions.text: file /bin/ls reports dynamically linked, interpreter /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2. What is that interpreter?
options: The shell that runs ls when it is started from a script
A compatibility layer that runs 32-bit programs
A debugger that the kernel attaches when the program crashes
The dynamic linker, which the kernel starts to load the shared libraries before main runs
questions.explanation: A dynamically linked ELF file has a PT_INTERP program header naming the dynamic linker, shown by readelf -l /bin/ls | grep interpreter. The kernel maps the program and this linker; the linker loads libraries such as libc.so.6, then jumps to the program's entry point.

questions.text: Which command prints the entry point address of an ELF executable?
questions.explanation: readelf -h shows the ELF header, including Class, Machine and Entry point address. readelf -l lists the program headers (segments and interpreter), and readelf -d lists the dynamic section with NEEDED libraries.

questions.text: You build gcc -static -o hello-static hello.c. What does ldd hello-static print?
options: The same list as for a dynamically linked build
questions.explanation: A static binary contains the library code it uses and has no PT_INTERP header, so there is nothing for ldd to resolve (it also exits with status 1). file describes such a binary as statically linked. Static binaries suit minimal initramfs environments.

questions.text:
You copy /bin/busybox from an Alpine container to an Ubuntu host. ls -l shows it, but ./busybox echo hi prints the error below. Why?

bash: ./busybox: cannot execute: required file not found
options: The file lost its execute permission during the copy
Its ELF interpreter /lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1 does not exist on the host
Ubuntu refuses to run binaries that were built on another distribution
The binary is for a different CPU architecture
questions.explanation: file busybox shows interpreter /lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1. When the interpreter is missing, execve fails with ENOENT, which bash 5.2 reports as required file not found (older versions say No such file or directory) although the program file exists. A wrong architecture gives Exec format error.

questions.text: A script named show has the first line #!/bin/echo hello. What does ./show a b print?
questions.explanation: For a #! file, the kernel runs the interpreter with the optional shebang argument, then the script's path, then the original arguments: /bin/echo hello ./show a b. That is how #!/bin/sh scripts end up as /bin/sh ./script args.

questions.text: A script starts with #!/usr/bin/env python3 -u. Running it on Linux prints /usr/bin/env: 'python3 -u': No such file or directory. Why?
options: Linux passes everything after the interpreter path as one argument, so env looks for a program named python3 -u
env cannot start Python and needs the full path /usr/bin/python3
The -u option is not valid for Python 3
Shebang lines may not contain spaces at all
questions.explanation: The kernel splits a shebang only once, after the interpreter path. GNU env -S splits the rest itself, so #!/usr/bin/env -S python3 -u works, as env's own hint says.

questions.text: A script copied from Windows runs fine with sh deploy.sh, but ./deploy.sh fails with cannot execute: required file not found. file deploy.sh reports with CRLF line terminators. What is wrong?
options: The script has no execute permission
/bin/sh is not installed on the system
The shebang line ends with a carriage return, so the kernel looks for an interpreter named /bin/sh\r
Windows scripts must be run through wine
questions.explanation: The kernel takes the interpreter path up to the newline, so the trailing \r becomes part of the file name, which does not exist. Running sh deploy.sh bypasses the shebang. Convert the file with dos2unix or sed -i 's/\r$//'.

questions.text: A script has mode -rw-r--r-- (644). What happens with ./s.sh and with bash s.sh?
options: Both run, because the file is readable
./s.sh runs; bash s.sh fails because bash checks the x bit
./s.sh fails with Permission denied (status 126); bash s.sh runs the script
questions.explanation: Executing a file with execve needs the execute bit. bash s.sh executes /bin/bash, which only reads the script, so read permission is enough. chmod +x s.sh lets ./s.sh work.

questions.text: You set mode --x--x--x (111) on a compiled binary hx and on a shell script s.sh, both owned by you. What happens when you run each with ./?
options: ./hx runs; ./s.sh fails because the interpreter cannot read the script
Both run, because both have execute permission
Both fail, because every executable also needs read permission
./s.sh runs; ./hx fails because the kernel must read the binary
questions.explanation: For an ELF binary the kernel maps the file itself, so execute permission is enough. For a script the kernel starts /bin/sh ./s.sh, and the shell must open the file for reading: /bin/sh: 0: cannot open ./s.sh: Permission denied.

questions.text: /t is mounted with noexec. Both /t/hello (an ELF binary) and /t/s.sh have mode 755. What happens?
options: Both run, because noexec only blocks setuid programs
/t/hello and /t/s.sh fail with Permission denied, but sh /t/s.sh still runs the script
