questions.explanation: NVMe names are controller, namespace and then p plus the partition number. /dev/nvme0n1 is the whole disk.

questions.text: You attach a new SATA disk and it appears as /dev/sdc. After you create one partition on it, what is that partition called?
questions.explanation: Partition numbers start at 1, so the first partition on /dev/sdc is /dev/sdc1. The p separator is only used when the disk name ends in a digit, such as NVMe.

questions.text: Which command lists disks and their partitions as a tree, with sizes and mount points?
questions.explanation: lsblk shows every block device, including unmounted partitions and LVM volumes, with TYPE and MOUNTPOINT columns. df lists only mounted filesystems.

questions.text:
What does this lsblk output tell you?

NAME   MAJ:MIN RM   SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINT
sda      8:0    0   500G  0 disk
├─sda1   8:1    0    50G  0 part /
└─sda2   8:2    0    50G  0 part /home
options: The disk is full because both partitions are mounted
/home is 500G in size because it is on sda
About 400G of the disk is not allocated to any partition
sda2 is the boot partition, since it is listed last
questions.explanation: The disk is 500G and its two partitions use 100G, so roughly 400G is unallocated and available for new partitions. lsblk does not print free space directly; you infer it.

questions.text: Which command shows the unallocated regions of /dev/sda together with its partitions?
questions.explanation: print free adds "Free Space" rows with their start, end and size. lsblk -f and blkid show filesystems and UUIDs, and df reports usage of mounted filesystems only.

questions.text: sudo fdisk -l /dev/sdb prints Disklabel type: dos. What does that mean?
options: The disk uses an MBR partition table
The disk is formatted with a FAT filesystem
The disk can only be read by DOS or Windows
The disk uses GPT with a legacy boot flag
questions.explanation: fdisk calls the MBR format "dos" (and parted calls it "msdos"). A GPT disk shows Disklabel type: gpt; the label says nothing about the filesystems inside the partitions.

questions.text: Inside fdisk, which command saves your partition changes to the disk and exits?
questions.explanation: fdisk keeps changes in memory until you press w. q quits without saving, which is a safe way to back out, p prints the table and n creates a partition.

questions.text: While creating a partition in fdisk (util-linux 2.39), what should you enter at the "Last sector" prompt to make it 50 GiB?
questions.explanation: A leading + gives a size from the first sector. -50G instead leaves 50 GiB free at the end, 50000 is an absolute sector (about 23 MiB here), and 50G without a sign is rejected as out of range.

questions.text: Which partitioning tool was designed specifically for GPT disks?
questions.explanation: gdisk is the GPT counterpart of fdisk, with commands such as o to create a new GPT. Modern fdisk also handles GPT, but it started as an MBR tool; lsblk and resize2fs do not edit partition tables.

questions.text: You just created /dev/sdb1 with fdisk. What must you do before you can store files on it?
options: Create a filesystem on it, for example mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1
Nothing, it can be mounted immediately with mount
Run lvcreate on it to make it usable
Mark it as active with the a command in fdisk
questions.explanation: A new partition is just raw space. A filesystem must be created on it before it can be mounted and used for files.

questions.text: You run sudo parted -s /dev/sdb mklabel gpt mkpart data ext4 1MiB 100%. Can you now mount /dev/sdb1 as ext4?
options: Yes, the ext4 argument made mkpart format the partition
No, ext4 is only a type hint; you still need mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1
Yes, but only after running resize2fs to fill the partition
No, GPT partitions cannot hold ext4, only FAT32 or XFS
questions.explanation: The fs-type argument of mkpart sets the partition type and creates no filesystem, so blkid finds nothing on it. Note that mklabel also replaces any existing partition table.

questions.text: What does deleting a partition with fdisk actually do?
options: Securely overwrites all data in that area with zeros
Moves its data into the neighbouring partition first
Removes its entry from the partition table and marks the area as free
Converts the area into unformatted swap space
questions.explanation: Deletion only removes the table entry. Old data may still be on disk until it is overwritten, so it is not a secure erase, and you should back up anything you need first.

questions.text: To grow /dev/sdb1 with fdisk, you delete it and create a larger partition 1. fdisk then reports "Partition #1 contains a ext4 signature". What must you get right to keep the data?
options: Start the new partition at the next free sector and remove the signature
Choose a different partition number so the old one is not overwritten
Run mkfs.ext4 on the new partition before writing the table
Start it at exactly the same first sector and keep the signature
questions.explanation: The filesystem begins at the old start sector, so the new entry must start there and only end later. Removing the signature erases the ext4 magic, so the filesystem is no longer recognized. After w, run resize2fs.

questions.text: You need to shrink the ext4 filesystem on /dev/sda1 and its partition. In what order should you work?
options: Back up, unmount, shrink the filesystem with resize2fs, then shrink the partition
Shrink the partition with fdisk, then run resize2fs
Run resize2fs while mounted, then reboot
Delete the partition and run mkfs.ext4 with a smaller size
questions.explanation: The filesystem must already fit inside the smaller space before the partition is cut down; doing it the other way round destroys data. ext4 can only be shrunk unmounted. When growing, reverse the order.

questions.text: You enlarged the partition /dev/sda1 into free space. Which command makes its ext4 filesystem use the new space?
questions.explanation: Without a size argument, resize2fs grows the filesystem to fill its partition. mkfs.ext4 would erase the data, and tune2fs -l only prints superblock information.

questions.text: A partitioning tool reports "Partition in use" when you try to change /dev/sda1. What is the usual fix?
options: Unmount the partition and close programs using it
Run mkfs on the partition first
questions.explanation: A mounted partition cannot safely be resized or deleted. Unmount it with umount, or for system partitions work from a live USB.

questions.text:
What does the final 2 in this /etc/fstab line mean?

UUID=3f1c8a2e-5b7d-4c11-9e0a-2d6f8b1c4e77  /mnt/data  ext4  defaults  0  2
options: Wait two seconds after boot before mounting the filesystem
Keep two backup copies of the filesystem with dump
The filesystem is on the second partition of its disk
fsck checks it at boot after the root filesystem, which uses 1
questions.explanation: The sixth field is fs_passno: 1 for root, 2 for other filesystems, 0 for no check. The fifth field (0) is the old dump flag. Test new entries with sudo mount -a before rebooting.

questions.text: Why do /etc/fstab entries usually use UUID= instead of names like /dev/sdb1?
options: Names like /dev/sdb1 can change between boots, while the UUID stays the same
UUIDs let the kernel mount the filesystem faster at boot
Plain device names like /dev/sdb1 are rejected in /etc/fstab
The UUID entry makes the filesystem encrypted at rest
questions.explanation: The UUID is stored in the filesystem itself, so it identifies the same filesystem wherever the disk appears. Find it with blkid or lsblk -f.

questions.text: In what order are the three LVM layers built, from the disk upward?
options: Logical volume, volume group, physical volume
Physical volume, volume group, logical volume
Volume group, physical volume, logical volume
Physical volume, logical volume, volume group
questions.explanation: Disks or partitions become physical volumes, PVs are pooled into a volume group, and logical volumes are carved from the VG. A filesystem then goes on the LV.

questions.text: What is an LVM physical volume (PV)?
options: A logical volume that has been mounted
A snapshot of a volume group
A disk or partition initialized with pvcreate for use by LVM
The filesystem created on a logical volume
questions.explanation: A PV is a device such as /dev/sdb or /dev/sdc1 labeled for LVM. It is not mounted directly; it contributes its space to a volume group.

questions.text: What is an LVM volume group (VG)?
options: A group of users allowed to manage LVM
A storage pool made from one or more physical volumes
A single partition on one disk
A list of mounted logical volumes
questions.explanation: A VG combines the capacity of its PVs, so its size is roughly the sum of theirs minus a little metadata. Logical volumes are allocated from that pool.

questions.text: Which statement about an LVM logical volume (LV) is true?
options: It must be exactly the same size as one of the physical disks
It can only be used for swap, not for regular filesystems
It is a type of extended partition stored in the MBR
It can be formatted and mounted like a partition, and can span several disks in the VG
questions.explanation: An LV behaves like a partition to the rest of the system, but it is allocated from the VG's pool, so it can use space from several PVs and be resized later.

questions.text: You have two blank disks, /dev/sdb and /dev/sdc, and want to start building LVM on them. Which command comes first?
questions.explanation: The devices must be initialized as PVs before they can join a volume group with vgcreate. LVs come after the VG, and the filesystem goes on the LV, not on the raw disk.

questions.text: Which command adds the physical volume /dev/sdd to the existing volume group TEST?
questions.explanation: vgextend grows a VG by adding PVs. vgcreate would try to make a new group, and lvextend resizes logical volumes, not groups.

questions.text: Which command creates a 20 GiB logical volume named vol_name_1 in the volume group TEST?
questions.explanation: -L sets the size (LVM's G means GiB) and -n the name, followed by the VG. The new LV appears as /dev/TEST/vol_name_1.

questions.text: How are /dev/TEST/vol_name_1 and /dev/mapper/TEST-vol_name_1 related?
options: The first is the LV and the second is its snapshot
The first is a PV and the second is the VG
They are two names for the same logical volume
The second is a backup copy of the first
questions.explanation: Both point to the same device-mapper device. LVM documents /dev/VG/LV as the stable name for scripts, because the /dev/mapper format is meant for internal use and escapes some characters.

questions.text: An Ubuntu server shows the device /dev/mapper/ubuntu--vg-ubuntu--lv. What are the volume group and logical volume names?
questions.explanation: In /dev/mapper names a single hyphen separates VG from LV, and hyphens inside the names are doubled. dmsetup splitname decodes it, and /dev/ubuntu-vg/ubuntu-lv is the same device.

questions.text: What is the difference between lvextend -L +10G /dev/TEST/data and lvextend -L 10G /dev/TEST/data?
options: +10G also resizes the filesystem, while 10G does not
+10G uses a new disk, while 10G uses free space in the VG
+10G adds 10 GiB to the current size, while 10G sets the total size to 10 GiB
questions.explanation: A leading + is relative. Without it the value is the target size, which lvextend refuses if it is not larger than the current size. Filesystem resizing is controlled by -r.

questions.text: After sudo lvextend -L +10G /dev/TEST/vol_name_1, df -h still shows the old size. What is missing?
options: A reboot, so the kernel reloads the partition table
Running vgextend so the volume group grows too
Growing the filesystem, for example with resize2fs, or using lvextend -r
Recreating the filesystem with mkfs.ext4 at the new size
questions.explanation: lvextend enlarges only the block device. The filesystem on it must be grown too; -r does both steps in one command.

questions.text: A filesystem on an LV is 100% full and vgs shows VFree as 0. What must you do before you can extend the LV?
options: Add storage with pvcreate and vgextend, or free space in the VG
Run lvextend -r anyway, since it allocates space automatically
Create a snapshot of the LV
questions.explanation: An LV can only grow into free extents in its VG. When VFree is 0, add a new PV to the group or remove or shrink other LVs first.

questions.text:
In a VG with the default 4 MiB extent size, lvextend fails with the message below. About how much free space does the VG have?

Insufficient free space: 1280 extents needed, but only 129 available
questions.explanation: LVM allocates in physical extents, so the free space is $129 \times 4\ \text{MiB} = 516\ \text{MiB}$. The request needed $1280 \times 4\ \text{MiB} = 5\ \text{GiB}$, which is what -L +5G asks for.

questions.text: In pvs output, what does the PFree column show?
options: The size of the largest LV on that disk
The number of free partitions on the disk
The unallocated space remaining on that physical volume
questions.explanation: PSize is the PV's total size and PFree is how much of it no LV uses yet. The volume group equivalent in vgs is VFree.

questions.text: lvs shows the attribute string -wi-ao---- for the LV data. What does the o in the sixth position mean?
options: The LV is the origin of a snapshot and cannot be removed
The device is open, for example because its filesystem is mounted
The LV is owned by root and other users cannot open it
The LV is offline and must be activated before use
questions.explanation: In lv_attr, position 5 a means active and position 6 o means open. An origin LV is shown by an o in the first position instead, as in owi-a-s---.

questions.text: What is the correct order for safely shrinking an ext4 filesystem on a logical volume?
options: Unmount, e2fsck -f, resize2fs to the new size, then lvreduce
resize2fs, then lvreduce, both while mounted
questions.explanation: The filesystem must be checked and shrunk to fit before the LV is reduced; reducing the LV first cuts off data. lvreduce -r performs the filesystem step for you. Back up beforehand.

questions.text: Why can't you shrink a logical volume that holds an XFS filesystem in the usual way?
options: XFS can be grown, and only while mounted, but has no general way to shrink
XFS cannot be placed on LVM logical volumes at all
XFS becomes read-only once it has been created
XFS must be shrunk with vgreduce instead of lvreduce
questions.explanation: xfs_growfs enlarges a mounted XFS filesystem, but XFS offers no normal shrink operation. To get a smaller XFS volume you back up, recreate the filesystem and restore.

questions.text: What happens to the space of a logical volume after lvremove /dev/TEST/vol_name_1?
options: It is lost until the disk is repartitioned
It returns to the volume group as free space
It is moved to a snapshot automatically
It becomes a new physical volume
questions.explanation: Removing an LV frees its extents in the VG, which vgs shows as VFree. Unmount the LV first, and remember its data is gone.

questions.text: You want to take the disk /dev/sdb out of the volume group TEST while its LVs stay online. Which sequence works, assuming the other PVs have enough free space?
questions.explanation: pvmove relocates the allocated extents to other PVs in the VG while the LVs stay in use. Only an empty PV can be removed with vgreduce, after which pvremove can wipe its label.

questions.text: You are dismantling a lab LVM setup with one LV on one VG. In what order do you remove the pieces after unmounting?
questions.explanation: Teardown reverses creation: remove the LVs, then the now-empty VG, then the LVM labels on the PVs. pvremove normally refuses a PV that still belongs to a VG.

questions.text: How does an LVM snapshot preserve the original state of a logical volume?
options: It copies the whole LV when the snapshot is created
It uses copy-on-write, keeping old blocks only as they change on the origin
It compresses the origin LV into a file
It mirrors all writes to a second disk
questions.explanation: A new snapshot is nearly empty. When a block on the origin is about to change, the old block is saved into the snapshot, so it only needs space for changed data.

questions.text: Which command creates a 1 GiB snapshot named snap1 of /dev/TEST/vol_name_1?
questions.explanation: lvcreate -s makes a snapshot of the origin LV, with -L reserving space for changed blocks. lvconvert --merge is used later to roll back to a snapshot.

questions.text: In lvs output, a snapshot's Data% reaches 100%. What does that mean?
options: The snapshot has been merged automatically
The snapshot ran out of space and is no longer valid
The snapshot is ready to be mounted
questions.explanation: Once the snapshot's space is used up by changed blocks, it can no longer represent the earlier state and is marked invalid (I in its attributes). The origin LV keeps working.

questions.text: A snapshot you still need shows Data% at 85% and the origin keeps changing. What should you do?
options: Run lvreduce on the origin to slow down changes
Nothing, LVM deletes old blocks from the snapshot when it fills
Give it more COW space with lvextend -L +1G on the snapshot LV
questions.explanation: Extending a copy-on-write snapshot adds room for changed blocks, and automatic extension can be configured. Size snapshots for the writes you expect and remove them when done.

questions.text: To test snapshot exhaustion, you run fallocate -l 200M bigfile on the ext4 origin of a 50 MiB snapshot, but the snapshot's Data% barely moves. Why?
options: fallocate reserves blocks as unwritten extents without writing data, so few origin blocks change
Snapshots only record changes to files that existed when the snapshot was created
ext4 writes new files into the snapshot instead of the origin
Data% is only updated after the origin is unmounted
questions.explanation: A COW snapshot fills only when blocks on the origin are overwritten. fallocate updates a little metadata; writing real data, for example with dd if=/dev/urandom ... conv=fsync, fills the snapshot.

questions.text: A risky upgrade broke the data on /dev/TEST/vol_name_1, which has the snapshot snap1. Which command rolls the LV back to the snapshot?
questions.explanation: Merging writes the snapshot's preserved state back into the origin and then removes the snapshot. If the origin or snapshot is open, the merge waits until both are closed and the LV is next activated, so unmount first.

questions.text: Why are LVM snapshots not a replacement for real backups?
options: Snapshots cannot be mounted, so files cannot be restored
Snapshots are deleted automatically at every reboot
Snapshots only store file names and metadata, not data
Snapshots live in the same VG as the origin, so a disk failure can destroy both
questions.explanation: A snapshot depends on the origin LV and sits in the same volume group. Keep separate backups on other storage for disaster recovery.

questions.text: After booting a rescue system, lvs lists your logical volumes but they cannot be mounted because they are inactive. Which command activates them?
questions.explanation: vgchange -ay activates all logical volumes in all volume groups, creating their device nodes. Check with lsblk afterwards, then mount them.

questions.text: Why must you be careful running pvcreate /dev/sdb?
options: It immediately mounts the disk under /dev/mapper
It overwrites the start of the disk, wiping its partition table or filesystem
It removes the disk from every volume group it belongs to
It renames the disk's device node to an LVM name
questions.explanation: pvcreate initializes the device for LVM, overwriting what was at its start; -f or -y suppress its confirmation prompts. Confirm the device with lsblk before running it.

questions.text: In a typical Linux server layout that uses LVM, which part is usually kept as a plain partition rather than a logical volume?
questions.explanation: Firmware must read the EFI system partition (and often /boot) directly, without LVM support, so they stay plain partitions. /, /home and /var benefit from LVM's resizing.

questions.text: Which command prints a one-time snapshot of every process on the system, with user, PID, CPU and memory columns?
questions.explanation: ps aux lists all processes for all users with %CPU, %MEM, STAT and the command. Plain ps shows only processes on the current terminal, top is a live view, and jobs lists only the current shell's jobs.

questions.text: Which ps option selects every process on the system in standard (UNIX) syntax, as in ps -ef?
questions.explanation: -e (same as -A) selects all processes, and -f adds full-format columns such as UID, PPID and start time. -a omits session leaders and processes without a terminal, -u filters by user and -p by PID.

questions.text: Which command lists only the processes owned by the user alice?
questions.explanation: ps -u alice selects processes by effective user. pgrep -u alice gives just their PIDs. -p expects PIDs, not user names.

questions.text: Which command prints only the parent PID of process 1234, with no header line?
questions.explanation: -o ppid= selects the PPID column and the trailing = removes its header; -p 1234 picks the process. pgrep -P 1234 does the reverse: it lists the children of 1234.

questions.text: Which command shows processes as a tree, making parent-child relationships easy to see?
questions.explanation: pstree draws the process hierarchy, and -p adds PIDs. ps fax gives a similar ASCII-art tree. ps aux and pgrep -l print flat lists.

questions.text: Which command prints the PIDs and names of all running processes called nginx?
questions.explanation: pgrep matches process names and prints PIDs; -l adds the name. Add -f to match against the full command line, -u user to filter by owner, or -n for the newest match.

questions.text: On Linux, pgrep systemd-journald prints a warning and finds nothing, although the daemon is running. Why?
options: pgrep matches the process name, which the kernel cuts to 15 characters (systemd-journal)
pgrep only lists processes owned by the current user unless you add -u root
pgrep needs the full path, such as /usr/lib/systemd/systemd-journald
pgrep skips daemons that have no controlling terminal
questions.explanation: By default pgrep compares against the short comm name, at most 15 characters. Use pgrep -f systemd-journald to match the full command line, or pgrep -x systemd-journal for the exact short name.

questions.text: Why does ps -ef | grep firefox often include an extra line that is not Firefox?
options: ps lists each Firefox thread as a separate process
ps -ef prints a header line containing the search term
The grep firefox process itself matches the pattern
Firefox starts a watchdog process with the same name
questions.explanation: The grep process's own command line contains firefox, so it matches. Use grep '[f]irefox', add grep -v grep, or switch to pgrep firefox.

questions.text: Which command writes a single, non-interactive top snapshot that you can redirect into a log file?
questions.explanation: -b (batch mode) prints plain text instead of redrawing the screen, and -n 1 stops after one update. -d sets the refresh delay, -p watches chosen PIDs and -H shows threads; on their own, all three stay interactive.

questions.text: While top is running, which key sorts the process list by memory usage?
questions.explanation: M sorts by %MEM and P sorts by %CPU. k prompts for a PID to signal, and r renices a process.

questions.text: In htop, what is the difference between pressing F4 and F3?
options: F4 kills the selected process and F3 stops it
F4 sorts by memory and F3 sorts by CPU
F4 filters out non-matching rows and F3 searches while keeping every row
F4 shows threads and F3 hides them
questions.explanation: F4 (Filter) hides processes that do not match the typed text, and F3 (Search) jumps to matches without hiding anything else. F9 sends a signal and F6 changes the sort column.

questions.text: What is PID 1 on a systemd-based distribution?
options: The kernel's scheduler, running as a special thread
systemd, the first user-space process, which starts services and adopts orphans
The login shell of the first user who logs in
kthreadd, the parent of every process on the system
questions.explanation: The kernel starts PID 1 (systemd or init), which brings up the user-space service tree and normally adopts orphaned processes. Kernel threads descend from kthreadd (PID 2), not from PID 1.

questions.text: A parent process exits while its child keeps running. What becomes the child's parent?
options: PID 1, or the nearest ancestor registered as a child subreaper, such as systemd --user
Nobody: the child's PPID is set to 0 until the child exits
Nothing changes, because the child is killed together with its parent
The child turns into a zombie until a new parent calls wait()
questions.explanation: Orphans are re-parented, normally to PID 1. In a desktop session they often go to systemd --user, which registers as a child subreaper, so ps can show an orphan's PPID as something other than 1.

questions.text:
How many hi lines does this program print, assuming both fork() calls succeed?

#include <stdio.h>
#include <sys/wait.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int main(void) {
  fork();
  fork();
  printf("hi\n");
  while (wait(NULL) > 0) {}
  return 0;
}
questions.explanation: Each fork() duplicates every process that reaches it, so 1 process becomes 2, then 4, and each prints once. fork() returns 0 in the child and the child's PID in the parent, which is how code tells them apart.

questions.text: A child process calls execl("/bin/ls", "ls", (char *)NULL) and it succeeds. What happens to the child's PID?
options: It stays the same, because exec replaces the program in the same process
The kernel assigns a new PID for ls
It becomes 1, because exec re-parents the process to init
questions.explanation: The exec family loads a new program image into the existing process; no new process is created. That is why shells use fork() first, then exec in the child.

questions.text: In Bash, which command normally runs without the shell creating a new process?
questions.explanation: echo is a Bash builtin, so the shell runs it itself; type echo reports echo is a shell builtin. External programs such as /bin/echo, ls and sleep need a fork() followed by an exec in the child.

questions.text: What is the main difference between a process and a thread?
options: Threads always run on a different CPU core from their process
A process can contain only one thread at a time
Threads have their own PIDs and memory, while processes share memory
Each process has its own address space, while threads in one process share memory
questions.explanation: Threads of one process share the same memory and open files but have separate stacks and registers. ps -eLo pid,tid,stat,comm lists threads with their thread IDs (TID).

questions.text: Which command sends SIGTERM, asking process 1234 to shut down cleanly?
questions.explanation: kill sends SIGTERM (15) by default, which a program may catch to clean up. -9 is SIGKILL and -STOP pauses the process. Signal 0 sends nothing: it only tests whether the PID exists and you may signal it.

questions.text: Which signal cannot be caught, blocked or ignored, so the program gets no chance to clean up before it dies?
questions.explanation: The kernel handles SIGKILL (9) itself, so no handler or cleanup code runs. Use it only after SIGTERM fails. SIGSTOP is likewise uncatchable, but it pauses the process instead of killing it.

questions.text: What happens when you press Ctrl+C while a command runs in the foreground?
options: The terminal sends SIGKILL to the command
The terminal sends SIGINT to the foreground process group
The shell sends SIGTSTP and parks the job
The terminal sends SIGHUP and closes the session
questions.explanation: Ctrl+C generates SIGINT (2) for every process in the foreground group, so both sides of sleep 9 | sleep 9 get it. Programs may catch it. Ctrl+Z generates SIGTSTP, which stops the job instead.

questions.text: Which command terminates every process named firefox without looking up PIDs first?
questions.explanation: pkill matches processes by name (like pgrep) and sends them a signal, SIGTERM by default. kill expects PIDs or job specs such as %1, not names.

questions.text: How can you pause process 1234 and later let it continue from where it stopped?
questions.explanation: kill -STOP 1234 freezes the process (state T), and kill -CONT 1234 resumes it. SIGSTOP cannot be caught or ignored. A killed process cannot be continued.

questions.text:
You run these commands in an interactive Bash shell. What does the last one print?

sleep 600 &
kill -STOP $!
kill $!
ps -o stat= -p $!
options: T, because the SIGTERM stays pending until the process is continued
Z, because the process was killed but not yet reaped
Nothing, because the process has already exited
S, because SIGTERM resumed the stopped process
questions.explanation: A stopped process does not act on most signals until it gets SIGCONT; only SIGKILL ends it straight away. Bash's kill %1 avoids this trap by also sending SIGCONT to a stopped job.

questions.text: Many daemons, such as nginx, do what when they receive SIGHUP?
options: Reload their configuration files without a full restart
Dump their memory to a core file
questions.explanation: SIGHUP originally meant "terminal hung up", and its default action is to terminate. Many daemons have no terminal, so they catch it and treat it as a request to reload configuration.

questions.text: What does kill -s TERM -- -2345 do?
options: Sends SIGTERM to the process with PID 2345
Sends SIGTERM to every process in process group 2345
Sends SIGTERM to every process the user may signal
Sends SIGTERM to process 2345 and its parent
questions.explanation: A negative target (other than -1) means a process group, and -- stops kill from reading -2345 as an option. Target -1 means all processes you may signal, and 0 means your own process group.

questions.text: How do you start ./backup.sh so that it runs in the background and you get the prompt back immediately?
questions.explanation: A trailing & starts the command as a background job and prints its job number and PID, such as [1] 3241. bg resumes an existing stopped job, and nohup alone still runs the command in the foreground.

questions.text: You press Ctrl+Z while long_task.sh runs in the foreground. What state is the job in afterwards?
options: Stopped, until you resume it with fg or bg
Terminated, with its exit status saved
Still running in the foreground, but with output hidden
questions.explanation: Ctrl+Z sends SIGTSTP, which stops (pauses) the job and returns the prompt. bg resumes it in the background and fg brings it back to the foreground.

questions.text: Which command brings job number 2 back to the foreground?
questions.explanation: %2 is a job spec for job 2 in this shell. bg %2 resumes it in the background instead, and kill -CONT 2 would target PID 2, not job 2.

questions.text:
In this Bash jobs -l output, what does the + after [2] mean?

[1]- 3241 Running                 sleep 1000 &
[2]+ 3250 Stopped                 vi notes.txt
options: Job 2 is the current job, used by fg and bg when no job is named
Job 2 has a higher scheduling priority
Job 2 has finished and is waiting to be cleared
questions.explanation: + marks the current job and - the previous one. Bash prefers a stopped job as the current job, so plain fg here resumes vi, while fg %- would bring back sleep.

questions.text: In a script, what does the wait builtin do?
options: Sleeps for a fixed number of seconds
Waits for the user to press Enter
Blocks until the script's background child processes have finished
Suspends the script until it receives SIGCONT
questions.explanation: wait with no arguments waits for all background children; wait PID waits for one and returns its exit status. Pausing for a duration is sleep.

questions.text: You start ./long_job.sh & over SSH, and the job dies when you log out. Which change keeps it running after logout?
questions.explanation: When the session hangs up, Bash sends SIGHUP to its jobs. nohup makes the command ignore SIGHUP; redirecting alone does not, it only avoids writing to a closed terminal. For critical work, a service manager, tmux or screen is better.

questions.text: A long job is already running as background job %1 in your SSH session. How do you keep it alive after logout without restarting it?
questions.explanation: disown removes the job from the shell's job table, so Bash does not pass SIGHUP on to it when the session hangs up. nohup only works when starting a command, and bg and SIGCONT merely resume a stopped job.

questions.text: What range of nice values does Linux use, and which end gets the most CPU time?
questions.explanation: Lower nice values mean higher priority, so -20 is the least "nice" to other processes. The default is 0, and ordinary users may only raise a value (lower the priority).

questions.text: Which command starts make with lower CPU priority so it does not slow down interactive work?
questions.explanation: nice -n 10 starts a new command with niceness 10, which is lower priority. A negative value raises priority and needs root. renice changes an already-running process and takes a PID, not a command.

questions.text: Which command changes the priority of the running process 4321 to niceness 5?
questions.explanation: renice adjusts existing processes by PID (-p), group or user. nice only launches new commands, so nice -n 5 4321 would try to run a program called 4321.

questions.text: As an ordinary user, you ran renice -n 5 -p 4321 on your own process. Now renice -n 2 -p 4321 fails with Permission denied. Why?
options: Ordinary users may only set nice values above 10
The process must be stopped before its priority can change again
renice needs -g instead of -p for processes you own
Lowering niceness raises priority, which needs CAP_SYS_NICE
questions.explanation: Unprivileged users can make their own processes nicer but cannot take that back, unless RLIMIT_NICE allows it. The first command raised niceness from 0 to 5, which is always allowed; going back to 2 is a priority increase.

questions.text: What is a zombie process (state Z)?
options: A process stuck in uninterruptible disk I/O
A process that has been stopped with SIGSTOP
A process whose parent died and that was adopted by PID 1
A child that has exited but whose parent has not yet collected its exit status
questions.explanation: A zombie has finished running and holds only a process-table entry until its parent calls wait(). Waiting on disk I/O is state D, stopped is T, and an adopted process is an orphan, not a zombie.

questions.text: ps keeps showing a zombie child of PID 800, even after kill -9 on the zombie. What actually removes it?
options: Sending SIGKILL again, in case the first one was lost
Sending SIGCONT, so the zombie can finish exiting
Having PID 800 reap it with wait(), or ending PID 800 so PID 1 adopts and reaps it
Running renice -n 19, so the scheduler drops its entry
questions.explanation: A zombie has already exited, so there is nothing left for a signal to kill. Only reaping removes the entry: fix or restart the parent, and if the parent dies, PID 1 (or a subreaper) adopts and reaps the zombie.

questions.text: Many processes sit in state D for a long time while vmstat shows high wa. What does this suggest?
options: A CPU bottleneck from compute-heavy threads
A parent process that is not reaping its children
Processes that were stopped with Ctrl+Z
An I/O bottleneck, such as a slow disk or a stuck network filesystem
questions.explanation: D is uninterruptible sleep, usually waiting on kernel I/O, and such tasks often cannot be killed until the I/O finishes. Many R tasks point to CPU pressure, many Z to a broken parent, and T to stopped jobs.

questions.text: In ps -eo pid,stat,comm output, what does a STAT value of S mean?
options: The process is stopped and must be resumed with SIGCONT
The process is a session leader and is currently running
The process is swapped out to disk
The process is in interruptible sleep, waiting for an event such as input or a timer
questions.explanation: S means interruptible sleep, which is normal for most processes most of the time. A trailing s (as in Ss) marks a session leader, + the foreground group, and l a multi-threaded process.

questions.text: In ps -o pid,stat,comm output, one process shows STAT T and another shows t. What is the difference?
options: T is stopped by job control or SIGSTOP; t is stopped by a tracer such as gdb
T is terminating; t has terminated and is waiting to be reaped
T is a multi-threaded process; t is one of its threads
T was stopped by root; t was stopped by an ordinary user
questions.explanation: Neither runs. T resumes on SIGCONT, for example from fg or bg, while t is a ptrace stop that the debugger controls. Exited processes that have not been reaped show Z.

questions.text: Which command shows the state, parent PID and thread count of process 1234 as labelled lines such as State: and Threads:?
questions.explanation: /proc/PID/status is human-readable, with State:, PPid: and Threads: lines. /proc/PID/stat holds similar data as unlabelled fields (the state is the third), cmdline holds the arguments, and task/ has one directory per thread.

questions.text: Which command shows the 1-, 5- and 15-minute load averages, along with uptime and logged-in user count?
questions.explanation: uptime prints a line such as up 1 day, 2 users, load average: 0.42, 0.35, 0.30. The same figures appear in the first line of top.

questions.text: A 4-core server shows a load average of 6.80, 4.10, 2.30, but CPU usage is low and vmstat shows high b and wa. What is driving the load?
options: Too much free memory being cached
Zombie processes using up CPU time
Tasks blocked on I/O, which Linux also counts in the load average
questions.explanation: Linux load counts runnable tasks and tasks in uninterruptible (D) sleep, so I/O waits raise it even when the CPU is idle. High b (blocked) and wa (I/O wait) confirm the cause. Zombies use no CPU.

questions.text: A 4-core server shows a load average of 8.10, 7.90, 7.50, and vmstat 1 shows r near 8, b 0, us 95, id 0 and wa 0. What is the likely bottleneck?
options: CPU saturation: about twice as many runnable tasks as cores
Disk I/O, because a load above the core count always means I/O wait
Memory, because the system must be swapping heavily
Zombie processes filling up the process table
questions.explanation: r counts tasks running or waiting for a CPU, so 8 runnable tasks on 4 cores with no idle time and no I/O wait means CPU saturation. High b and wa would point to I/O instead.

questions.text: In ps -ef output, systemd-journald and cron show ? in the TTY column. What does that tell you?
options: Their terminal was closed and they are about to exit
They have no controlling terminal, as is typical for daemons
ps lacks permission to read their terminal
They are kernel threads rather than user-space processes
questions.explanation: Daemons are background services, usually started by a service manager such as systemd, and are not attached to any terminal, so ps shows ?. Kernel threads show ? too, but their names appear in brackets, like [kthreadd].

questions.text: Which command lists every thread of every process, with a thread ID column?
questions.explanation: -L shows one row per thread, and tid is the thread ID. Threads of one process share its PID but have their own TIDs and states, which helps spot the one thread using CPU.

questions.text: In a shell with background jobs, what is the difference between kill %1 and kill 1?
options: They are the same; % is optional
kill %1 sends SIGKILL, while kill 1 sends SIGTERM
%1 means job 1 of this shell; 1 means the process with PID 1
kill %1 signals the first process listed by ps
questions.explanation: %N is a job spec that the shell translates into the job's processes. A plain number is a PID, and PID 1 is systemd or init, which an ordinary user's kill fails on with Operation not permitted.

questions.text: In ps aux, a Java process shows VSZ 4096000 and RSS 1210000 (both in KiB). Which statement is correct?
options: It is using about 4 GB of physical RAM right now
About 1.2 GB is in RAM; VSZ is the whole virtual address space
RSS counts the process's swap usage, and VSZ counts its physical RAM
The two values only differ when the process uses shared libraries
questions.explanation: RSS is the resident set in physical RAM. VSZ also counts mapped but untouched, swapped-out and reserved memory. RSS includes shared pages, so summing it over many processes overcounts total RAM use.

questions.text:
free -h shows the output below. About how much memory can new programs get without swapping?

               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:            15Gi       5.4Gi       410Mi       300Mi       9.2Gi       8.9Gi
Swap:          2.0Gi          0B       2.0Gi
options: About 410 MiB, since only free memory can be handed out
About 9.2 GiB, since buff/cache is memory reserved for programs
About 2.0 GiB, since new programs are placed in free swap first
About 8.9 GiB, the available estimate, since most of the cache can be reclaimed
questions.explanation: Linux uses spare RAM for the page cache and gives it back on demand. available estimates what new programs can use without swapping, so a low free figure alone is normal, not a sign of memory pressure.

questions.text: vmstat 1 keeps showing large non-zero si and so values, high wa, and the system feels frozen. What is happening?
options: Swap thrashing: memory is short, so pages keep moving between RAM and swap
The CPU is overheating and the kernel is throttling it
Network sockets are being opened and closed very rapidly
The disk is nearly full, so the kernel keeps retrying writes
questions.explanation: si and so are memory swapped in from and out to disk per second. Some swap use is harmless, but continuous swapping both ways means the working set does not fit in RAM; check free -h and the top %MEM processes.

questions.text: A file has mode -rw-r--r--, yet nginx running in the httpd_t domain gets "Permission denied" reading it on an enforcing SELinux system. Which statement explains this?
options: SELinux overrides the file mode, so the Unix permissions are ignored once SELinux is enforcing
The file mode only applies to root, while SELinux rules apply to service accounts
Access needs both the normal permissions (DAC) and the SELinux policy (MAC) to allow it
SELinux denies every read until the file owner grants access with chmod
questions.explanation: SELinux adds Mandatory Access Control on top of Discretionary Access Control; it does not replace it. A request succeeds only if DAC allows it and the policy allows the process domain to access the object's type.

questions.text:
In the context below, which field is the SELinux type?

system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0
questions.explanation: A context is user:role:type:level, so the third field is the type. system_u is the SELinux user, object_r the role used for files and s0 the MLS/MCS level. Everyday troubleshooting focuses on the type.

questions.text: Under the targeted policy, what does type enforcement mainly compare when httpd tries to read a file?
options: The domain of the process with the type of the file, against the loaded policy rules
The Linux user ID of the process with the file's owner and group
The full path of the file with a list of paths allowed for httpd
The SELinux user field of the process with the SELinux user field of the file
questions.explanation: Policy rules have the form "domain X may do Y to type Z", such as httpd_t reading httpd_sys_content_t. Paths matter only because they decide which label a file gets; UIDs are the separate DAC check.

questions.text: On an SELinux-enabled system, what does ls -Z /var/www/html/index.html print?
options: The long listing of the file plus a column naming the process allowed to open it
The file's security context followed by its name, without mode, owner or size
Only the type field of the context, such as httpd_sys_content_t
The extended ACL entries of the file, in the same format as getfacl
questions.explanation: With GNU ls, -Z prints the context (for example system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0) before the name. Combine it with -l (ls -lZ) to see mode, owner and size as well; add -d for a directory itself.

questions.text: Which command shows which SELinux domain the running sshd processes are in?
questions.explanation: ps -Z adds a LABEL column with each process's context, such as system_u:system_r:sshd_t:s0-s0:c0.c1023. ls -Z shows the label of the executable file, which is not the same as the domain of the running process.

questions.text: What happens to an action that the policy would deny while SELinux is in permissive mode?
options: It is blocked, but no AVC message is written to the audit log
It is blocked and logged, exactly as in enforcing mode
It is allowed and nothing is logged, as if SELinux were disabled
It is allowed, and an AVC denial is logged as if it had been blocked
questions.explanation: Permissive mode keeps SELinux and its policy loaded but only audits violations. That makes it useful for diagnosis. In disabled mode no policy is loaded and no denials are logged.

questions.text:
An AVC record ends with permissive=1. What does that tell you?

avc:  denied  { read } for  pid=1234 comm="nginx" path="/srv/mywebsite/index.html" scontext=system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0 tcontext=unconfined_u:object_r:default_t:s0 tclass=file permissive=1
options: The read was logged as a denial but was actually allowed to proceed
The read was blocked, and SELinux will allow it next time it is attempted
The file is labeled with a permissive type that any domain may read
The AVC message was generated by audit2allow rather than by the kernel
questions.explanation: permissive=1 means the check failed but was not enforced, because the system or that domain was permissive. In enforcing mode the same record shows permissive=0 and the read fails.

questions.text: getenforce prints Disabled. What happens if you run sudo setenforce 1?
options: SELinux is loaded immediately and starts enforcing until the next reboot
It fails; SELinux has to be enabled in the boot configuration and the system rebooted
SELinux switches to permissive mode first and then to enforcing after a relabel
The setting is written to /etc/selinux/config and takes effect at the next login
questions.explanation: setenforce only switches an enabled SELinux between enforcing and permissive. To enable a disabled SELinux you change the boot configuration (/etc/selinux/config, kernel parameters) and reboot, usually with a relabel.

questions.text:
sestatus shows the lines below. What mode will SELinux be in after the next reboot, assuming nothing else changes?

SELinux status:                 enabled
Current mode:                   permissive
Mode from config file:          enforcing
Policy name:                    targeted
options: Permissive, because the current mode is saved at shutdown
Disabled, because the running mode and the config file disagree
Enforcing, because the mode in /etc/selinux/config applies at boot
questions.explanation: Someone ran setenforce 0, which lasts only until reboot. At boot the SELINUX= value in /etc/selinux/config is used, here enforcing. To make permissive permanent you would edit that file.

questions.text: SELinux was disabled for months and is now being re-enabled. Why do administrators usually run touch /.autorelabel before rebooting?
options: It tells the kernel to load the targeted policy instead of the MLS policy
It resets all SELinux booleans to their default values during boot
Files created while SELinux was off have no labels, so the boot relabels them from policy
It switches SELinux to permissive mode for one boot so services can start
questions.explanation: With SELinux disabled, new and changed files do not get labels. The /.autorelabel flag makes the boot process relabel the file systems according to policy, which can take a while on large disks.

questions.text:
Under the Fedora targeted policy, files under /srv/mywebsite have type var_t, which httpd_t cannot read. You run the commands below. What type does index.html have afterwards?

sudo chcon -R -t httpd_sys_content_t /srv/mywebsite
sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/mywebsite
options: var_t, because restorecon applies the policy's default label for that path
httpd_sys_content_t, because chcon stores the new label as a permanent rule
httpd_sys_content_t, because restorecon only changes files that have no label
default_t, because restorecon removes custom labels and leaves the generic type
questions.explanation: chcon writes a label to the file but adds no file-context rule. restorecon relabels from the rules, and the rule for /srv/.* says var_t, so the change is undone. That is why chcon is for testing only.

questions.text: Which pair of commands permanently labels a custom web root /srv/mywebsite so that the label survives restorecon and full relabels?
options: restorecon -Rv /srv/mywebsite then semanage fcontext -l | grep mywebsite
questions.explanation: semanage fcontext -a adds a local file-context rule and restorecon applies it to existing files. A later relabel uses the same rule. httpd_sys_content_t is a type, not a boolean.

questions.text: You add a rule with semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/mywebsite(/.*)?", but ls -Z /srv/mywebsite/index.html still shows var_t. Why?
options: The rule only applies to files created after the next reboot
semanage fcontext changes the labeling rules, not existing files; run restorecon to apply them
The rule needs setenforce 1 before the kernel will read it
ls -Z caches labels, so the new type appears only after ls --clear-cache
questions.explanation: The rule is stored in the policy's local file contexts. Files keep their existing labels until something relabels them, usually restorecon -Rv /srv/mywebsite. New files may still inherit the parent directory's label.

questions.text: What does the path expression "/srv/mywebsite(/.*)?" match in a semanage fcontext rule?
options: Only files directly inside /srv/mywebsite, not the directory itself
Only the directory /srv/mywebsite, not anything inside it
Any path containing the word mywebsite anywhere on the system
The directory /srv/mywebsite itself and everything below it
questions.explanation: File-context specs are regular expressions anchored to the whole path. (/.*)? optionally matches a slash followed by anything, so the rule covers the directory and all of its contents. Quote it so the shell does not expand it.

questions.text: A file has context unconfined_u:object_r:var_t:s0, and the matching file-context rule says system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0. What context does the file have after restorecon -v (without -F)?
questions.explanation: According to restorecon(8), a file that already has a context only has its type changed. -F forces the user, role and range to be reset as well. The SELinux user rarely matters in the targeted policy.

questions.text:
semanage boolean -l shows the line below. What happens to the boolean at the next reboot?

httpd_can_network_connect      (on   ,  off)  Allow httpd to can network connect
options: It goes back to off, because it was turned on with setsebool without -P
It stays on, because semanage only lists booleans that were set with -P
It stays on until the next policy update, and then it is reset to off
It goes back to off only if SELinux is switched to permissive mode
questions.explanation: The columns are the current state and the persistent default. setsebool name on changes only the running value; setsebool -P name on also writes it to the policy on disk so it survives reboots.

questions.text: A PHP application behind Apache must open TCP connections to an API server on another host. The firewall allows it, but ausearch shows denied { name_connect } for httpd_t. What is the usual fix?
options: setenforce 0 in the Apache unit's ExecStartPre= line
questions.explanation: name_connect is an outgoing connection, and the targeted policy gates it for httpd_t with the httpd_can_network_connect boolean. Labeling a port http_port_t controls which ports httpd may listen on (name_bind), not where it may connect.

questions.text: You move nginx to listen on TCP 8085. It fails to start and the audit log shows denied { name_bind } ... src=8085. Assuming 8085 has no SELinux port type yet, which command fixes it?
questions.explanation: name_bind is the right to listen on a port, and httpd_t may bind to ports of type http_port_t. semanage port -a labels the port; if it already has another type, use -m instead. Check with semanage port -l | grep http_port_t.

questions.text:
In the AVC denial below, what was blocked?

type=AVC msg=audit(1609459200.123:456): avc:  denied  { read } for  pid=1234 comm="nginx" name="index.html" scontext=system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0 tcontext=unconfined_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0 tclass=file
options: A process in the user_home_t domain tried to read a file labeled httpd_t
The user nginx tried to read a file owned by unconfined_u
A process in httpd_t tried to read a directory called index.html
A process in httpd_t tried to read a file labeled user_home_t
questions.explanation: scontext is the source (the process), tcontext the target object and tclass its class. Here the web server domain was denied read on a regular file with a home-directory type, which suggests content copied or moved from a home directory.

questions.text: What time range does ausearch -m avc -ts recent search?
options: Only the most recent single AVC event
questions.explanation: In ausearch(8), recent means 10 minutes ago, today means since midnight and boot means since the last boot. -m avc limits the search to AVC records; add -c nginx to filter by command name.

questions.text: What does piping AVC records into audit2why give you?
options: A reason for each denial, such as a missing allow rule or a boolean that is off
A compiled policy module that allows the denied accesses from then on
A list of the files with wrong labels, which it then relabels automatically
The list of booleans that setsebool -P changed since the last boot
questions.explanation: audit2why (the same as audit2allow -w) translates denials into reasons, for example a missing type enforcement rule or a boolean that would allow the access. It changes nothing; you still choose the fix.

questions.text:
httpd_t is denied reading files under /srv/mywebsite labeled var_t. audit2allow suggests the rule below. Why is installing it a bad fix?

allow httpd_t var_t:file read;
options: Generated rules apply only in permissive mode, so the denial would come back
It lets the web server read every var_t file on the system, when the real fault is a wrong label
semodule refuses modules created by audit2allow unless they are signed
The rule only lasts until the next reboot, like setsebool without -P
questions.explanation: audit2allow generates rules that would have permitted the logged accesses, often far more broadly than needed. Here the right fix is to label the content httpd_sys_content_t. Check labels, booleans and port types before writing custom policy.

questions.text: After reviewing the output, you run ausearch -m avc -c myapp | audit2allow -M myapp_local. What do you have to do next for the rules to take effect?
options: Nothing; audit2allow -M loads the module into the kernel immediately
Run restorecon -Rv / so the new rules are applied to every file
Reboot, because policy modules are only read at boot
Install the generated package with semodule -i myapp_local.pp
questions.explanation: -M writes a type enforcement source file (myapp_local.te) and a compiled package (myapp_local.pp) but does not load it. Read the .te file first, then load the package with semodule -i.

questions.text: With the targeted policy, which processes are confined in their own SELinux domains?
options: Every process, including users' login shells, under strict per-user rules
Only processes started by root; processes of regular users run unrestricted
Selected services such as httpd, sshd and named, while most user processes run unconfined
Only processes inside containers; host processes are never confined
questions.explanation: The targeted policy, the default on Fedora and RHEL, confines chosen services and leaves ordinary user sessions in unconfined domains. The MLS policy confines far more and is harder to administer.

questions.text: A colleague's fix for every SELinux problem is SELINUX=disabled. What is the better first step when a service gets "Permission denied"?
options: Run chcon -R -t unconfined_t / so that all files are readable by every domain
Check the AVC denial, then fix the label, boolean or port type it points to
Reinstall the selinux-policy-targeted package to reset the policy
Set the service's domain to permissive permanently in /etc/selinux/config
questions.explanation: Most denials come from wrong file labels, a boolean that is off or an unlabeled port, and each has a narrow fix. Disabling SELinux removes the protection for every service. Permissive mode is for short-term diagnosis only.

questions.text: Where does SELinux write AVC denials when auditd is running?
questions.explanation: With auditd running, AVC records go to /var/log/audit/audit.log, which ausearch, audit2why and sealert read. Without auditd, they go to the kernel log, so look in dmesg or the journal.

questions.text: What is the key difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
options: Symmetric uses one shared secret key; asymmetric uses a public and a private key
Symmetric is used for files only; asymmetric is used for network traffic only
Symmetric needs no key at all; asymmetric needs a password to be shared first
Symmetric is always more secure than asymmetric, but it is much slower
questions.explanation: With symmetric ciphers such as AES, both sides must already share the secret. Asymmetric schemes let anyone encrypt to a published public key that only the private key can decrypt. Symmetric ciphers are usually much faster.

questions.text: A colleague wants to "decrypt" a SHA-256 value back into the original file. What is wrong with that idea?
options: SHA-256 can only be decrypted with the private key that created it
SHA-256 output can be reversed only by the root user
A hash is a one-way fixed-length digest, not encryption, so there is no key to reverse it
SHA-256 is symmetric encryption, so the same password is needed to reverse it
questions.explanation: Hash functions map any input to a fixed-size digest and are designed so the input cannot be recovered from it. They are used to check integrity and to store passwords; encryption is reversible with the right key.

questions.text:
Why do these two commands print different SHA-256 digests?

echo hello | sha256sum
echo -n hello | sha256sum
options: sha256sum mixes in a random salt each time it runs
echo adds a trailing newline, so the first input is six bytes
-n makes sha256sum switch to printing SHA-512 output
Reading from a pipe makes sha256sum include a timestamp
questions.explanation: SHA-256 is deterministic, but any change in the input, even a trailing newline, gives a completely different digest. The second command hashes exactly hello and prints 2cf24dba...9824.

questions.text: SUMS was created with sha256sum p.txt > SUMS. Then a line is appended to p.txt. What does sha256sum -c SUMS do?
options: Prints p.txt: OK, because the file name and size are unchanged
Updates SUMS with the new digest and prints p.txt: UPDATED
Prints the new digest and leaves the comparison to the user
Prints p.txt: FAILED, warns that a checksum did not match and exits with status 1
questions.explanation: -c recomputes each listed file's digest and compares it with the stored one. A changed file prints FAILED and the exit status is non-zero, which makes it easy to use in scripts.

questions.text: You want to send a file to Jane that only she can read. Which key do you encrypt it with?
questions.explanation: Anything encrypted to Jane's public key can be decrypted only with Jane's private key, which never leaves her hands. Signing is the operation that uses your own private key.

questions.text: Which statement about GPG digital signatures is correct?
options: You sign with the recipient's public key, and they verify with their private key
A signature encrypts the file so only people with your public key can read it
Signing and verifying both need the same shared passphrase
You sign with your private key, and anyone with your public key can verify it
questions.explanation: A signature proves the data was signed by the holder of the private key and has not changed since. It does not hide the content; use encryption for confidentiality, or both together.

questions.text: What does gpg -e -r jane@example.com file.txt produce by default?
options: A binary file file.txt.gpg that only Jane's private key can decrypt
An ASCII file file.txt.asc that anyone with Jane's public key can decrypt
The ciphertext printed to standard output, leaving no file behind
A detached signature file.txt.sig made with Jane's key
questions.explanation: Without --armor, GPG writes binary OpenPGP data to file.txt.gpg. With -a/--armor the output is text in file.txt.asc, which is easier to paste into an email. -o chooses another output name.

questions.text: A project ships release.tar.gz and release.tar.gz.sig. You have imported its public key. Which command verifies the download?
questions.explanation: A detached signature is verified by giving --verify the signature first and then the data file. If even one byte of the tarball changed, GPG prints BAD signature and exits non-zero.

questions.text:
gpg --verify prints the output below for a key you imported from a key server. What does it mean?

gpg: Good signature from "Jane Smith <jane@example.com>" [unknown]
gpg: WARNING: This key is not certified with a trusted signature!
gpg:          There is no indication that the signature belongs to the owner.
options: The signature matches the key, but nothing confirms the key really belongs to Jane
The file was modified after it was signed, so the signature no longer matches
The key has expired, so the signature can no longer be checked
GPG could not find the public key, so it checked only the file's checksum
questions.explanation: The maths checks out for that key, but anyone can create a key with Jane's name. Compare the fingerprint (gpg --fingerprint jane@example.com) with Jane through a trusted channel before relying on it.

questions.text: What does gpg --symmetric file.txt do?
options: Encrypts file.txt with a key derived from a passphrase, writing file.txt.gpg
Encrypts file.txt to your own public key and signs it with your private key
Creates a new key pair whose public and private halves are identical
Prints a hash of file.txt that can be compared on another machine
questions.explanation: Symmetric mode needs no key pair: anyone who knows the passphrase can decrypt with gpg -d. Current GnuPG uses AES-256 by default. The hard part is getting the passphrase to the other person safely.

questions.text: Why should you keep a revocation certificate for your GPG key somewhere safe?
options: It contains a copy of your private key for disaster recovery
It lets you declare the key invalid even after losing the private key
It must be supplied every time you sign or decrypt a file
It extends the key's expiry date automatically each year
questions.explanation: Publishing the certificate tells others to stop trusting the key. GnuPG 2.1 and later create one automatically under ~/.gnupg/openpgp-revocs.d/ when you generate a key. Anyone holding it can revoke your key, so protect it.

questions.text: Which GPG command asks you to choose the key type, size and expiry when creating a key?
questions.explanation: In GnuPG 2.1 and later, --gen-key asks only for name, email and passphrase and uses the default algorithm. --full-generate-key (--full-gen-key) shows all the prompts. --edit-key changes an existing key, for example with addkey.

questions.text: You run chmod 755 ~/.gnupg. What happens the next time you run gpg --list-keys?
options: GPG refuses to run until the directory is owned by root
GPG deletes the private keys to protect them
GPG still works but prints WARNING: unsafe permissions on homedir
Nothing; GPG does not check the permissions of its home directory
questions.explanation: GPG checks that its home directory is not accessible to other users and warns when it is. The private keys inside should not be readable by anyone else; chmod 700 ~/.gnupg fixes it.

questions.text:
ssh -i mykey user@host prints the warning below and refuses to use the key. How do you fix it?

WARNING: UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE!
Permissions 0644 for 'mykey' are too open.
questions.explanation: OpenSSH refuses a private key file that group or others have any access to, because someone else could have copied it. Mode 600 (owner read/write) fixes it. The .pub file may stay world-readable.

questions.text:
openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -in p.txt -out p.enc prints the warning below (OpenSSL 3.0). What should you add?

*** WARNING : deprecated key derivation used.
Using -iter or -pbkdf2 would be better.
options: -nosalt, so the output does not include a random salt
-base64, so the ciphertext is stored as text
-pbkdf2, so the key is derived from the password with PBKDF2
-md5, so a faster digest is used for the key
questions.explanation: Without -pbkdf2 or -iter, enc turns the password into a key with a single fast hash, which makes guessing easy. The same option must be given when decrypting with -d. -a only changes the output encoding.

questions.text: Which command creates a new 2048-bit RSA private key in key.pem?
questions.explanation: genpkey generates private keys for any algorithm; here the file starts with -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----. openssl pkey -in key.pem -pubout extracts the public key. req and x509 work with requests and certificates.

questions.text: What does openssl req -new -key key.pem -subj "/CN=www.example.com" -out req.csr create?
options: A new RSA private key, protected by a passphrase you choose
A copy of the server certificate fetched from www.example.com
A certificate signing request to send to a certificate authority
questions.explanation: A CSR holds the public key and the requested subject, signed with the private key to prove you hold it. The CA returns a certificate; the private key never leaves your server. Adding -x509 would produce a self-signed certificate instead.

questions.text: In openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -noenc -keyout k.pem -out c.crt -days 365, what does -noenc do?
options: It produces a certificate whose public key is not encrypted
It writes the new private key without passphrase protection
It disables encryption on TLS connections that use the certificate
It skips signing, so the certificate has no signature
questions.explanation: -noenc (called -nodes before OpenSSL 3.0) stores the key unencrypted, as unattended services usually need. Without it, OpenSSL asks for a passphrase and writes an encrypted private key. Either way, keep the key file at mode 600.

questions.text: Which command shows when the certificate in c.crt expires?
questions.explanation: openssl x509 reads certificates; -enddate prints notAfter=..., -dates shows both validity dates and -noout suppresses the PEM output. -checkend 86400 exits non-zero if it expires within a day.

questions.text:
echo | openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:44330 prints the output below, and the TLS session is still established. Why?

subject=CN = test
issuer=CN = test
Verify return code: 18 (self-signed certificate)
options: s_client reports failed verification but continues unless given -verify_return_error
Self-signed certificates are always trusted when connecting to 127.0.0.1
Return code 18 means that the certificate chain was verified successfully
s_client never checks certificates unless the -showcerts option is given
questions.explanation: s_client is a debugging tool, so it shows the result of verification and keeps the connection open even when it fails. Here the subject equals the issuer and no trusted CA signed it. Real clients such as curl would refuse.

questions.text: Why do you pass -servername www.example.com to openssl s_client -connect 203.0.113.10:443?
options: It sends the name via SNI, so a multi-site server returns the matching certificate
It makes s_client resolve the name through DNS instead of using the IP
It checks that the server's reverse DNS record matches the given name
It sets the HTTP Host: header for the request typed after connecting
questions.explanation: With Server Name Indication the client names the site in the handshake. Without it, a server with many virtual hosts may present a default certificate that does not match. Recent OpenSSL sends SNI from a host name given in -connect, but not from an IP address.

questions.text: What does cryptsetup luksFormat /dev/sdb1 do to a partition that already holds an ext4 file system with data?
options: Encrypts the existing ext4 file system in place, keeping the data
Creates an encrypted copy of the data on /dev/mapper/sdb1
Writes a new LUKS header and keyslots, so the old data should be treated as lost
Asks for a passphrase, then mounts the partition at /mnt/sdb1
questions.explanation: luksFormat initializes a new LUKS container and asks you to type YES. Afterwards you cryptsetup open it to get a /dev/mapper/NAME device, run mkfs on that mapping once, and mount it.

questions.text: A LUKS volume is unlocked with a passphrase. You add a second passphrase with cryptsetup luksAddKey. Why is this fast even on a large disk?
options: It only encrypts new data; existing blocks keep using the old passphrase
It copies the disk in the background after the command returns
It stores the new passphrase in plain text inside the LUKS header
Each keyslot encrypts the same volume key, so the data itself is not re-encrypted
questions.explanation: The data is encrypted with a volume key, and every passphrase or key file unlocks a keyslot holding a copy of it. Adding, changing or removing a passphrase only rewrites keyslots. Losing the header loses the data, so back it up with luksHeaderBackup.

questions.text: You have finished with an opened LUKS volume mounted at /mnt/secure. What is the correct order to lock it again?
options: cryptsetup close secure first, then umount /mnt/secure
umount /mnt/secure first, then cryptsetup close secure
questions.explanation: The file system on /dev/mapper/secure must be unmounted before the mapping can be removed. cryptsetup close then removes the mapping and wipes the key from kernel memory.

questions.text:
nginx.service is stopped. You run the commands below. What does the last one print?

sudo systemctl enable nginx.service
systemctl is-active nginx.service
questions.explanation: enable only sets up boot-time activation; it does not start anything. The service stays stopped until you run systemctl start, or use enable --now to do both in one step.

questions.text: Which command stops sshd.service now and also keeps it from starting at the next boot?
questions.explanation: disable only removes the boot-time symlinks and leaves a running service running; stop (and kill) affect only the current state. --now makes disable stop the unit as well.

questions.text: The unit file has WantedBy=multi-user.target in its [Install] section. What does sudo systemctl enable app.service do on disk?
options: Creates a symlink to the unit in /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/
Copies the unit file from /usr/lib/systemd/system/ to /etc/systemd/system/
Adds app.service to the DefaultUnits= list in /etc/systemd/system.conf
Starts the unit and records its main PID under /run/systemd/units/
questions.explanation: enable reads [Install] and creates the matching .wants/ symlink, so multi-user.target pulls the unit in at boot. [Install] is read only by install commands such as enable and disable, never when the unit starts.

questions.text:
You run the commands below. What happens?

sudo systemctl mask cups.service
sudo systemctl start cups.service
options: cups starts, because masking only affects what happens at boot
cups starts with a warning, and is stopped again at the next boot
cups starts only if another unit lists it in Requires=
The start fails with Unit cups.service is masked.
questions.explanation: mask links the unit name to /dev/null, so neither a manual start nor a dependency can start it. A disabled unit can still be started by hand; a masked one needs systemctl unmask first.

questions.text: A unit file has no [Install] section and is started only by another unit that lists it in Wants=. What does systemctl is-enabled print for it?
questions.explanation: static means the unit has no install information, so there is nothing for enable to do; running enable on it prints a notice instead. Such units are started by other units or by socket, timer or D-Bus activation.

questions.text:
You change ExecStart= in /etc/systemd/system/app.service and then run the command below without anything else. What does systemd run?

sudo systemctl restart app.service
options: The old ExecStart=, with a warning that the unit file changed on disk
The new ExecStart=, because restart always rereads the unit file
Nothing; restart refuses to run until you reload systemd
The new ExecStart=, but only after the old process exits by itself
questions.explanation: systemd works from the unit definitions it has loaded in memory. Until systemctl daemon-reload, a restart uses the old command and systemctl prints "changed on disk. Run 'systemctl daemon-reload'".

questions.text: You want to change a setting of the packaged /usr/lib/systemd/system/nginx.service so that the change survives package upgrades. What is the usual way?
options: Add a drop-in under /etc/systemd/system/nginx.service.d/, for example with systemctl edit nginx
Add the setting under a [nginx.service] section in /etc/systemd/system.conf
questions.explanation: Files under /etc/systemd/system take precedence over /usr/lib/systemd/system, which upgrades overwrite. systemctl edit creates override.conf there and reloads systemd. /run is lost at reboot.

questions.text:
app.service has Type=simple. You add the drop-in below, run daemon-reload, and systemctl start app fails with "bad unit file setting". Why?

# /etc/systemd/system/app.service.d/override.conf
[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/app --verbose
options: Drop-ins may only contain [Unit] settings, so the [Service] section is ignored
The drop-in must be named app.service.conf and live next to the unit file
ExecStart= paths in a drop-in must be relative to WorkingDirectory=
The drop-in adds a second ExecStart=; an empty ExecStart= line must clear the original first
questions.explanation: ExecStart= is a list, so a drop-in appends to it. Only Type=oneshot may have several; others are refused. Put ExecStart= (empty) before the new line to reset the list.

questions.text:
systemctl status backup.service shows the lines below for a Type=oneshot unit. What do they tell you?

     Active: inactive (dead)
    Process: 3600 ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/backup.sh (code=exited, status=0/SUCCESS)
options: The script ran and finished successfully; inactive is normal after a oneshot completes
The script crashed, and systemd gave up after too many restart attempts
The unit is disabled, so the script was never started by systemd
The script is still running in the background, detached from systemd
questions.explanation: A oneshot unit is active only while its command runs, then goes back to inactive; status=0/SUCCESS shows a clean exit. With RemainAfterExit=yes it would stay active (exited) instead.

questions.text: legacyd forks into the background and its parent process exits at once. Its unit uses Type=simple. What happens after systemctl start legacyd?
options: systemd follows the fork and adopts the child as the new main PID
systemd sees the main process exit, marks the unit inactive and kills the forked daemon
The daemon keeps running, but systemctl status reports it as failed
systemd restarts the parent process in an endless loop
questions.explanation: With Type=simple the ExecStart= process is the service; when it exits, systemd stops the unit and kills what is left in its cgroup. Use Type=forking (with PIDFile=) or run the daemon in foreground mode.

questions.text: A unit has Restart=on-failure. Its main process exits with status 0. What does systemd do?
options: Restarts it after RestartSec= has passed
Marks the unit failed and restarts it once
Leaves it stopped, because a clean exit is not a failure
questions.explanation: on-failure restarts only after a non-zero exit code, a fatal signal, a timeout or a watchdog failure. Restart=always would restart it even after a clean exit.

questions.text: A service with Restart=always crashes right after every start. After a few quick restarts, systemctl status shows failed and "Start request repeated too quickly". Why did systemd stop restarting it?
options: Restart=always allows only five restarts over the unit's whole lifetime
journald stopped accepting its messages, so systemd killed it
RestartSec= expired before the service reached the active state
It hit the start rate limit, StartLimitBurst= starts within StartLimitIntervalSec=
questions.explanation: By default a unit may start 5 times in 10 seconds; after that systemd refuses and marks it failed. Fix the crash, then systemctl reset-failed clears the counter and the failed state.

questions.text: A shell script must check whether nginx.service is running. Which test is reliable?
options: systemctl is-active --quiet nginx, which exits with status 0 only when the unit is active
systemctl is-enabled --quiet nginx, which exits with status 0 when the service is running
systemctl status nginx, which always exits with status 0 if the unit file exists
systemctl cat nginx, which fails when the main process is not running
questions.explanation: is-active reports the runtime state and returns non-zero (3 for inactive) otherwise; --quiet hides the output. is-enabled only tells you about boot-time setup, and cat just prints the unit file.

questions.text: You fixed a broken unit, but systemctl --failed still lists it from the earlier attempt. Which command clears that state?
questions.explanation: systemd remembers a unit's failed result until it starts successfully or you run reset-failed. daemon-reload rereads unit files but keeps unit state, and journal commands only affect logs.

questions.text: What is the difference between systemctl reload app and systemctl restart app?
options: reload rereads the unit file; restart rereads the application's config
reload works only for disabled units; restart only for enabled ones
They are aliases; both stop and start the process with a new PID
reload asks the running process to reread its config; restart stops and starts it
questions.explanation: reload runs the unit's ExecReload= (often a SIGHUP), so the main PID survives. Not every service supports it; reload-or-restart falls back to a restart. Rereading unit files is daemon-reload.

questions.text: app.service contains only After=postgresql.service in [Unit]. PostgreSQL is stopped. What happens when you run systemctl start app?
options: PostgreSQL is started first, then app
app starts and PostgreSQL stays stopped
