app waits until someone starts PostgreSQL
app refuses to start because PostgreSQL is inactive
questions.explanation: After= only orders units that are both being started in the same transaction; it never pulls a unit in. Add Wants= or Requires= to have PostgreSQL started too.

questions.text: db.service fails to start. One app unit has Requires=db.service and After=db.service; another has Wants=db.service and After=db.service. Which statement is true?
options: The Requires= app is not started; the Wants= app starts anyway
Both apps start; Requires= only logs a warning about the failure
Neither app starts, because both wait for db.service
The Wants= app is not started; the Requires= app starts after a retry
questions.explanation: Both settings pull db.service in, but only Requires= (with After=) makes the start job of the app fail with "A dependency job failed". Wants= is the weak form: a failed dependency is ignored.

questions.text: app.service has Requires=db.service but no After= or Before=. db.service fails to start. What happens when you start app.service?
options: app is not started, because Requires= always waits for the result
systemd delays app until db has been retried
app starts anyway, because both start jobs run in parallel
systemd refuses the transaction as an ordering cycle
questions.explanation: Without an ordering dependency, systemd starts both at the same time and does not wait for db's result. A failed required unit blocks the requiring unit only when After= is also set.

questions.text: app.service has Requires=db.service and After=db.service, and both are running. What happens when you run systemctl stop db.service?
options: Only db stops; app keeps running until it is restarted
systemd refuses to stop db while app needs it
db stops, and app is restarted to reconnect
questions.explanation: With Requires=, explicitly stopping or restarting the required unit also stops or restarts the units that require it. With Wants=, app would keep running.

questions.text: A service fails at boot because it starts before the network is fully configured. Which [Unit] lines express "start the network-online milestone too, and start me after it"?
questions.explanation: Wants= pulls the target into the boot and After= orders the service after it. network.target only means the network stack started, not that addresses are configured. Before= reverses the order, and WantedBy= belongs in [Install].

questions.text: Which systemd target corresponds to SysV runlevel 3 (multi-user, networking, no GUI)?
questions.explanation: systemd ships runlevel3.target as a symlink to multi-user.target. Runlevel 5 maps to graphical.target, 1 to rescue.target, 0 to poweroff.target and 6 to reboot.target.

questions.text: You want a server to boot into text mode from now on, without ending the current graphical session. Which command?
questions.explanation: set-default repoints the default.target symlink, which affects future boots only. isolate switches the running system right away and stops units the new target does not need, such as the display manager.

questions.text: What is the main difference between rescue.target and emergency.target?
options: emergency.target mounts all filesystems and starts networking; rescue.target mounts none
rescue.target needs a network connection for remote repair; emergency.target does not
They are aliases of the same target, kept only for SysV compatibility
rescue.target mounts local filesystems and starts basic services; emergency.target starts almost nothing
questions.explanation: Rescue mode is single-user mode with filesystems mounted. Emergency mode gives a shell with no other mounts or services, which helps when /etc/fstab or a filesystem check breaks the boot.

questions.text: In the GRUB menu you press e to edit the boot entry. What do you append to the linux line to boot once into rescue mode on a systemd system?
questions.explanation: systemd reads systemd.unit= from the kernel command line; single or 1 work too. Editing in GRUB lasts for one boot. init= expects a program path, not a unit name.

questions.text: Which timer setting runs a job every 15 minutes, like the cron schedule */15 * * * *?
questions.explanation: *:0/15 means any hour, minutes starting at 0 in steps of 15; systemd-analyze calendar '*:0/15' shows the next run times. *:15:00 fires once an hour at minute 15, and OnUnitActiveSec= takes a time span.

questions.text: A laptop is often switched off at 03:00, when backup.timer (OnCalendar=*-*-* 03:00:00) should fire. Which line makes the missed run happen at the next boot?
questions.explanation: With Persistent=true systemd stores the last trigger time on disk and runs the service at once if a scheduled run was missed while the timer was inactive. It affects only OnCalendar= timers.

questions.text: You enable backup.timer, which has no Unit= line. Which unit does it start when it fires?
options: No unit, until you add Unit=
questions.explanation: A timer activates the service with the same name by default; the ACTIVATES column of systemctl list-timers shows it. timers.target is only what timers are usually WantedBy=.

questions.text: Which statement describes an advantage of a systemd timer over a cron job?
options: A timer uses the same five-field schedule syntax as crontab
A timer can run a command without any matching unit file
Each run is a service unit, so its output and result show up in the journal and systemctl status
A timer runs its job in the owner's login shell with the crontab environment
questions.explanation: A timer starts a service unit, so you get journal logs, dependencies, resource limits and status for free. Cron needs its own logging or mail; timers need a .service file and their own OnCalendar= syntax.

questions.text: Which [Timer] settings run a job 10 minutes after boot and then 1 hour after each time it was last activated?
questions.explanation: OnBootSec= and OnUnitActiveSec= are monotonic timers, measured from boot and from the last activation of the unit. OnCalendar= takes calendar expressions such as hourly, and AccuracySec= only sets how precisely a timer fires.

questions.text: Which order matches a typical Linux boot?
options: Bootloader, firmware POST, initramfs, kernel, PID 1
Firmware POST, kernel, bootloader, PID 1, initramfs
Firmware POST, bootloader, kernel, initramfs, PID 1
Firmware POST, initramfs, bootloader, kernel, PID 1
questions.explanation: Firmware tests hardware and finds a boot target, the bootloader loads the kernel and initramfs, the initramfs prepares and mounts the real root, then switch_root runs PID 1 (systemd), which starts services.

questions.text: Which statement correctly contrasts BIOS and UEFI booting?
options: BIOS loads a .efi file from a FAT partition; UEFI runs code from the first disk sector
BIOS runs boot code from the disk's first 512-byte sector; UEFI loads a .efi file from the EFI System Partition
BIOS reads boot entries from NVRAM; UEFI always boots the first disk in the system
Both load the kernel straight from /boot without a bootloader
questions.explanation: The MBR holds 446 bytes of boot code that can only chain to a bigger loader. UEFI reads a boot entry from NVRAM and runs an EFI program such as shimx64.efi or grubx64.efi from the ESP, usually mounted at /boot/efi.

questions.text: On Ubuntu you want to add a kernel parameter to every future boot. What is the usual way?
options: Edit /boot/grub/grub.cfg directly, since GRUB reads it at every boot
Append the parameter to /proc/cmdline, then reboot the machine
Add the parameter to /etc/sysctl.conf and apply it with sysctl -p
Add it to GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT in /etc/default/grub, then run sudo update-grub
questions.explanation: grub.cfg is generated, so manual edits are lost the next time it is rebuilt. Red Hat-style systems use grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg (or grubby). /proc/cmdline is read-only.

questions.text: Which command shows the parameters the running kernel was booted with?
questions.explanation: /proc/cmdline holds the exact command line the bootloader passed, such as root=UUID=... ro quiet splash. /etc/default/grub describes future boots and may have changed since; sysctl -a lists runtime tunables.

questions.text: The root filesystem is on LVM inside a LUKS-encrypted partition. Why does this system need an initramfs?
options: The kernel can only mount ext4 directly, so all other filesystems need it
The initramfs holds the GRUB menu and the kernel parameters
systemd refuses to run as PID 1 from an encrypted disk
The tools and drivers that unlock and assemble the root device must run before that root is available
questions.explanation: The initramfs is a small filesystem in RAM with storage drivers, cryptsetup, LVM tools and scripts. It prepares and mounts the real root, then hands over with switch_root.

questions.text:
After booting a self-built kernel you see the message below. What is the most likely cause?

Kernel panic - not syncing: VFS: Unable to mount root fs on unknown-block(0,0)
options: No usable initramfs or built-in driver for the root device, or a wrong root= parameter
sshd.service failed to start, so systemd could not finish the boot
The GRUB menu timeout is too short for the kernel to load its drivers
/etc/fstab has a wrong UUID for the /home filesystem
questions.explanation: The kernel could not find any block device to mount as root. Typical fixes: build the storage and filesystem drivers in, generate an initramfs for the new kernel, or correct root=. /etc/fstab is read later, by systemd.

questions.text: On Ubuntu you added blacklist nouveau under /etc/modprobe.d/, but the module still loads early in boot. Which command is usually needed next?
questions.explanation: The initramfs carries its own copy of the modules and modprobe configuration, so it must be rebuilt to see the change. On RHEL/Fedora the equivalent is sudo dracut -f.

questions.text:
ps -p 1 -o comm,args prints the line below on Ubuntu. Why does the command name differ from the arguments?

COMMAND         COMMAND
systemd         /sbin/init splash
options: PID 1 is SysV init, which starts systemd as a child process
systemd renames itself after it finishes the boot
The kernel always reports PID 1 as /sbin/init
/sbin/init is a symlink to systemd, and the kernel started it by that path
questions.explanation: The kernel runs /sbin/init by default (or the init= parameter); here it links to /usr/lib/systemd/systemd. comm is the executable's name, while args shows how it was invoked. splash came from the kernel command line.

questions.text: What happens if PID 1 exits on a running Linux system?
options: Another process is promoted to PID 1 and the system continues
The kernel panics, because there must always be an init process
systemd restarts itself from the initramfs within a few seconds
Only user sessions end; system services keep running
questions.explanation: PID 1 reaps orphaned processes and manages the system, so the kernel cannot continue without it and panics with "Attempted to kill init!". That is why a crash of the init process is fatal.

questions.text:
In a RHEL root password reset you boot with rd.break and run the commands below. Why is the last command needed?

mount -o remount,rw /sysroot
chroot /sysroot
passwd root
touch /.autorelabel
options: It tells GRUB to drop rd.break from the kernel command line at the next boot
It forces fsck to check the root filesystem during the next boot
SELinux relabels files at the next boot, fixing the label of the newly written /etc/shadow
It makes /sysroot writable again after leaving the chroot
questions.explanation: In the initramfs SELinux policy is not loaded, so passwd writes /etc/shadow without its proper label. Without a relabel, logins can fail. rd.break itself lasts only for the edited boot.

questions.text: systemd-analyze blame lists backup-check.service at the top with 20 s, yet removing it does not shorten the boot. What explains this?
options: blame reports time spent in the firmware and loader, not in user space
blame measures the CPU time used by each unit, not wall-clock time
Units start in parallel, so a slow unit off the critical path does not delay the target
The times are cached and only updated after two more reboots
questions.explanation: blame sorts units by their own start-up time. systemd-analyze critical-chain shows the chain of units that actually determined when the default target was reached.

questions.text: After adding a USB backup disk to /etc/fstab, the system drops to emergency mode whenever the disk is unplugged. Which mount option lets boot continue without it?
questions.explanation: With nofail, a missing device no longer fails local-fs.target, so boot carries on. errors=remount-ro only changes what ext4 does on errors after the mount succeeded.

questions.text:
lsmod prints the lines below. What does 1 ipt_REJECT in the last column mean?

Module                  Size  Used by
ipt_REJECT             12288  0
nf_reject_ipv4         12288  1 ipt_REJECT
options: nf_reject_ipv4 was loaded once, by the user ipt_REJECT
One module, ipt_REJECT, depends on nf_reject_ipv4, so it cannot be unloaded first
nf_reject_ipv4 is built into the kernel image of ipt_REJECT
ipt_REJECT is waiting for nf_reject_ipv4 to finish loading
questions.explanation: The number is the use count and the list names dependent modules. modprobe -r nf_reject_ipv4 would fail while ipt_REJECT uses it; lsmod just formats /proc/modules.

questions.text: sudo insmod ./btrfs.ko fails with "Unknown symbol in module", while sudo modprobe btrfs works. Why?
options: insmod works only for modules outside /lib/modules
modprobe ignores signature checks that insmod enforces
insmod loads only the named file; modprobe loads its dependencies first
questions.explanation: modprobe uses modules.dep under /lib/modules/$(uname -r) to load modules such as raid6_pq and xor before btrfs; modprobe --show-depends btrfs lists them. insmod does no dependency handling.

questions.text: /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-nouveau.conf contains blacklist nouveau. What happens when an admin runs sudo modprobe nouveau?
options: modprobe loads it only after the next reboot
The module loads, because blacklist only stops loading by alias
modprobe removes the blacklist line and loads the module
questions.explanation: blacklist makes modprobe ignore the module's aliases, so hardware detection no longer pulls it in, but loading it by name still works. To block that too, add install nouveau /bin/false.

questions.text: You put net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1 in /etc/sysctl.d/90-router.conf. Which command applies it now without a reboot?
questions.explanation: --system loads every file in the sysctl configuration directories, including /etc/sysctl.d/. Plain sysctl -p reads only /etc/sysctl.conf unless you name a file. sysctl -w changes a value only until reboot.

questions.text: Which command shows the same value as sysctl vm.swappiness?
questions.explanation: sysctl names are paths under /proc/sys/ with dots in place of slashes. Writing to the file (as root) has the same effect as sysctl -w, and both are lost at reboot.

questions.text: Where can you read the current parameter values of the loaded kvm module?
questions.explanation: sysfs (/sys) exposes the kernel's device, driver and module model, with one file per module parameter. /etc/modprobe.d/ holds options for future loads, and /lib/modules holds the module files.

questions.text: In make menuconfig, what does <M> next to a driver mean, compared with [*]?
options: <M> means mandatory; [*] means optional
<M> builds it as a loadable module; [*] builds it into the kernel image
<M> marks a modified option; [*] marks the default
<M> enables it for multiprocessor systems only
questions.explanation: Built-in code is always present from boot. A module is a separate .ko file installed under /lib/modules/<version> and loaded on demand. [ ] leaves the feature out.

questions.text: A web server fails with "Too many open files" at about 1024 open sockets, although fs.file-max is very large. Which limit is it most likely hitting?
options: The listen backlog of the socket, net.core.somaxconn
The per-process open-file limit, ulimit -n or LimitNOFILE= in its unit
questions.explanation: fs.file-max caps file handles for the whole system. Each process also has its own RLIMIT_NOFILE, often a soft limit of 1024; for a systemd service raise it with LimitNOFILE=.

questions.text: A program calls read() on a file. Which statement describes what happens?
options: The C library reads the disk blocks itself and returns them to the program
The kernel copies the program into kernel space and runs the read there
The disk driver is mapped into the program and runs in user space
The CPU switches to kernel mode, the kernel does the I/O, and data is copied into the program's buffer
questions.explanation: User-space code cannot touch hardware or kernel memory. A system call enters the kernel, whose filesystem and driver code performs the request and returns the result to the process.

questions.text: What is the difference between a terminal and a shell?
options: They are two names for the same program
The shell draws the window; the terminal runs the commands
The terminal is the window you type into; the shell interprets the commands
A terminal is used only for remote sessions, a shell only for local ones
questions.explanation: A terminal emulator such as GNOME Terminal or xterm provides the window and keyboard input. The shell (Bash, Zsh, and so on) runs inside it, parses commands and starts programs.

questions.text: Which file lists the shells that may be used as login shells, and is checked by chsh?
questions.explanation: chsh -s /bin/zsh normally refuses a shell that is not listed in /etc/shells. Each user's chosen login shell is then stored in the last field of their /etc/passwd entry.

questions.text: Your login shell is Bash, but you have just typed zsh to try it out. Which command reliably shows the shell you are running right now?
questions.explanation: $$ is the PID of the current shell, and ps prints its command name. $SHELL normally holds your default login shell, so it would still say /bin/bash.

questions.text: echo "$0" prints -bash. What does the leading dash tell you?
options: The shell is running in POSIX compatibility mode
The shell was started as a login shell
The shell is a non-interactive subshell
The shell is running with restricted permissions
questions.explanation: By convention, a login shell's argv[0] starts with -. Login shells read /etc/profile and then the first of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login or ~/.profile that exists.

questions.text: You log in over SSH, and Bash starts as a login shell. A user has both ~/.bash_profile and ~/.profile. Which files does Bash read?
questions.explanation: A login shell reads /etc/profile, then only the first user file it finds out of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login and ~/.profile. Here ~/.profile is skipped because ~/.bash_profile exists.

questions.text: Which file does Bash read when you open a new terminal tab in a desktop session (an interactive, non-login shell)?
questions.explanation: Interactive non-login shells read ~/.bashrc, often after a system-wide file such as /etc/bash.bashrc. Aliases, functions and prompt settings usually live there.

questions.text: Aliases defined in ~/.bashrc are missing when you log in over SSH. What is the usual fix?
options: Add export in front of each alias
questions.explanation: SSH starts a login shell, which reads ~/.bash_profile rather than ~/.bashrc. Adding if [ -f ~/.bashrc ]; then . ~/.bashrc; fi to ~/.bash_profile gives both kinds of shell the same settings.

questions.text: Which file does Bash run when an interactive login shell exits?
questions.explanation: ~/.bash_logout runs when a login shell exits, which makes it handy for cleanup such as clearing the screen. Non-login shells, such as a new terminal tab on most desktops, do not read it.

questions.text: You edited ~/.bashrc to add an alias. How do you apply it to the current shell without opening a new terminal?
questions.explanation: source (or .) runs the file inside the current shell, so its aliases and variables stay defined. bash ~/.bashrc runs it in a child process whose changes vanish when it exits.

questions.text:
What does this print?

export MODE=dev
bash -c 'MODE=prod; exec sh -c "echo child: \$MODE"'
echo "parent: $MODE"
questions.explanation: The inner bash gets its own copy of the environment, and exec keeps that copy because it replaces the program, not the process. Nothing a child does reaches the parent's copy, so the parent still prints dev.

questions.text: A cron job must run /srv/app/app.py with the packages installed in /srv/app/.venv. Which command does that without activating the venv?
questions.explanation: The venv's own interpreter already uses the venv's site-packages; activation only puts .venv/bin first on PATH. Setting VIRTUAL_ENV alone does not change python3, and activate is not executable, so running it fails.

questions.text:
What does this print, given the difference between ( ) and { }?

COLOR=blue
( COLOR=red )
echo "$COLOR"
{ COLOR=green; }
echo "$COLOR"
questions.explanation: Parentheses run commands in a subshell, so its assignment is lost. Braces group commands in the current shell, so green sticks. Braces need spaces and a trailing ; before }.

questions.text:
What does printenv show for a variable that was set but never exported?

count=5
printenv count
options: Nothing, because count was never exported
5, because printenv reads shell variables
A syntax error, because it needs $count
questions.explanation: printenv is an external program and sees only exported variables. Run export count first. echo "$count" would still print 5, because the shell expands the variable itself.

questions.text: What does DEBUG=1 ./app do?
options: Puts DEBUG=1 in the environment of ./app only
Sets DEBUG permanently in the current shell and runs ./app
Runs ./app with debug tracing turned on in Bash
questions.explanation: A NAME=value prefix adds the variable to that one command's environment. Afterwards echo "$DEBUG" in the shell prints nothing.

questions.text: Which line adds ~/bin to the front of the command search path for this shell and its children?
questions.explanation: PATH entries are separated by colons and searched left to right, so prepending puts ~/bin first. PATH=~/bin throws away the existing directories, and ; is not a separator on Linux.

questions.text: What does env -i bash --norc give you?
options: A Bash shell that runs as root
A new Bash shell that starts with no inherited environment variables
A copy of the current shell, including its unexported variables
A Bash shell that ignores PATH lookups
questions.explanation: env -i clears the environment before starting the command; Bash then sets only a few variables itself, such as PWD and SHLVL. This shows whether a script secretly depends on your personal variables.

questions.text: What does readonly MAX_RETRIES=5 followed by MAX_RETRIES=3 do?
options: Changes the value to 3 and prints a warning
Changes the value to 3 only in child processes
questions.explanation: Read-only variables cannot be reassigned or unset in that shell, so Bash reports an error and the value stays 5. This is useful for constants in scripts.

questions.text: A script starts with : "${API_KEY:?API_KEY is required}". What happens if API_KEY is unset?
options: API_KEY is set to the text API_KEY is required and the script goes on
The line is ignored, because : is a comment
The script prompts the user to type a value
The script prints the message to stderr and exits with a non-zero status
questions.explanation: ${VAR:?msg} aborts a non-interactive shell with msg if VAR is unset or empty. : is a no-op command that still expands its arguments, so the check runs.

questions.text:
What does this print when using the ${x:-7} default-value expansion?

x=5; echo "${x:-7}"; unset x; echo "${x:-7}"
questions.explanation: ${x:-7} uses the default 7 only when x is unset or empty, and does not assign it. The ${x:=7} form would also store 7 in x.

questions.text: Which shebang finds bash through the user's PATH, so the script works where Bash is not at /bin/bash?
questions.explanation: env searches PATH for bash, which helps on systems such as FreeBSD or macOS with Homebrew. #!/bin/sh may be Dash, which lacks Bash features, and the kernel never searches PATH for a shebang interpreter, so #!bash fails.

questions.text: A script deploy.sh has a valid shebang. What lets you run it as ./deploy.sh?
questions.explanation: Without execute permission, ./deploy.sh fails with Permission denied; with it, the kernel reads the shebang to pick the interpreter. bash deploy.sh runs the script without needing +x, but that is not ./deploy.sh.

questions.text: A script is run as ./greet.sh Ann Bob. Inside it, what are $0, $1 and $#?
questions.explanation: $0 is the name the script was invoked by, $1 is the first argument, and $# counts the arguments, not including $0.

questions.text:
What does this print, comparing "$@" with "$*"?

count() { echo "$#"; }
set -- "a b" c
count "$@"; count "$*"
questions.explanation: "$@" expands to each argument as a separate word, keeping a b intact, so you get 2. "$*" joins every argument into one string, so you get 1. Use "$@" to pass arguments through safely.

questions.text: What do $?, $$ and $! hold?
options: The PID of the last background job, the exit status, and the shell's PID
The argument count, the shell's PID, and the last exit status
The last command's exit status, the current shell's PID, and the PID of the last background job
The current shell's PID, the parent's PID, and the last exit status
questions.explanation: $? is 0 on success and non-zero on failure. $$ is the shell's own PID, and $! is set when you start something with &, which makes it useful with wait "$!".

questions.text:
In Bash, the first line below prints 4100 4100. What does the second line print?

echo "$$ $BASHPID"
( echo "$$ $BASHPID" )
options: A new PID twice, such as 4105 4105
4100 followed by a different PID, such as 4100 4105
A new PID followed by 4100, such as 4105 4100
questions.explanation: $$ always expands to the PID of the main shell, even inside a subshell, while $BASHPID is the PID of the process actually running the code. Use $BASHPID when a subshell needs its own PID.

questions.text: What does echo "Today is $(date +%A)" do?
options: Stores the output of date in a variable called A
Runs date +%A and puts its output into the string
questions.explanation: $(...) is command substitution: the command's stdout, without trailing newlines, replaces the expression. Backticks do the same thing but are harder to nest.

questions.text: With name=World, what does echo 'Hello $name' print?
questions.explanation: Single quotes keep every character literal. Double quotes, as in "Hello $name", still expand variables and command substitutions but prevent word splitting and globbing.

questions.text:
You run this in an otherwise empty directory. What happens?

f="my file.txt"
touch "$f"
rm $f
options: rm deletes my file.txt, because $f holds the whole name
rm deletes every file in the directory, because the space acts as a wildcard
rm gets the two arguments my and file.txt, fails on both, and my file.txt remains
Bash refuses to run rm, because an unquoted $f contains a space
questions.explanation: An unquoted expansion is split into words on IFS characters and then globbed, so $f becomes two arguments. Write rm -- "$f" to pass the name as a single argument.

questions.text:
What does this print?

data="red,green,blue"
IFS=, read -r first second third <<< "$data"
echo "$second"
printf '%q\n' "$IFS"
questions.explanation: A VAR=value prefix on read sets IFS for that one command, so the line is split on commas while the shell's IFS keeps its default of space, tab and newline. Changing IFS globally can break later commands.

questions.text: Which alias definition makes ll run ls -la?
questions.explanation: There must be no spaces around =, and the value needs quotes because it contains a space. alias with no arguments lists all aliases, and unalias ll removes one.

questions.text:
What happens when you run this script with bash script.sh?

#!/usr/bin/env bash
alias ll='ls -la'
ll
options: It fails with ll: command not found, as scripts do not expand aliases
It runs ls -la, because the alias is defined before it is used
It prints the definition alias ll='ls -la'
It fails with a syntax error on the alias line
questions.explanation: Bash expands aliases only in interactive shells unless shopt -s expand_aliases is set. In scripts, use a function such as ll() { ls -la "$@"; } instead.

questions.text: You want a shortcut backup notes.txt that copies a file to notes.txt.bak. Why use a function instead of an alias?
options: Aliases cannot contain the cp command
A function can use its argument as $1 anywhere in its body
Functions run faster because they are compiled
Aliases are deleted when the terminal is resized
questions.explanation: An alias is only text substitution at the start of a command, so it cannot reuse an argument. backup() { cp -- "$1" "$1.bak"; } can. Use aliases for simple shortcuts and functions for logic.

questions.text: Which of these is a valid Bash function definition?
questions.explanation: The body is a brace group, which needs a space after { and a ; or newline before }. Without the semicolon, Bash keeps reading and reports a syntax error.

questions.text: In PS1='\u@\h:\w\$ ', what do \u, \h and \w expand to?
options: Username, hostname, and current working directory
User ID, home directory, and time
Uptime, history number, and window title
Username, home directory, and week day
questions.explanation: PS1 is the primary prompt. \h is the hostname up to the first dot, and \$ shows $ for normal users and # for root.

questions.text: What is the difference between HISTSIZE and HISTFILESIZE?
options: They are two names for the same setting, kept for compatibility
HISTSIZE limits commands kept in memory; HISTFILESIZE limits lines saved in ~/.bash_history
HISTSIZE is measured in kilobytes; HISTFILESIZE is in lines
HISTSIZE applies to root; HISTFILESIZE applies to other users
questions.explanation: During a session, Bash keeps up to HISTSIZE commands. When the shell exits, the history file is cut down to HISTFILESIZE lines.

questions.text: In an interactive Bash shell, what does sudo !! do?
options: Runs sudo with no arguments twice
Re-runs the previous command with sudo in front
Opens the history list in an editor
Repeats the last command that used sudo
questions.explanation: !! is history expansion for the previous command line, and Bash echoes the expanded command before running it. !$ expands to the last argument of the previous command. Scripts have history expansion turned off.

questions.text: Which redirection sends both stdout and stderr of make to build.log, overwriting the file?
questions.explanation: Redirections are processed left to right: stdout goes to the file, then stderr is pointed at the same place. 2>&1 > build.log points stderr at the old stdout (the terminal) first. Bash's &> build.log is a shorter form.

questions.text: Which command adds a line to the end of notes.txt instead of replacing its contents?
questions.explanation: >> appends, while > truncates the file first. < redirects input, and 2> redirects only stderr.

questions.text: How do you run find / -name core and throw away its "Permission denied" messages, while still seeing the results?
questions.explanation: Error messages go to file descriptor 2, so 2>/dev/null discards just those. > /dev/null would discard the results, and &> would discard both streams.

questions.text: Which command shows output on screen and also appends it to run.log?
questions.explanation: tee copies stdin to the screen and to a file, and -a appends instead of overwriting. The redirect-only versions show nothing on screen.

questions.text: Which Bash command shows both the output and the error messages of make on screen and also saves both to build.log?
questions.explanation: |& is Bash shorthand for 2>&1 |, so both streams enter the pipe and tee copies them to the screen and the file. A plain | carries only stdout, so error messages bypass tee and are not saved.

questions.text:
A #!/bin/sh script on Ubuntu, where /bin/sh is Dash, contains this line. What happens?

echo hi &> out.log
options: Both stdout and stderr of echo go to out.log, as in Bash
echo hi runs in the background, and out.log is created empty
Dash stops with a syntax error at &>
Only stderr of echo goes to out.log
questions.explanation: POSIX sh has no &> operator, so Dash reads echo hi & followed by > out.log, an empty command whose redirection truncates the file. The portable form is echo hi > out.log 2>&1.

questions.text:
What does this here-document print when its delimiter is quoted?

name=World
cat <<'EOF'
Hello $name
EOF
options: It fails because the delimiter is quoted
questions.explanation: Quoting the here-document delimiter ('EOF') turns off expansion in the body. With an unquoted EOF, the shell would expand $name and print Hello World.

questions.text: What does diff <(ls dir1) <(ls dir2) do?
options: Compares two files literally named ls dir1 and ls dir2
Copies dir1 into dir2, then compares them
Compares the outputs of the two ls commands as if they were files
Fails, because diff cannot read from pipes
questions.explanation: Process substitution <(cmd) runs the command and passes a path such as /dev/fd/63 that reads its output. That lets programs that expect filenames read command output. It is a Bash feature; Dash reports a syntax error.

questions.text: What does set -e change in a script?
options: It echoes each command to stderr before running it
The script exits when a command fails, outside tests such as if or &&
It exports every variable it sets to child processes
It turns expanding an unset variable into an error
questions.explanation: set -e (errexit) stops the script at the first unchecked failure. Commands used as conditions are exempt. Tracing is set -x, and unset-variable errors are set -u.

questions.text:
What does this script print?

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e
count=0
((count++))
echo "count is $count"
options: Nothing: the script exits with status 1 at ((count++))
count is 0, because count++ is a post-increment
An unbound variable error for count
questions.explanation: count++ evaluates to the old value, 0, and an arithmetic command whose value is 0 returns status 1, so set -e ends the script silently. count=$((count + 1)) always succeeds.

questions.text:
What does this script print?

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e
f() { false; echo "in f"; }
f || echo "f failed"
echo "end"
options: Nothing, because the script exits at false
in f, f failed, then end
questions.explanation: set -e is ignored for everything run as the left side of || or &&, including commands inside a function called there. So false does not stop f, f returns the echo status 0, and f failed never prints.

questions.text:
What does this script do when it uses an unset variable?

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
echo "Count is $count"
echo "after"
options: Count is then after, as $count expands to nothing
Count is $count then after, printed literally
Count is 0 then after, as unset numbers default to 0
An error like count: unbound variable, and the script stops
questions.explanation: set -u (nounset) makes expanding an unset variable an error, which ends a non-interactive shell. Without it, $count silently becomes an empty string and hides the bug.

questions.text:
What does this print in Bash, before and after enabling pipefail?

false | true; echo $?
set -o pipefail
false | true; echo $?
questions.explanation: A pipeline's status is normally that of its last command, so the failing false is hidden. With pipefail, a pipeline fails if any command in it fails.

questions.text:
On Ubuntu 24.04, /bin/sh is Dash 0.5.12. What happens when you run this script with sh check.sh?

false | true
echo "first: $?"
set -o pipefail
echo "after set"
options: It prints first: 0 and after set, ignoring the option
It prints first: 1, then after set on the next line
It prints first: 0, then Dash reports Illegal option -o pipefail and exits
It fails with a syntax error before running any line
questions.explanation: This Dash version does not implement pipefail, and an error in the special builtin set ends a non-interactive shell. Use a bash shebang and run the script with Bash when you rely on pipefail.

questions.text: Which line is the usual "strict mode" at the top of a Bash script: exit on error, error on unset variables, and fail pipelines on any error?
questions.explanation: -e exits on unchecked errors, -u treats unset variables as errors, and -o pipefail makes pipeline failures visible. A + prefix turns options off instead of on.

questions.text: What does set -x do?
options: Prints each command, after expansion, before it runs
Exits the script as soon as any command fails
Marks the script file as executable for its owner
Exports every variable that the script creates
questions.explanation: set -x (xtrace) prints each command to stderr with a + prefix, which is useful for debugging. Turn it off again with set +x.

questions.text:
What does this trap line do in a script?

tmp=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT
options: Deletes the temporary file immediately, before the next line
Stops the script from being interrupted with Ctrl+C
Prevents other users from reading the temporary file
Removes the temporary file whenever the script exits, including after an error
questions.explanation: Bash runs an EXIT trap on a normal end, on exit, after a set -e failure, and when a signal such as SIGINT or SIGTERM kills the script. Nothing can run after SIGKILL, so cleanup is skipped then.

questions.text:
You build an image from this Dockerfile with docker build --build-arg APP_VERSION=1.2.3 -t myapp . and then run docker run myapp. What is printed?

FROM python:3.12-slim
ARG APP_VERSION
CMD ["python", "-c", "import os; print(os.environ.get('APP_VERSION'))"]
options: Nothing, because the build fails without a default for the ARG
questions.explanation: ARG values exist only while the image is being built. To keep a non-secret value at runtime, add ENV APP_VERSION=$APP_VERSION, or pass it with docker run -e APP_VERSION=1.2.3.

questions.text: A Docker build needs a private package token only during one RUN pip install step. Which approach keeps the token out of the image's layers and history?
options: docker build --build-arg PIP_TOKEN=... with ARG PIP_TOKEN used in the RUN step
ENV PIP_TOKEN=... before the RUN step and ENV PIP_TOKEN= after it
COPY .env . before the RUN step and RUN rm .env after it
questions.explanation: A BuildKit secret is mounted under /run/secrets/ only for that RUN step and is not saved in a layer. A build arg used by RUN shows up in docker history, and later ENV or rm steps cannot erase earlier layers.

questions.text: Which command connects to server.example.com as user deploy?
questions.explanation: The form is ssh user@host. The equivalent option form is ssh -l deploy server.example.com; ssh has no -u or -user option.

questions.text: How do you run df -h on server and see its output locally, without opening an interactive shell?
questions.explanation: A command after the host runs on the remote side, and its output comes back to your terminal. In ssh user@server; df -h the df runs locally after the session ends, and -N runs no command at all.

questions.text:
Local user alice (home /home/alice) runs the command below in bash. What does it print?

ssh bob@server "echo $HOME"
questions.explanation: Inside double quotes the local shell expands $HOME before ssh runs, so the remote side receives echo /home/alice. Single quotes, 'echo $HOME', pass the variable through unexpanded and print /home/bob.

questions.text: ssh user@server tty prints not a tty, and full-screen programs such as top misbehave when run this way. Which option forces a pseudo-terminal?
questions.explanation: When a remote command is given, ssh does not allocate a terminal by default. -t requests one, so ssh -t user@server top works. -T explicitly disables terminal allocation, -N runs no command and -X forwards X11.

questions.text: The SSH server listens on port 2222. Which command connects to it?
questions.explanation: ssh takes a lowercase -p for the port. scp and sftp use uppercase -P because their -p means "preserve times and modes". user@host:2222 is not port syntax for ssh; the URI form ssh://user@host:2222 is.

questions.text: Which command generates a new Ed25519 key pair?
questions.explanation: ssh-keygen -t TYPE creates a key pair, here ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 and id_ed25519.pub. Since OpenSSH 9.5 Ed25519 is also the default type. For RSA, ssh-keygen defaults to 3072 bits; avoid anything below 2048.

questions.text: After running ssh-keygen -t ed25519, which file must stay secret?
questions.explanation: The file without .pub is the private key; anyone holding it can log in as you wherever the public key is trusted. The .pub file is meant to be copied to servers.

questions.text: Which command installs your public key on a server so that later logins can use key authentication?
questions.explanation: ssh-copy-id appends the public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server, creating it if needed. Copying the private key, as in the scp option, defeats the point of key pairs.

questions.text: On the server, which file lists the public keys allowed to log in to a user account?
questions.explanation: sshd checks the target user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys during public-key authentication. known_hosts is the client's record of server host keys.

questions.text: During public-key authentication, what does the client send to prove its identity?
options: The private key, encrypted with the server's public key
A signature made with the private key, which the server checks against the public key
The user's password, hashed with the private key
The public key alone, with no further proof
questions.explanation: The private key never leaves the client. The server verifies the signature using the public key in authorized_keys, all inside the already-encrypted session.

questions.text: ssh refuses to use your key and warns UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE!. Which command fixes it?
questions.explanation: OpenSSH ignores a private key that the group or other users can access, so even 640 is rejected as "too open". Mode 600 (or 400) limits the file to its owner. The ~/.ssh directory itself is normally 700.

questions.text: Your public key is in the server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, yet sshd keeps rejecting it. On the server, ls -ld ~ shows drwxrwxrwx. What is the likely cause?
options: The key type is not supported by the server
The client's known_hosts entry for the server is stale
sshd's StrictModes check rejects keys when the home directory is writable by others
questions.explanation: With the default StrictModes yes, sshd ignores authorized_keys if the home directory, ~/.ssh or the file is writable by group or others, since anyone could have added a key. Run chmod 755 ~ (or go-w) and check the server's auth log.

questions.text: Which option tells ssh to use a specific private key file?
questions.explanation: -i selects the identity (private key) file. -f sends ssh to the background, and -p sets the port.

questions.text: What does ssh-agent do?
options: It generates new key pairs on demand
It runs on the server and checks authorized_keys
It copies public keys to remote servers
It holds decrypted private keys in memory so you enter each passphrase only once
questions.explanation: The agent keeps unlocked keys in memory and answers signing requests from ssh. You add keys to it with ssh-add. The server-side checks are done by sshd.

questions.text: Which command loads your private key into the running ssh-agent?
questions.explanation: ssh-add asks for the passphrase once and gives the key to the agent. ssh-add -l lists loaded keys. Running ssh-agent FILE would try to run FILE as a command.

questions.text: Which command prints the fingerprint of the key in ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub?
questions.explanation: -l shows the fingerprint, such as 256 SHA256:... (ED25519), and -f names the file. -p changes a key's passphrase, and -R removes a host from known_hosts.

questions.text: What is stored in the client's ~/.ssh/known_hosts file?
options: Public keys of users allowed to log in to this machine
Host keys of servers you have connected to, used to detect impersonation
Hostnames and aliases for your saved connections
A log of past SSH sessions
questions.explanation: On first connection you accept the server's host key, and later connections check it against this file. Aliases belong in ~/.ssh/config, and user keys in authorized_keys.

questions.text: ssh warns REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED! for a server. What is the right first step?
options: Generate a new client key with ssh-keygen
Confirm the server's new host-key fingerprint through a trusted channel before trusting it
questions.explanation: A changed host key may mean a reinstall, or a man-in-the-middle attack. Verify it first; only then remove the old entry with ssh-keygen -R host. Deleting entries or disabling checking removes the protection.

questions.text: A server was rebuilt, and you have verified its new host key. Which command removes only its old entry from ~/.ssh/known_hosts?
questions.explanation: ssh-keygen -R host deletes that host's keys from known_hosts and keeps a backup in known_hosts.old. -F only finds and prints the entry, ssh-add -d removes keys from the agent, and deleting the file discards every saved host key.

questions.text:
With this block in ~/.ssh/config, what does ssh web do?

Host web
    HostName 203.0.113.10
    User deploy
    Port 2222
options: Connects to 203.0.113.10 on port 2222 as user deploy
Looks up a host named web in DNS and connects on port 22
Connects to 203.0.113.10 on port 22 as your local username
Fails, because Host entries are read only by sshd
questions.explanation: A Host block defines an alias, and the keywords under it apply when you connect to that alias. ssh -G web prints the resulting settings without connecting, and command-line options such as -p override the file.

questions.text:
~/.ssh/config contains the blocks below, in this order. Which port does ssh web use?

Host *
    Port 2000

Host web
    HostName 203.0.113.10
    Port 2222
options: 2222, because the web block is more specific
2000, because the first value obtained for each keyword wins
22, because two conflicting Port lines cancel out
2222, because later blocks override earlier ones
questions.explanation: ssh reads the file top to bottom and keeps the first value it finds for each keyword, and Host * matches every host. Put specific Host blocks first and general Host * defaults at the end.

questions.text: Which file configures the SSH server daemon, as opposed to the client?
questions.explanation: The extra d stands for daemon: sshd_config controls the server, while ssh_config and ~/.ssh/config control the client.

questions.text: Which pair of sshd_config settings blocks direct root logins and allows only key-based logins?
questions.explanation: PermitRootLogin no blocks root over SSH, and PasswordAuthentication no stops password logins (also check KbdInteractiveAuthentication). PubkeyAuthentication no would turn off keys, the opposite of what you want.

questions.text: sudo sshd -T on a stock OpenSSH server shows permitrootlogin without-password, the alias of the default prohibit-password. What does this allow?
options: Root can log in with a key, but not with a password
Root cannot log in over SSH by any method
Root can log in with a password, but not with a key
Root can log in by any method once PasswordAuthentication yes is set
questions.explanation: prohibit-password disables password and keyboard-interactive logins for root only, whatever PasswordAuthentication says; key logins still work. Use PermitRootLogin no to block root entirely.

questions.text:
On Ubuntu, you add PasswordAuthentication no at the end of /etc/ssh/sshd_config, yet sudo sshd -T | grep -i passwordauth prints passwordauthentication yes. The files are shown below. Why?

# /etc/ssh/sshd_config (first lines)
Include /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf

# /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/50-cloud-init.conf
PasswordAuthentication yes
options: sshd -T shows compiled-in defaults, not the configuration files
Files in sshd_config.d always override the main file, wherever the Include is
sshd keeps the first value it reads, and the included file is read before your line
The setting only takes effect after the server is rebooted
questions.explanation: Like the client, sshd uses the first value obtained for most keywords. The Include at the top is read first, so its yes wins. Change or remove the drop-in, then check with sshd -T before reloading.

questions.text: You edited /etc/ssh/sshd_config on a remote server. What is the safest way to apply the change?
options: Run sudo sshd -t, reload the service, and test a new connection before closing the current one
Run sudo systemctl stop ssh, then start it again from the new session
Close your session first, then reconnect to load the new settings
questions.explanation: sshd -t catches syntax errors before they can lock you out. Reloading keeps existing sessions alive, so if the new login fails you can still fix the config from the open session.

questions.text: You changed sshd to listen on port 2222 on a server with UFW. Which firewall step is needed so you can still connect?
questions.explanation: SSH uses TCP, so the new port must be allowed before you rely on it; then remove the old port 22 rule. A non-standard port reduces scan noise but does not replace strong authentication.

questions.text: On Ubuntu 24.04, where sshd is socket-activated through ssh.socket, you change Port 22 to Port 2222 in sshd_config. What makes it listen on the new port?
options: sudo systemctl daemon-reload, then sudo systemctl restart ssh.socket
questions.explanation: systemd, not sshd, owns the listening socket. A generator copies Port and ListenAddress into ssh.socket, so you must re-run it with daemon-reload and restart the socket. Restarting only ssh.service keeps port 22, and socket units cannot be reloaded.

questions.text: Which command makes the SSH service start automatically at boot on Debian 12?
questions.explanation: enable creates the links that start the unit at boot, and start runs it now; enable --now does both. On RPM-based systems the unit is named sshd, and on Ubuntu 22.10+ ssh.socket starts it on the first connection.

questions.text: Which option increases ssh output so you can see where a connection or authentication is failing?
questions.explanation: -v prints debug messages, and -vv or -vvv add more detail. -V prints the version, -q suppresses warnings, and -N skips the remote command.

questions.text: What does ssh -L 8080:localhost:5432 user@db.example.com do?
options: Opens port 8080 on db.example.com and forwards it to port 5432 on your machine
Starts a SOCKS proxy on local port 8080
Copies the database on port 5432 to local port 8080
Opens port 8080 on your machine and forwards it through SSH to port 5432 on db.example.com
questions.explanation: -L local_port:dest_host:dest_port is local forwarding. localhost is resolved on the server side, so connecting to localhost:8080 on your machine reaches the server's local port 5432.

questions.text: After you run ssh -N -L 8080:localhost:5432 user@db.example.com, a colleague on your LAN cannot connect to port 8080 on your machine. Why?
options: Local forwarding works only for the user who started ssh
By default ssh binds the forwarded port to 127.0.0.1 and ::1 only
The colleague must also authenticate to db.example.com
-N makes the tunnel accept only one connection
questions.explanation: Forwarded ports listen on loopback unless you ask otherwise, which ss -tln confirms. To share it, bind explicitly, for example -L 0.0.0.0:8080:localhost:5432 (or use -g), and consider the security impact first.

questions.text: Which option creates a reverse tunnel, so that a port on the remote server forwards back to a service on your machine?
questions.explanation: -R remote_port:host:port opens the listening port on the server and sends connections back through the tunnel; with the server's default GatewayPorts no it binds to loopback there. -L listens locally, -D starts a SOCKS proxy, and -X forwards X11.

questions.text: What does ssh -D 1080 user@host provide?
options: A debug log written to port 1080
A local SOCKS proxy on port 1080 that sends traffic out through host
A forward from local port 1080 to the same port on host
A disconnect after 1080 seconds of inactivity
questions.explanation: -D sets up dynamic port forwarding. Applications configured to use localhost:1080 as a SOCKS proxy reach any destination as if they were connecting from host.

questions.text: Why add -N to a command such as ssh -N -L 8080:localhost:80 user@host?
options: It disables host-key checking for the tunnel
It uses numeric IP addresses only
It keeps the tunnel open without running a remote command or shell
It compresses traffic through the tunnel
questions.explanation: -N is for forwarding-only sessions. It is often combined with -f to send ssh to the background after authentication. Compression is -C.

questions.text: Which option connects to an internal server through the bastion host jump.example.com in a single command?
questions.explanation: -J (ProxyJump) connects to the jump host first and tunnels the SSH connection to the target through it. In ~/.ssh/config the same thing is written as ProxyJump.

questions.text: What does ssh -X user@host enable?
options: X11 forwarding, so graphical programs on host display on your screen
questions.explanation: -X forwards X11 connections through the encrypted tunnel. The server must allow it with X11Forwarding yes.

questions.text: Which command copies report.pdf from your machine to /srv/docs/ on server?
questions.explanation: scp works like cp: scp SOURCE DEST, with remote paths written as user@host:path. Without the colon, server/srv/docs/ is just a local path.

questions.text: Which command downloads /var/log/app.log from server into the current local directory?
questions.explanation: The remote file is the source, so it comes first, and . (the current directory) is the destination. Without the colon, user@server is treated as a local file name.

questions.text: Which command copies the whole site/ directory to a server whose SSH daemon listens on port 2222?
questions.explanation: scp uses uppercase -P for the port and -r to copy directories. Without -r it refuses with "site" is not a regular file, and lowercase -p preserves times and modes.

questions.text:
/tmp/dd does not exist on server. You run the same command twice. Which files exist on the server afterwards?

scp -r d1 user@server:/tmp/dd   # d1 contains one file, f
scp -r d1 user@server:/tmp/dd
options: Only /tmp/dd/f, overwritten by the second copy
Only /tmp/dd/f, because the second command fails
questions.explanation: Like cp -r, the first copy creates /tmp/dd as a copy of d1. The second time /tmp/dd already exists, so d1 is copied inside it. Copy into an existing parent, such as user@server:/tmp/, for repeatable results.

questions.text: Since OpenSSH 9.0 (Ubuntu 24.04 ships 9.6), what protocol does the scp command use by default, and how do you force the legacy one?
options: The SCP/rcp protocol; force SFTP with -s
The SFTP protocol; force the legacy SCP protocol with -O
FTP over TLS; force SCP with -T
The rsync protocol; force SCP with -L
questions.explanation: Modern scp requests the server's sftp subsystem for its transfers. Against a server without that subsystem it fails, and -O switches back to the original SCP/rcp protocol, which runs scp -t on the remote side.

questions.text: In an interactive sftp session, which commands upload a local file and download a remote file?
questions.explanation: put local_file uploads to the remote working directory and get remote_file downloads it. ls, cd, mkdir and rm act on the remote side, and exit ends the session.

questions.text: How is SFTP related to SSH?
options: SFTP runs as a subsystem over an SSH connection, using the same port and authentication
SFTP is FTP with TLS added on top
SFTP needs its own daemon listening on port 21
SFTP sends data unencrypted after logging in over SSH
questions.explanation: SFTP is enabled through a Subsystem sftp line in sshd_config. It uses SSH's encryption and logins, typically on port 22. FTP with TLS is FTPS, a different protocol.

questions.text: Which command copies the contents of the local site directory directly into /var/www/html/, without creating /var/www/html/site/?
questions.explanation: For rsync, a trailing slash on the source means "the contents of this directory". Without it, the directory itself is copied, giving /var/www/html/site/. The slash on the destination makes no difference.

questions.text: The server's SSH daemon listens on port 2222. How do you point rsync at it?
questions.explanation: -e sets the remote shell command, so the SSH options go there. In rsync, -P means --partial --progress, not port.

questions.text:
What does this command do?

ssh user@remotehost "tar -czf - /srv/data" > data.tar.gz
options: Copies the local data.tar.gz to the remote host
Extracts data.tar.gz into /srv/data on the remote host
Creates data.tar.gz on the remote host and leaves it there
Creates a compressed archive on the remote host and streams it into a local file
questions.explanation: -f - makes tar write the archive to stdout, ssh carries that stdout back, and the local > saves it. No temporary archive is written on the server.

questions.text: Which plain-text protocol should you avoid on untrusted networks, because it sends logins and data unencrypted?
questions.explanation: Plain FTP sends credentials and files in clear text. SFTP and SCP run over SSH, and FTPS adds TLS encryption to FTP.

questions.text: Which command finds lines containing error, Error or ERROR in app.log?
questions.explanation: -i ignores case. -r recurses into directories, -v inverts the match and -w matches whole words only, all of them still case-sensitive.

questions.text:
app.log has 3 lines, one of which contains error twice. What does grep -c error app.log print?

error: disk full, error: retry failed
ok
error: timeout
questions.explanation: -c counts matching lines, not matches. To count every occurrence, use grep -o error app.log | wc -l, which prints 3 here.

questions.text: What does grep -o change about the output?
options: It prints only the matched part of each line, one match per line
It prints only the names of matching files
It prints only the number of matching lines
It prints only lines that do not match
questions.explanation: -o outputs each matching substring on its own line, which is handy for extracting values such as IP addresses. Filenames only is -l, counts are -c, and inverted matching is -v.

questions.text: Which command shows the active lines of sshd_config, dropping both comment lines and empty lines?
questions.explanation: ^(#|$) matches lines that start with # or are empty, and -v removes them. Without -E, the | is a literal character, and without -v you would print only the lines you wanted to remove.

questions.text: Which command lists the files under src/ that contain main(, printing only their names?
questions.explanation: -r recurses, -l prints only the names of files with a match, and -F makes the pattern a fixed string, so ( is never regex syntax (under -E it would open a group). -L lists files without a match, and -n prints the matching lines.

questions.text:
Given these lines, which command matches foo and bar foo but not foobar?

foo
foobar
bar foo
questions.explanation: -w requires the match to be a whole word, so foobar is excluded. -x would match only the line that is exactly foo. -F and -i would still match foobar.

questions.text:
What does grep '[^0-9]' data.txt print for the lines below?

12345
hello123
no_digits_here
questions.explanation: [^0-9] matches one character that is not a digit, and a line matches if it contains such a character anywhere, so only the all-digit line is skipped. To print lines made only of digits, use grep -E '^[0-9]+$'.

questions.text: Why does grep 'abc|def' file.txt find nothing, while grep -E 'abc|def' file.txt finds both words?
options: In basic regex | is a literal character; -E turns on extended syntax
Basic grep needs the pattern in double quotes to read |
-E makes the search case-insensitive, so it finds more lines
Basic grep stops reading the file after the first match
questions.explanation: In basic regex | is literal. With -E, |, +, ? and () work as operators. You can also use grep -e abc -e def to give several patterns.

questions.text: Which command searches for the literal string 1.2.3.4, so that . does not match any character?
questions.explanation: -F treats the pattern as a fixed string. In every regex mode an unescaped . matches any character, so 1x2y3z4 would also match. You can also escape the dots instead.

questions.text: Which command shows each line containing panic along with the 3 lines that follow it?
questions.explanation: -A means "after" context. -B shows lines before the match, and -C shows lines on both sides.

questions.text: Which command searches the contents of every *.conf file anywhere under /etc for Listen?
questions.explanation: --include=GLOB limits a recursive search to files whose base name matches; the quotes stop the shell expanding the glob. /etc/*.conf names only top-level files, and piping find into grep searches the list of names, not the files' contents.

questions.text: What does sed 's/foo/bar/' input.txt do to the line foo foo foo?
options: Changes it to bar bar bar
Changes it to foo foo bar
Changes it to bar foo foo
Leaves it unchanged unless -i is given
questions.explanation: Without flags, s replaces only the first match on each line. Add g (s/foo/bar/g) to replace every match. Without -i, sed prints the result and leaves the file alone.

questions.text: What does echo 'concatenate cat' | sed 's/cat/dog/g' print?
questions.explanation: s matches the text anywhere, including inside words, and g replaces every match on the line. To change only the whole word, GNU sed accepts s/\bcat\b/dog/g, which prints concatenate dog.

questions.text: Which command replaces /usr/local with /opt/tools on every line of paths.txt?
questions.explanation: The character after s is the delimiter, so | avoids escaping every /. Unescaped slashes end the fields early, the escaped version lacks its closing delimiter, and y maps single characters one-to-one instead of replacing strings.

questions.text: Which command deletes every line containing DEBUG from app.log in place, keeping a backup as app.log.bak?
questions.explanation: -i.bak edits the file in place after saving the original with a .bak suffix. Redirecting to the same file truncates it before sed reads it, so you lose the data.

questions.text: Which command prints only the lines from START to END, inclusive?
questions.explanation: A /start/,/end/ address selects a range of lines. -n turns off automatic printing, so only p produces output. Without -n, every line prints once and the range prints twice. /START/p;/END/p prints only the two marker lines.

questions.text: Which command deletes all empty lines from file.txt, printing the result?
questions.explanation: ^$ matches a line with nothing between the start and the end, and d deletes it. s/^$// replaces nothing with nothing, so the empty lines stay. /$/ matches every line.

questions.text: With GNU sed, which command inserts a line # generated before the first line of config.ini, writing the result to stdout?
questions.explanation: i\ inserts text before the addressed line, a\ appends after it, and c\ replaces it. Address 1 is the first line and $ is the last. The one-line form is a GNU extension; POSIX sed wants the text on the next line.

questions.text:
What does this sed command with capture groups print?

echo 'user=alice' | sed -E 's/(.*)=(.*)/\2=\1/'
questions.explanation: With -E, parentheses are capture groups, and \1 and \2 in the replacement refer back to them. Without -E you would write \(.*\)=\(.*\).

questions.text: Which command removes the third character from every line?
questions.explanation: ^(..). captures two characters and matches the third, and \1 puts back only the two. s/.//3g deletes the third and every later character, basic regex reads {3} literally, and y needs two equal-length character lists.

questions.text: Which awk command prints the username (field 1) and UID (field 3) from /etc/passwd?
questions.explanation: /etc/passwd is colon-separated, so set the field separator with -F:. By default awk splits on runs of whitespace. The action must be inside braces.

questions.text: What does awk '{ print NF, $NF }' print for the line a b c d?
questions.explanation: NF is the number of fields in the current line, and $NF is the last field. NR would be the line (record) number.

questions.text: Which command prints the total of the numbers in column 2 of sales.txt?
questions.explanation: The main block runs for every line, adding up $2, and END runs once after the last line. print sum += $2 prints a running total on every line, and BEGIN runs before any input is read.

questions.text: Which command prints the names of users whose UID is 1000 or higher?
questions.explanation: A condition before the action limits which lines it runs on. > 1000 would leave out UID 1000 itself, if needs parentheses around its condition, and /1000/ matches the text 1000 anywhere in the line.

questions.text: The shell variable limit holds a number. Which command prints field 1 of every line whose field 3 is greater than it?
questions.explanation: -v name=value sets an awk variable before input is read. Inside single quotes the shell expands nothing, so awk reads $limit as a field reference and "$limit" as literal text. -F sets the field separator.

questions.text: Which command prints x,z for the input x:y:z?
questions.explanation: -F: splits the input on colons, and OFS is the output field separator that print places between comma-separated items. RS is the record separator, and $1 $3 joins the fields with nothing in between.

questions.text:
What does this command print?

printf 'a\nb\n' | awk '{ printf "%s", $1 }'
options: a and b on separate lines
ab, with no newline at the end
questions.explanation: Unlike print, printf adds neither OFS nor a newline, so the fields run together. Put \n in the format string, as in printf "%s\n", $1, to get one value per line.

questions.text: Which command counts how often each value in column 1 of access.log appears?
options: awk '{c[$1]++} END {for (k in c) print k, c[k]}' access.log
questions.explanation: c[$1]++ uses an associative array keyed by the first field, and the END loop prints each key with its count. The order of for (k in c) is unspecified, so pipe the output to sort if needed.

questions.text: What does sort numbers.txt output for lines 10, 9 and 100?
questions.explanation: Without options, sort compares lines as text, character by character, so 1… sorts before 9. Use sort -n to compare numerically and get 9, 10, 100.

questions.text: Which command sorts scores.txt numerically by its second column, highest first?
questions.explanation: -k2 sorts on a key starting at field 2 (-k2,2 stops it there), -n compares numbers and -r reverses the order. -t sets the field delimiter, not the key.

questions.text: Why does uniq usually appear after sort in a pipeline?
options: uniq only works on numeric data
uniq reverses the order of its input
uniq removes only adjacent duplicate lines
sort adds the line numbers that uniq needs
questions.explanation: uniq compares each line with the one before it. Sorting first puts identical lines next to each other, so printf 'b a b ' | uniq keeps all three lines. sort -u does both steps at once.

questions.text: Which pipeline lists the most frequent lines in ips.txt first, each with its count?
questions.explanation: sort groups duplicates, uniq -c prefixes each distinct line with its count, and sort -rn puts the biggest counts first. uniq -d prints only the duplicated lines, without counts.

questions.text: Which command prints the usernames (the first colon-separated field) from /etc/passwd?
questions.explanation: -d: sets the delimiter and -f1 picks the first field. Without -d, cut splits on tabs, and -c1 would print only the first character.

questions.text: Which command turns hello world into HELLO WORLD?
questions.explanation: tr SET1 SET2 maps each character in the first set to the matching one in the second. 'a-z' 'A-Z' also works for ASCII text. -d deletes characters and -s squeezes repeats.

questions.text: What does echo 'a1b2c3' | tr -d '0-9' print?
questions.explanation: tr -d deletes every character in the given set, here the digits, leaving abc.

questions.text:
What does this command print?

printf 'first\nsecond' | wc -l
questions.explanation: wc -l counts newline characters, and the last line, second, has no trailing newline, so the count is 1. 12 is what wc -c would print, since the input is 12 bytes.

questions.text:
What ends up in out.txt after you run this command?

ls /nonexistent . 2>&1 > out.txt
options: Both the listing of . and the error message
Only the listing of .; the error still appears on the terminal
Nothing, because the two redirections cancel out
questions.explanation: Redirections are applied left to right. 2>&1 points stderr at the current stdout, the terminal, and only then does > out.txt move stdout to the file. Write > out.txt 2>&1, or &> out.txt in Bash, to capture both.

questions.text:
What does this script print?

name=World
cat <<'EOF'
Hello $name
EOF
options: Hello followed by an empty value
Nothing; cat waits for keyboard input
questions.explanation: Quoting the delimiter ('EOF') turns off expansion in the here-document, so $name is printed literally. With an unquoted EOF, the shell expands the variable and prints Hello World.

questions.text: Which Bash command compares the sorted contents of a.txt and b.txt without creating temporary files?
questions.explanation: Process substitution <(command) runs the command and passes diff a path such as /dev/fd/63 to read its output from. $(...) would paste the sorted lines in as file names, and < redirects from a file, not a command.

questions.text: Which command finds regular files larger than 100 MiB under the current directory?
questions.explanation: +N means more than N, -N means less than N, and a bare N means exactly N (rounded up to whole units). A bare number with no suffix counts 512-byte blocks. find has no -bigger test.

questions.text: A directory holds three files of 0 bytes, 100 bytes and 500 KiB. Which of them does GNU find . -type f -size -1M list?
questions.explanation: find rounds each size up to whole units before comparing, so every non-empty file counts as 1 MiB, and "less than 1" leaves only empty files. Use -size -1024k (or -size -1048576c) for files under 1 MiB.

questions.text: The current directory contains a.log, and sub/ contains a.log and b.log. What does find . -name *.log (unquoted) print?
options: An error saying paths must precede the expression
questions.explanation: The shell expands *.log to a.log before find runs, so find looks for files named exactly a.log. If two names matched in the current directory, find would fail with "paths must precede expression". Quote the pattern: -name '*.log'.

questions.text: Which command finds files under /home that are not owned by guest?
questions.explanation: ! (or -not) negates the test that follows it. -user !guest would look for a user literally named !guest.

questions.text: What is the difference between -exec rm -- {} \; and -exec rm -- {} + in find?
options: \; deletes directories and + deletes only files
+ asks before each deletion, while \; does not
\; runs rm once per file, while + passes many files to each rm
\; is for GNU find only, while + works everywhere
questions.explanation: {} + batches pathnames like xargs, creating far fewer processes. Both forms handle spaces in names safely. Asking before each command is what -ok does.

questions.text: Which find action asks for confirmation before running the command on each match?
questions.explanation: -ok works like -exec but prompts before each command, which is a safer way to delete. -delete removes matches without asking.

questions.text: Which command uses the locate database to find paths containing readme, whether written README, Readme or readme?
questions.explanation: -i ignores case. -b matches only the base name and -c prints the number of matches, both still case-sensitive. locate searches a prebuilt database, so run sudo updatedb first if the files are very new.

questions.text: In Bash on Ubuntu, which ls prints /usr/bin/ls, but typing ls runs ls --color=auto. Which command shows the alias as well as the files on PATH?
questions.explanation: type is a Bash builtin that reports aliases, functions, builtins and files on PATH, in the order the shell resolves them. Ubuntu's external which searches only PATH, and whereis only standard directories.

questions.text:
What does this xargs -n 2 pipeline print?

printf '%s\n' one two three four five | xargs -n 2 echo
options: one two, three four, then five on separate lines
one two three four five on one line
Each word on its own line
questions.explanation: -n 2 passes at most two arguments to each echo, so echo runs three times. Without -n, xargs puts as many arguments as fit into a single command.

questions.text: Why does printf '%s\n' a.tmp b.tmp | rm fail with rm: missing operand?
options: printf writes to stderr, so the pipe receives nothing
rm needs -f before it reads names from a pipe
The names must be separated by NUL bytes, not newlines
rm takes file names as arguments and ignores stdin; xargs rm -- would pass them
questions.explanation: A pipe connects stdout to stdin, but rm never reads stdin. xargs turns its input into command-line arguments (stdin to argv). NUL separators make that safe for odd names, but they are not what is missing here.

questions.text: Which pipeline safely deletes every *.tmp file, even when names contain spaces or newlines?
questions.explanation: -print0 ends each pathname with a NUL byte, and xargs -0 splits only on NUL, so whitespace stays part of the name. By default xargs splits on blanks, so a b.tmp becomes two bad arguments.

questions.text: In xargs rm --, which program is the -- for, and why is it there?
options: It is for rm, so that file names starting with - are not read as options
It is for xargs, telling it to read NUL-separated input
It is for the shell, to end the pipeline
It is for rm, to make it delete directories recursively
questions.explanation: xargs adds the input items after rm --, and -- tells rm that everything after it is a filename. Without it, a file named -rf would be read as options.

questions.text: Which command runs gzip on each listed file, with up to 4 compressions running at once?
questions.explanation: -P 4 allows four parallel processes, and -n 1 gives each gzip a single file. -n 4 alone runs gzip with four files at a time, one invocation after another.

questions.text: What does printf '%s\n' web1 web2 | xargs -I {} ssh {} uptime do?
options: Runs a single ssh with both hostnames as arguments
Runs ssh web1 uptime, then ssh web2 uptime
Runs ssh in parallel on both hosts
Prints the commands without running them
questions.explanation: -I {} swaps each input line in for {} and runs one command per item. Parallelism needs -P, and printing each command as it runs needs -t.

questions.text: On GNU systems, find . -name '*.bak' -print0 | xargs -0 rm -- finds no files. How do you stop rm from running at all in that case?
questions.explanation: GNU xargs normally runs the command once even with empty input; -r (--no-run-if-empty) skips it. -r is not in POSIX, so find ... -exec rm -- {} + is the portable alternative.

questions.text: Which command creates a gzip-compressed archive project.tar.gz from the directory project/?
questions.explanation: -c creates, -z compresses through gzip and -f names the archive. -x extracts and -t lists. gzip -r compresses each file separately and makes no archive.

questions.text: Why does tar -cfz backup.tar.gz project/ not create a compressed backup.tar.gz?
options: -z must always come before -c in a bundled option group
tar refuses to create archive names that end in .gz
-f takes z as the archive name, so backup.tar.gz is treated as a file to add
-cfz creates a bzip2-compressed archive instead of gzip
questions.explanation: -f needs an argument, and in a bundled option group it takes the rest of the group. GNU tar writes an uncompressed archive named z and complains that backup.tar.gz does not exist. Keep f last: -czf backup.tar.gz project/.

questions.text: How do you list the contents of backup.tar.gz without extracting anything?
questions.explanation: -t lists the archive's members, and with -v it shows permissions, owner, size and date like ls -l. gzip -d would decompress the file into backup.tar.

questions.text: Which command extracts project.tar.gz into /opt/restore instead of the current directory?
questions.explanation: -C DIR makes tar change into that directory before extracting. Redirecting stdout does not move the extracted files, and -c would create an archive instead.

questions.text: Which command extracts only docs/readme.txt from archive.tar.gz?
questions.explanation: Member names given after the archive limit extraction to those paths, which must match how they appear in tar -tzf. The archive name must come straight after -f.

questions.text: Which command archives app/ but leaves out its app/tmp/ contents?
questions.explanation: In GNU tar, --exclude is position-sensitive and must come before the file operands it applies to; placed last, tar 1.35 warns that it "has no effect" and keeps the files. The quotes stop the shell from expanding the pattern.

questions.text: Which tar option compresses with xz, as in archive.tar.xz?
questions.explanation: -z is gzip (.tar.gz), -j is bzip2 (.tar.bz2) and capital -J is xz (.tar.xz). Lowercase -x means extract.

questions.text: In ssh user@host 'tar -czf - /srv/data' > data.tar.gz, what does the - after -f do?
options: It tells tar to read the list of files from standard input
It makes tar write the archive to stdout, which ssh carries to the local file
It turns off compression for the network transfer
It names the archive - on the remote host
questions.explanation: As the archive name, - means standard output when creating (and standard input when extracting). The archive travels over the SSH connection and the local shell redirects it into data.tar.gz, so no copy is left on the remote host.

questions.text: You need to split big.tar into 100 MiB pieces for upload, then rebuild it later. Which pair of commands works?
options: split -b 100M big.tar part_, then cat part_* > big.tar
split -l 100 big.tar part_, then tar -xf part_*
questions.explanation: split -b cuts the file into byte-sized chunks named part_aa, part_ab and so on (100M means 100 MiB). The glob expands in sorted order, so cat puts them back together correctly. -l splits by lines.

questions.text: Which command compresses log.txt to log.txt.gz but also keeps the original file?
