questions.explanation: By default gzip replaces the file with the .gz version. -k keeps the original, -d decompresses and -l lists compression statistics.

questions.text: Which crontab line runs /opt/backup.sh at 7:30 AM, Monday to Friday?
questions.explanation: The five fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week. 1-5 in the fifth field means Monday to Friday; in the third field it would mean the 1st to the 5th of the month.

questions.text: When does the crontab entry */15 * * * * /opt/check.sh run?
options: 15 minutes after cron starts, then every 15 minutes from that point
Once at 15 minutes past each hour
At minutes 0, 15, 30 and 45 of every hour
questions.explanation: Cron schedules are calendar matches, not timers. */15 in the minute field is a step value that matches minutes divisible by 15. 15 alone would run once an hour at minute 15.

questions.text: When does the crontab entry 0 9 13 * 5 /opt/report.sh run?
options: At 9:00 only on Fridays that fall on the 13th
At 9:00 on every 13th of the month and also on every Friday
questions.explanation: When both day of month and day of week are restricted (neither is *), cron runs the job when either one matches. To run only on Friday the 13th, keep one field and test the other inside the command.

questions.text: A cron job 0 2 * * * tar -czf /backup/$(date +%F).tar.gz /data never produces a correctly named file. Why?
options: Cron cannot run tar unless it is given as /usr/bin/tar
Command substitution $(...) is not allowed in cron jobs
An unescaped % is special in crontab commands and must be written as \%
Cron jobs are not permitted to write into /backup
questions.explanation: Cron turns % into a newline, and text after the first % is sent to the command's stdin. Write date +\%F, or move the logic into a script.

questions.text: A script runs fine from your terminal, but its cron job fails with mytool: command not found. What is the most likely cause?
options: Cron cannot run shell scripts, only binaries
Cron jobs always run as root, which cannot see user programs
The crontab line is missing the username field
Cron starts jobs with a minimal environment whose PATH lacks the directory of mytool
questions.explanation: Cron runs jobs through /bin/sh with a small environment (typically PATH=/usr/bin:/bin), without your shell startup files. Use absolute paths or set PATH= at the top of the crontab. User crontabs have no username field.

questions.text: How do lines in /etc/crontab differ from lines you add with crontab -e?
options: They have an extra username field between the time fields and the command
They have no time fields, only a user and a command
They use seconds as an extra first field before the minute
They must spell out months and weekdays by full name
questions.explanation: System crontabs (/etc/crontab and /etc/cron.d/) say which user runs each job. User crontabs already belong to one user, so they have only the five time fields and the command.

questions.text: A laptop is often off at night, and you want a daily job to still run once it boots. Which tool suits this better than plain cron?
questions.explanation: Plain cron skips jobs whose time passes while the machine is off. anacron tracks when each periodic job last ran and catches up after boot, which suits machines that are not always on.

questions.text: In the /etc/anacrontab line 7 10 cron.weekly run-parts /etc/cron.weekly, what does 10 mean?
options: Wait 10 minutes after anacron starts before running the job
Keep the last 10 timestamps for the job
questions.explanation: The fields are the period in days (7), the delay in minutes (10), the job identifier, which names its timestamp file in /var/spool/anacron/, and the command. Anacron has no time-of-day field.

questions.text: Which file lists local user accounts with their UID, home directory and login shell?
questions.explanation: Each line of /etc/passwd describes one account: name, password placeholder, UID, primary GID, comment, home directory and shell. Password hashes live in /etc/shadow.

questions.text: Which file stores the password hashes and password-aging data for local accounts?
questions.explanation: /etc/shadow holds salted one-way hashes plus aging fields and is not world-readable: Ubuntu lets only root and the shadow group read it, and Fedora gives it mode 000. World-readable /etc/passwd only holds an x placeholder.

questions.text:
What does this /etc/passwd line tell you about the account?

deploy:x:1001:2000:Deploy User:/srv/deploy:/usr/sbin/nologin
options: UID 2000, primary GID 1001, home /srv/deploy, and the password is x
UID 1001, primary GID 2000, home /srv/deploy, and no interactive login shell
UID 1001, primary GID 2000, and the password stored in plain text in field 2
questions.explanation: The fields are name, password placeholder (x means "see /etc/shadow"), UID, primary GID, comment, home and shell. A shell of nologin is typical for service accounts.

questions.text: In /etc/shadow, what does a password field that starts with ! mean?
options: The account has no password and anyone can log in
The password must be changed at next login
Password authentication is disabled for the account
questions.explanation: A hash prefixed with ! (or a field of *) cannot match any password, so password logins fail. passwd -l locks accounts this way, but other methods such as SSH keys may still work.

questions.text: Which command creates the user adam with a home directory populated from /etc/skel, whatever the distribution's default?
questions.explanation: -m creates the home directory and copies the skeleton files into it. Without it, the result depends on CREATE_HOME in /etc/login.defs: Fedora creates a home, Ubuntu does not. -M explicitly skips it, and usermod changes existing accounts.

questions.text: After useradd -m bob on Ubuntu, where do the .bashrc and .profile files in /home/bob come from?
options: They are copied from the skeleton directory /etc/skel
They are generated from the settings in /etc/login.defs
They are copied from root's home directory
Bash creates them the first time bob logs in
questions.explanation: useradd -m copies everything in /etc/skel (or the directory given with -k) into the new home and gives it to the user. Changing /etc/skel affects only accounts created later.

questions.text: How do useradd and adduser differ?
options: adduser can only create system accounts, while useradd creates regular users
useradd always prompts for the full name and password, while adduser never does
adduser is an interactive front end on Debian/Ubuntu but just a link to useradd on Fedora
useradd only works on Red Hat systems, and adduser only on Debian
questions.explanation: Debian's adduser asks for a password and details and creates the home for you; Fedora's /usr/sbin/adduser is a symlink to useradd. Because adduser varies (and minimal images may lack it), useradd is the safer choice in portable scripts.

questions.text: Which command adds the existing user bob to the supplementary group docker without removing his other groups?
questions.explanation: -a appends to the supplementary group list. useradd would try to create a new user, and groupadd creates groups rather than adding members.

questions.text: You run usermod -aG docker bob while bob is logged in. In his existing shell, id -Gn still does not list docker. Why?
options: Group membership is read at login, so his running shell keeps its old group list
usermod changes only take effect after the system is rebooted
-aG writes the change to /etc/gshadow only, not to /etc/group
Bob must run passwd before a new group membership becomes active
questions.explanation: A process's supplementary groups are fixed when the login session starts. /etc/group is updated immediately, so a new login (or newgrp docker / su - bob) picks it up; no reboot is needed.

questions.text: What happens if you run usermod -G docker bob without -a?
options: Bob is added to docker and keeps all of his other supplementary groups
Bob's primary group changes to docker, and his supplementary groups stay
The command fails, because -a is mandatory whenever -G is used
Bob's supplementary groups are replaced, so he leaves every group except docker
questions.explanation: Without -a, -G sets the complete list of supplementary groups. Forgetting -a is a classic way to accidentally remove someone from sudo or wheel.

questions.text: Which command removes user adam from the group admins?
questions.explanation: gpasswd -d deletes a single member from a group. groupdel removes the whole group and userdel deletes the user account.

questions.text: A line in /etc/group reads admins:x:1001:adam,eve. What does 1001 represent?
questions.explanation: The fields are group name, password placeholder, GID and a comma-separated member list. getent group admins prints the same format.

questions.text: What does id adam display?
options: Adam's UID, primary GID and group memberships
questions.explanation: id prints something like uid=1000(adam) gid=1000(adam) groups=1000(adam),27(sudo). Expiry details come from chage -l and logins from last.

questions.text: Which command changes the login shell of user carol to /bin/zsh?
questions.explanation: chsh -s updates the shell field in /etc/passwd (as does usermod -s). useradd creates new accounts, and exporting SHELL only affects the current session.

questions.text: An admin runs useradd -m -p 'Secret123' carol. What happens when carol tries to log in with the password Secret123?
options: Login fails, because -p expects an already hashed password and stores the text as-is
Login works, because useradd hashes the value before storing it
Login works only after carol first logs in with an empty password
Login fails, because -p is accepted only together with -r
questions.explanation: -p writes its argument straight into the hash field of /etc/shadow, and Secret123 is not a valid hash, so no password can match it. Set passwords with passwd carol or chpasswd instead.

questions.text: Which command locks the password of user dave so password logins fail?
questions.explanation: -l prefixes the hash with !. It does not disable the account entirely, so SSH key logins may still work. -d removes the password, -e forces a change at next login and -S shows status.

questions.text: Which command forces user alice to choose a new password the next time she logs in?
questions.explanation: chage -d 0 sets the last-change date to day 0, so the password counts as expired and must be changed at login; passwd -e alice does the same. chage -l only displays aging data, while passwd -l and usermod -L lock the password.

questions.text: Which command deletes the user eve together with her home directory and mail spool?
questions.explanation: -r removes the home directory and mail spool along with the account. Plain userdel leaves the files behind, and deleting the directory alone leaves the account in place.

questions.text: What UID does the root account have?
questions.explanation: The kernel grants superuser privileges to UID 0, whatever the account is called. Regular users usually start at 1000, and 65534 is commonly nobody.

questions.text: You change adam's UID with usermod -u 2001 adam; it used to be 1001. What does ls -l show as the owner of a file he owned in /tmp?
options: adam, because usermod updates every file on the system
root, because orphaned files are handed to root
1001, because usermod only updates files in his home directory and mail spool
nobody, because unknown UIDs are shown as 65534
questions.explanation: Files store a numeric UID. usermod -u fixes ownership only inside the home directory and mail spool, so elsewhere the file keeps UID 1001, which no longer has a name. Fix it with find / -xdev -uid 1001 -exec chown -h adam {} +.

questions.text: What is the difference between su adam and su - adam?
options: su - adam switches user without asking for adam's password
su adam switches to root first and only then to adam
su - adam runs a single command as adam and then exits
su - adam starts a login shell with adam's environment and startup files
questions.explanation: The - (or -l) option simulates a full login: adam's environment variables are loaded and you start in his home directory. Plain su adam keeps much of the caller's environment.

questions.text: Which command runs whoami as user adam and then returns to your own session?
questions.explanation: su -c passes a single command to the target user's shell, and the output appears in your terminal. Here it prints adam.

questions.text: To give user adam administrative rights through the default sudoers setup, which group do you add him to on Debian/Ubuntu versus RHEL/Fedora?
options: sudo on Debian/Ubuntu and wheel on RHEL/Fedora
wheel on Debian/Ubuntu and sudo on RHEL/Fedora
questions.explanation: Debian-based systems grant %sudo full rights, while Red Hat-based systems use %wheel. For example, usermod -aG wheel adam on RHEL.

questions.text: Why should you edit /etc/sudoers with visudo rather than a regular editor?
options: visudo locks the file and checks its syntax before installing the change
visudo encrypts the file so that other users cannot read the rules
Regular editors cannot open files in /etc without special flags
visudo automatically grants the current user full sudo rights
questions.explanation: A syntax error in sudoers can stop sudo from working at all, locking you out of administration. visudo validates the file and refuses to install a broken version.

questions.text: What does the sudoers line %wheel ALL=(ALL) ALL do?
options: Grants the user named wheel full sudo rights
Lets all members of the wheel group run any command as any user on any host
Lets all users run commands as members of the wheel group
Denies the wheel group any sudo rights
questions.explanation: % marks a group. The fields are hosts (ALL), the users you may become ((ALL)) and the allowed commands (ALL). By default users still have to enter their own password.

questions.text: What does the sudoers line adam ALL = NOPASSWD:/sbin/reboot allow?
options: Adam can run /sbin/reboot through sudo without being asked for a password
Adam can run any command without a password
Adam can reboot only after entering the root password
Every user can reboot without a password
questions.explanation: The rule names one user and one command, and the NOPASSWD: tag skips authentication for it. Other commands still follow the remaining rules.

questions.text: Which sudoers line lets user alice run only /usr/bin/systemctl as root, still asking for her password?
questions.explanation: Listing one command restricts alice to it, and without NOPASSWD: she must authenticate. ALL would allow every command, and ! would forbid systemctl instead.

questions.text: What does sudo -l show?
options: All processes currently running as root on this host
The sudo log of commands the user has already run
The members of the sudo group and their privileges
Which commands the invoking user may run with sudo on this host
questions.explanation: sudo -l (list) prints the user's allowed and forbidden commands according to the sudoers policy. It is the quickest way to check what a new rule grants.

questions.text: Which sudo option starts a login shell as the target user, reading that user's profile files?
questions.explanation: sudo -i runs the target user's shell as a login shell, much like su -. -E preserves your environment, -l lists privileges and -u only chooses the target user.

questions.text: Which command runs make install as root while asking sudo to keep your current environment variables?
questions.explanation: -E (--preserve-env) requests that your environment be kept, if the security policy allows it. -i uses a login environment and -k discards cached credentials.

questions.text: Which sudoers Defaults setting makes commands run with a minimal, clean environment instead of the caller's variables?
questions.explanation: env_reset (on by default) discards most of the caller's environment. env_keep lists exceptions that are kept, and secure_path sets the PATH used for commands.

questions.text: What does the execute (x) permission mean on a directory?
options: The directory can be entered and traversed to reach entries inside it
Programs stored in the directory can be run by any user
New files can be created in the directory by group members
The names of the entries in the directory can be listed
questions.explanation: For directories, r lists names, w lets you create, delete and rename entries (together with x), and x allows access through the directory. Without x, cd and opening files inside fail.

questions.text: Bob has write and execute permission on /shared, which has no sticky bit. A file there is owned by alice with mode 444. Can bob delete it?
options: No, because the file's mode 444 makes it read-only for everyone
Yes, because deletion needs write and execute permission on the directory, not the file
No, because only the owner of a file can ever delete it
Yes, but only if bob is also a member of alice's primary group
questions.explanation: Removing a file removes a directory entry, so the directory's permissions decide. rm may ask about a write-protected file, but it succeeds. The sticky bit is what prevents this in shared directories.

questions.text: Which symbolic permissions does octal mode 754 represent?
questions.explanation: Each digit is the sum of read 4, write 2 and execute 1: 7 = rwx for the owner, 5 = r-x for the group and 4 = r-- for others.

questions.text: Which octal mode does chmod u=rw,go=r file.txt set?
questions.explanation: u=rw gives the owner 6 and go=r gives group and others 4 each. The = operator sets the permissions exactly rather than adding to them.

questions.text: What is the effect of chmod o-rwx file.txt?
options: It removes read, write and execute for others, leaving owner and group unchanged
It grants read, write and execute permission to others
It removes all permissions for the owner, leaving group and others
It makes the file immutable, so nobody else can change it
questions.explanation: o selects others and - removes the listed bits. Owner (u) and group (g) permissions are not touched.

questions.text: With umask 027, what permissions does a new regular file get when the program requests mode 666?
questions.explanation: The umask clears bits: 666 with group write and all of others' bits masked gives 640. Directories requested as 777 would become 750.

questions.text: With umask 033, which modes do a new file (requested as 666) and a new directory (requested as 777) get?
questions.explanation: The umask clears bits (mode & ~umask); it is not subtraction. 033 removes write and execute for group and others, so 666 becomes 644 and 777 becomes 744.

questions.text: Why can ordinary users change their own password even though /etc/shadow is writable only by root?
options: /etc/shadow has the sticky bit set
Users are temporarily added to the root group
/usr/bin/passwd is setuid root, so it runs with the file owner's privileges
Password changes are written to the user's home directory
questions.explanation: The setuid bit makes an executable run with its owner's user ID. Because setuid programs run as root, they must be audited carefully.

questions.text: On Linux, you run chmod 4755 on a root-owned shell script /usr/local/bin/backup.sh that runs id -u. What does it print when alice runs it?
options: 0, because the setuid bit makes the script run as root
Alice's own UID, because Linux ignores setuid on interpreted scripts
0, but only if the script starts with #!/bin/bash
Nothing, because the kernel refuses to run setuid scripts
questions.explanation: The kernel honours setuid and setgid only on binary executables; for a #! script it starts the interpreter with the caller's IDs. Grant the access with a narrow sudo rule instead.

questions.text: ls -l shows -rwSr--r-- for a file. What does the uppercase S mean?
options: The setuid bit is set, but the owner has no execute permission
The file is a socket, shown by S in the owner field
The sticky bit is set, and others have no execute permission
The file is a symbolic link to a setuid program
questions.explanation: A lowercase s means setuid plus execute, while S means the special bit is present without the underlying x, which usually signals a mistake.

questions.text: Which permission on a shared project directory makes new files inherit the directory's group?
questions.explanation: With setgid on a directory, new files get the directory's group and new subdirectories inherit setgid. It does not grant group write; use a suitable umask or a default ACL for that.

questions.text: /srv/proj has mode drwxrwsr-x. After chmod 0775 /srv/proj with GNU coreutils, what does ls -ld /srv/proj show?
options: drwxrwxr-x, because the leading 0 clears all special bits
drwxrwsr-x, because GNU chmod keeps a directory's setgid bit here
drwxrwSr-x, because the group execute bit is removed
drwxr-xr-x, because 0775 resets the group bits
questions.explanation: For directories, GNU chmod preserves the setuid and setgid bits when a numeric mode does not mention them explicitly. Clear the bit with chmod g-s /srv/proj or a five-digit mode such as chmod 00775 /srv/proj.

questions.text: What does the sticky bit do on a world-writable directory such as /tmp?
options: It makes every file created in the directory executable
It prevents anyone, including root, from deleting files
It makes the system empty the directory at every reboot
Only a file's owner, the directory's owner or root can delete or rename the file
questions.explanation: Without the sticky bit, anyone with write permission on the directory could remove other users' files. ls -ld /tmp shows it as a t in the last position (drwxrwxrwt).

questions.text: Which command lists every file on the system that has the setuid bit set?
questions.explanation: In octal, 4000 is setuid, 2000 is setgid and 1000 is the sticky bit. -perm /4000 matches files with that bit set; 2>/dev/null hides permission errors.

questions.text: What does find / -perm /2000 -type f -o -type d match?
options: Setgid regular files, plus every directory on the system
Only setgid regular files and setgid directories
Nothing, because -o must be written inside parentheses
questions.explanation: The implicit AND binds tighter than -o, so this reads (-perm /2000 -type f) -o -type d. Group the type tests to get setgid files and directories: find / \( -type f -o -type d \) -perm /2000.

questions.text: Which command recursively sets mode 755 on every directory under project/ without changing regular files?
questions.explanation: find -type d selects only directories and passes them to chmod. chmod -R would also make every regular file executable, and the glob only reaches the top level.

questions.text: Which command changes the owner of script.sh to user alice and its group to devs in one step?
questions.explanation: chown user:group sets both at once; chgrp changes only the group. chmod changes permission bits, not ownership.

questions.text: Which command grants user bob read and write access to report.txt through an ACL, keeping existing ACL entries?
questions.explanation: setfacl -m (modify) adds or updates one entry and leaves others intact. -x removes entries, and getfacl only displays ACLs.

questions.text: Which command removes only the ACL entry for group sales from budget.xls?
questions.explanation: -x deletes the named entry; no permissions are given in the spec. -b would remove every extended entry, and -m g:sales:--- keeps an entry that denies access.

questions.text: Which command removes all extended ACL entries from data/, keeping only the standard owner, group and other permissions?
questions.explanation: -b (--remove-all) strips named user, named group and mask entries, plus any default ACL, but retains the base permissions. -x needs an entry to remove, and chmod a-rwx would clear the base permissions instead.

questions.text: Which command makes every file later created in project/ grant group devs read and write access by default?
questions.explanation: -d sets a default ACL, which new items in the directory inherit. Without -d, the entry applies only to the directory itself, and setgid changes group ownership, not permissions.

questions.text: Directory shared/ has the default ACL entry default:group:devs:rw-. A program running with umask 077 creates shared/new, requesting mode 666. What happens?
options: The umask applies as usual, so new is rw------- and devs has no access
Default ACLs apply only to new subdirectories, not to files
new copies the directory's own access ACL instead
The umask is not applied; new inherits the default ACL, so group devs can read and write it
questions.explanation: When the parent has a default ACL, the new item's ACL comes from it, limited only by the mode the program requested; the umask is ignored. A program asking for 600 would still leave devs without effective access.

questions.text:
getfacl notes.txt shows the lines below. What access does user joe actually have?

user:joe:rwx        #effective:r--
mask::r--
options: rwx, because named user entries ignore the mask
No access, because the mask overrides all entries
Read only, because the mask limits named users and groups
Read and execute, the default for named users
questions.explanation: The mask is the upper bound for named users, named groups and the owning group. Joe's entry says rwx, but only the bits also present in the mask, r--, take effect.

questions.text: A file has extended ACL entries. What does running chmod g=r on it change?
options: Only the owning group's own ACL entry
The ACL mask, which can reduce named users' and groups' effective access
Nothing, because chmod is ignored on files with ACLs
It deletes all named ACL entries
questions.explanation: With an extended ACL, the group bits shown by ls -l represent the mask. Changing them with chmod therefore changes the mask and limits every named entry.

questions.text: In the DN uid=jdoe,ou=users,dc=example,dc=com, what does ou=users represent?
options: The organizational unit (container) that holds the entry
The domain the directory belongs to
questions.explanation: A DN is read from the most specific part to the most general, like a path: uid=jdoe is the entry, ou=users its container, and dc=example,dc=com the domain.

questions.text: What is the conventional base DN for a directory serving the domain example.com?
questions.explanation: Each part of the DNS name becomes a domain component (dc). Searches and new entries are placed under this base, such as ou=users,dc=example,dc=com.

questions.text: Which TCP ports do plain LDAP and LDAP over SSL (LDAPS) use by default?
questions.explanation: LDAP listens on 389, where StartTLS can upgrade the connection, and LDAPS uses TLS from the start on 636. Ports 53/853 are DNS, 88/464 are Kerberos and 443/8443 are HTTPS.

questions.text: Which command searches the subtree dc=example,dc=com for the user jdoe using simple authentication?
questions.explanation: -x selects simple authentication, -b sets the search base, and the filter comes after it. ldapadd creates entries and ldapwhoami only tests a bind.

questions.text: Which LDAP filter matches entries that are of class person and have an email address?
questions.explanation: LDAP filters use prefix notation: & is AND, | is OR and ! is NOT. (mail=*) is a presence test that matches any entry with a mail attribute.

questions.text: Which file format is used to add, modify or export LDAP entries in bulk with tools such as ldapadd and ldapmodify?
questions.explanation: LDIF (LDAP Data Interchange Format) is plain text listing a dn: line followed by attributes. For example, ldapadd -x -D "cn=admin,dc=example,dc=com" -W -f user.ldif loads it.

questions.text: A user entry in LDAP has only the inetOrgPerson object class, and getent passwd jdoe returns nothing. What is missing for Linux login?
options: The posixAccount class with uidNumber, gidNumber, homeDirectory and loginShell
A mail attribute holding the user's email address
An ou=groups entry listing the user's groups
The organization object class on the user's entry
questions.explanation: inetOrgPerson describes a person, but NSS needs POSIX attributes to build a Unix account. Adding posixAccount (and often shadowAccount) with those attributes lets getent passwd jdoe resolve.

questions.text: On a host whose users come from LDAP through SSSD, grep jdoe /etc/passwd finds nothing. Which command shows whether the system can resolve jdoe as an account?
questions.explanation: getent asks every source listed in /etc/nsswitch.conf (such as files and sss), while /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow hold only local accounts. A directory user's home may not exist until the first login.

questions.text: ldapsearch -x -b "dc=wrong,dc=com" "(uid=jdoe)" ends with result: 32 No such object. What does that tell you?
options: The client could not contact the LDAP server
The server answered, but the search base DN does not exist
The search ran but no entry matched the filter
questions.explanation: Code 32 means the base or target DN is missing. An unreachable server gives Can't contact LDAP server (-1), a wrong password Invalid credentials (49), and a search with no matches result: 0 Success with no entries.
